This report thus mentions love, knowledge, and justice, which together encompass all goodness. Something that must be understood is that, in matters of loving Allah Most High, one must not entertain the notions associated with loving others, such as unfounded reproach, abandonment, estrangement without cause, and the like. Some groups fall into this error, even speaking of love for Him in the same terms they use for loving someone who spurns them and severs ties though they have done no wrong, or who keeps those seeking closeness at a distance. This is not permissible even if some authors have fallen into this error in their treatises, to the point that the substance of their words amounts to making a case against Allah. Rather, to Allah belongs the conclusive argument.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever remembers Me to himself, I remember him to Myself. Whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it. Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a cubit. Whoever draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by an armspan. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.’”

In some transmitted reports, Allah Most High says:

“Those who remember Me are those who sit in My company; those who thank Me are those who visit Me; those who obey Me are those whom I honour. As for those who disobey Me, I do not make them despair of My mercy. If they repent, I am the One who loves them”—for Allah loves those who repent—“and if they do not repent, I am their physician: I afflict them with hardships until I cleanse them of their faults.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer need fear neither injustice nor deprivation.”

They explained: Injustice means being made to bear another’s sins, while deprivation means having one’s own good deeds diminished.

Allah Most High has also said:

“We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.”

In an authentic hadith, Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another.

O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I guide, so seek My guidance and I will guide you.

O My servants, all of you are hungry except those whom I feed, so ask Me for food and I will feed you.

O My servants, all of you are naked except those whom I clothe, so ask Me for clothing and I will clothe you.

O My servants, you sin by night and by day, and I forgive sins and do not mind doing so. Ask My forgiveness and I will forgive you.

O My servants, you can never harm Me, nor can you ever benefit Me.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts like that of the most pious man among you, that would add nothing to My dominion.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts like that of the most wicked man among you, that would diminish My dominion in no way.

O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, gathered on a single plain and asked of Me, and I gave each one what he asked for, that would diminish My dominion no more than a needle diminishes the sea when dipped into it.

O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you, then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.’”

Another example is what al-Bukhārī narrated in his Sahīh from Shaddād ibn Aws, who said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for a servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but Allah. You created me, and I am Your servant. I abide by Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your blessings upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with firm conviction and dies that day will enter Paradise. Whoever says it in the evening with firm conviction and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

The servant is always between a blessing from Allah that calls for gratitude and a sin of his own that calls for seeking forgiveness. Both are constant duties for the servant, for he continually enjoys Allah’s blessings and bounties and continually needs to repent and seek forgiveness. This is why Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the foremost of Adam’s descendants and the leader of the God-fearing—would seek forgiveness in every circumstance.

In the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O people, repent to your Lord, for I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.”

In Sahīh Muslim, he said:

“A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness a hundred times a day.”

ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar said:

“In a single gathering, we would count the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying a hundred times: ‘My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of repentance, the All-Forgiving.’”

For this reason, seeking forgiveness is prescribed at the conclusion of acts of worship. Allah Most High says:

“And those who seek forgiveness before dawn.”

Some said: “They spent the night in prayer, and when the time before dawn came, they were commanded to seek forgiveness.” An authentic hadith states:

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, finished his prayer, he would seek forgiveness three times and say: ‘O Allah, You are Peace, and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Then, when you depart from ʿArafāt, remember Allah at the Sacred Monument,”

up to His words:

“And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

After His Prophet had conveyed the message, striven for Allah as He deserves, and fulfilled Allah’s commands to a degree attained by no one else, Allah commanded him, saying:

“When Allah’s help and victory come, and you see people entering Allah’s religion in crowds, then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

For this reason, religion rests upon affirming Allah’s oneness and seeking forgiveness, as Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then set forth in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware: ‘Worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good tidings. And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance; He will grant you good enjoyment’”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High says:

“So take a straight course towards Him and seek His forgiveness.”

And Allah Most High says:

“So know that there is no god but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women.”

For this reason, it is related in a hadith:

“Satan says: ‘I destroyed people through sins, but they destroyed me by saying “There is no god but Allah” and seeking forgiveness.’”

Jonah said: “There is no god but You; glory be to You!

Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mounted his riding animal, “he would praise Allah, then proclaim Allah’s greatness three times and say: ‘There is no god but You; glory be to You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me.’”

The supplication of expiation with which he would conclude a gathering was:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.”

Allah knows best. May Allah bless Muhammad and grant him peace.

Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

All praise is due to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray, and whoever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him, his family and his Companions, and grant them abundant peace.

Section: The Sickness of Hearts and Their Healing

Allah Most High said concerning the hypocrites:

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease.”

And He, Most High, said:

“So that He may make what Satan casts forth a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and those whose hearts are hardened.”

and He said:

“If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is disease, and those who spread alarming rumours in Medina do not desist, We will surely stir you up against them; then they will remain your neighbours there only a little while.”

And He said:

“And so that those given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, ‘What does Allah intend by this as an example?’”

And He, Most High, said:

“There has come to you an admonition from your Lord, a healing for what is in the hearts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.”

And He said:

“And heal the hearts of a believing people”

“And remove the rage from their hearts.”

“Illness of the body” is the opposite of its health and soundness. It is a disorder within the body that impairs its perception and natural functioning. Its perception may disappear, as in blindness and deafness, or it may perceive things other than as they really are: something sweet may taste bitter, or it may imagine things that have no external reality. As for the impairment of its natural functioning, its digestive capacity may weaken, or it may develop an aversion to the foods it needs and a liking for things that harm it. It experiences pain accordingly.

Despite this illness, however, the body has neither died nor perished. Rather, it retains, in general, some capacity to perceive voluntary movement. This gives rise to pain in the body, owing to a disorder of either quantity or quality. The first involves either a deficiency of substance, in which case nourishment is needed, or an excess of it

Likewise, “illness of the heart” is a kind of corruption that impairs its perception and its will. Its perception is impaired by the doubts that arise within it, until it no longer sees the truth, or sees it as other than it really is. Its will is impaired such that it hates beneficial truth and loves harmful falsehood. This is why illness is sometimes explained as doubt and uncertainty, as when Mujāhid and Qatādah explained His words:

“In their hearts is disease”

as meaning doubt. At other times, it is explained as the desire for illicit intercourse, as in the explanation of His words:

“Lest he in whose heart is disease should covet.”

For this reason, al-Kharā’itī composed The Book of the Ailments of Hearts—that is, their illness—by which he meant their affliction with lust.

A sick person is hurt by things that do not hurt a healthy person. Even slight heat, cold, exertion, and similar things harm him, because the weakness caused by his illness leaves him unable to withstand them. Illness generally weakens the sick person, diminishing his strength so that he cannot bear what can be borne by

a strong person. Health is preserved by like conditions and lost through contrary ones, while illness is aggravated by conditions like those that caused it and dispelled by their opposite. If a sick person encounters something like the cause of his illness, his illness increases and his strength diminishes further, until he may even perish. If, however, he encounters what restores his strength and dispels his illness, the opposite occurs.

“Illness of the heart” is pain that arises in the heart, such as rage at an enemy who has overpowered you, for this causes the heart pain. Allah Most High says:

“and heal the hearts of a believing people”

“and remove the rage from their hearts.”

Their healing consists in the removal of the pain that has arisen in their hearts. Thus, one says, “So-and-so’s rage has been soothed.” Retaliatory execution likewise brings relief to the slain person’s next of kin, and there are other such examples. This is healing from distress, rage, and sorrow, all of which are pains that arise in the soul.

“Doubt and ignorance” likewise cause the heart pain. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is simply to ask.”

Someone who doubts something and is uncertain about it feels pain in his heart until he attains knowledge and certainty. One may say to a scholar whose answer makes the truth clear, “He has healed me with his answer.”

Illness falls short of death: the heart dies through complete ignorance and becomes ill through a particular kind of ignorance. Thus, it experiences death, illness, life, and healing. Its life, death, illness, and healing are more consequential than those of the body. Hence, when a doubt or desire comes upon a diseased heart, it aggravates its illness; but if wisdom and admonition reach it, they are among

the means of restoring its soundness and healing it.

Allah Most High says:

“so that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is disease”

This is because it gives rise to doubt in them. As for those whose hearts are hardened, their hardness is due to their dryness. The hearts of the former are weakened by illness, so what Satan casts becomes a trial for them; the hearts of the latter are hardened against faith, so it becomes a trial for them as well.

He also says:

“If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is disease, and those who spread alarming rumours in Medina do not desist”

And likewise:

“and so that those in whose hearts is disease may say”

Their hearts have not died as the hearts of the disbelievers and hypocrites have, nor are they healthy and sound like the sound hearts of the believers. Rather, they suffer from the illness of doubt and desires. Likewise, He says:

“lest he in whose heart is disease should be moved to desire”

This is the illness of lust. Someone with a sound heart would pay no attention to a woman even if she made advances to him. By contrast, a heart diseased with lust, because of its weakness, inclines towards such temptations as present themselves, to a degree corresponding to the severity of its illness. Thus, when women soften their speech, the man whose heart is diseased is moved to desire.

The Quran is a healing for what is in people's hearts. For those whose hearts suffer from the illnesses of doubts and desires, it contains clear proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood. It thereby dispels the illnesses of doubt that corrupt knowledge, understanding, and perception, enabling a person to see things as they truly are. It also contains wisdom and good admonition—through encouragement, warning, and instructive narratives—that restore the heart to soundness. The heart then desires what benefits it and turns away from what harms it. It thus comes to love right guidance and hate error, after having desired error and hated right guidance.

translated_text:
Thus, the Quran removes the diseases that give rise to corrupt desires, until the heart becomes sound, its desires are set right, and it returns to the innate disposition upon which it was created, just as the body returns to its natural state. The heart draws from faith and the Quran the nourishment that makes it flourish and strengthens it, just as the body feeds on what promotes its growth and soundness. For the heart’s flourishing is like the body’s growth.

“Zakāh in its linguistic sense” means growth and increase in goodness. Something is said to flourish when it grows in goodness. The heart needs nurturing so that it grows and develops until it becomes complete and sound, just as the body needs to be nurtured with wholesome foods. Alongside this, whatever harms it must be kept away. The body grows only when it receives what benefits it and is protected from what harms it. Likewise, the heart can flourish, grow, and attain complete soundness only by receiving what benefits it and warding off what harms it. Crops, too, flourish only in this way.

Since “charity” extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, it causes the heart to flourish. This flourishing is something beyond its purification from sin. Allah Most High says:

“Take charity from their wealth to purify them and cause them to grow thereby.”

Likewise, abandoning indecencies causes the heart to flourish. So too does abandoning sins, for they are like harmful humours in the body and weeds among crops. When the body is purged of harmful humours—for example, by removing excess blood—its natural strength is freed of its burden and finds relief, allowing the body to grow. So too with the heart: when

it repents of sins, it is purged of the admixture produced by combining righteous deeds with evil ones. When it repents of sins, its strength and will are freed for righteous deeds, and it finds relief from the corrupt influences that had arisen within it. The heart thus flourishes, growing and attaining completeness.

Allah Most High says:

“Were it not for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, not one of you would ever have become pure.”

And He Most High says:

“If you are told to go back, then go back; that is purer for you.”

And He says:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what they do.”

And He Most High says:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself, remembers the name of his Lord, and prays.”

And He Most High says:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it, and failed indeed is the one who corrupts it.”

And He Most High says:

“What could make you know? Perhaps he might purify himself.”

And He Most High says:

“Then say, ‘Would you be willing to purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord so that you may fear Him?’”

Although the primary meaning of tazkiya is growth, blessing, and an increase in goodness, this is achieved only by removing evil. Thus, purification encompasses both meanings.

And He says:

“Woe to those who associate partners with Allah, who do not give zakāh.”

Here, zakāh refers to affirming Allah’s oneness and to faith, through which the heart flourishes. This entails rejecting within the heart the divinity of anything besides the True One and affirming His divinity within it. This is the true meaning of “There is no god but Allah,” and it is the foundation upon which hearts flourish.

Tazkiya means making something pure, either in itself or in how it is regarded and spoken of;

just as one says, “I have rendered him upright,” meaning either that one has made him upright in himself or established his uprightness in people’s estimation. Allah Most High says:

“So do not claim purity for yourselves.”

That is, do not declare yourselves pure. This differs from His saying:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it.”

Hence He says:

“He knows best who is mindful of Him.”

Zaynab’s name had been Barrah, but it was said that she was thereby claiming purity for herself, so the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, named her Zaynab.

As for His saying:

“Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, Allah purifies whom He wills.”

This means that He makes a person pure and declares him to be so, just as someone who vouches for witnesses attests to their uprightness.

“Justice” means balance, and balance is the soundness of the heart, just as wrongdoing is its corruption. Thus, whenever a person sins, he wrongs himself. Wrongdoing is the opposite of justice: he has not treated himself justly, but has wronged himself. The heart’s soundness therefore lies in justice, and its corruption in wrongdoing. When a servant wrongs himself, he is both the wrongdoer and the one wronged. Likewise, when he acts justly, he is both the one who acts justly and the one treated justly. The deed proceeds from him, and its fruit, whether good or evil, returns to him.

Allah Most High says:

“Each soul will have the good it has earned and bear the evil it has earned.”

A deed affects the heart—benefiting it, harming it, or setting it right—before its effects appear outwardly. Setting the soul right is to do it justice, while corrupting it is to wrong it. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own benefit; and whoever does evil, it is to his own detriment.”

And He Most High says:

“If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against yourselves.”

One of the early generations said: “A good deed indeed produces light in the heart, strength in the body, radiance in the face, abundance in provision, and love in people’s hearts; an evil deed, by contrast, produces darkness in

the heart, darkness in the face, weakness in the body, diminished provision, and hatred in people’s hearts.”

Allah Most High says:

“Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned.”

And He Most High says:

“Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned.”

And He says:

“And remind through it, lest a soul be given up to destruction for what it has earned. It will have no protector or intercessor besides Allah. Even if it offers every ransom, none will be accepted from it. Those are the ones given up to destruction for what they have earned.”

To be “given up” means to be held in pledge, confined, and taken captive. Likewise, when the body recovers from illness, its temperament is said to have regained its balance; illness arises from a disturbance of that temperament. Yet perfect equilibrium, free from humoral admixture, is unattainable; rather, one seeks the best attainable balance, then the next best. Similarly, the heart’s health and soundness lie in justice, while its illness arises from deviation, wrongdoing, and crookedness. Absolute justice in everything is unattainable, in both knowledge and practice; rather, one seeks the best, then the next best.

Hence one says, “This is better,” and the way of the early generations is called “the best way.”

Allah Most High says:

“You will never be able to be completely just between wives, even if you strive to do so.”

And He Most High says:

“Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

Allah Most High sent the messengers and revealed the Books so that people might uphold justice. The greatest justice is to worship Allah alone, without any partner; then to deal justly with people concerning their rights; then to deal justly with oneself.

And injustice is of “three kinds”: all injustice is a disease of the heart, while justice is its health and soundness.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said to someone, “If you were sound, you would fear no one.” That is, your fear of created beings arises from a disease within you, such as the disease of associating partners with Allah or committing sins.

The foundation of the heart’s soundness is its life and illumination. Allah Most High says:

“Is one who was dead, then We gave him life and provided him with light by which to walk among people, like one who is in darkness from which he cannot emerge?”

Thus, Allah mentions the life and light of hearts, and their death and darkness, in several places. For example, He says:

“To warn whoever is alive, and so that the word may be fulfilled against the disbelievers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.”

Then He says:

“And know that Allah intervenes between a person and his heart, and that to Him you will be gathered.”

And Allah Most High says:

“He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living.”

One instance of this is that He brings forth a believer from a disbeliever and a disbeliever from a believer. An authentic hadith states:

“The likeness of a house in which Allah is remembered and a house in which Allah is not remembered is that of the living and the dead.”

Another authentic hadith states:

“Perform some of your prayers in your homes, and do not turn them into graves.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Those who deny Our signs are deaf and mute, in darkness.”

He—glorified be He—mentioned the verse of light and the verse of darkness, saying:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth

; the likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp. The lamp is within glass, the glass like a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, whose oil almost shines even without being touched by fire. Light upon light.”

This is a likeness of the light of faith in the believers’ hearts. Then He says:

“As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage on a level plain, which a thirsty person mistakes for water, until, when he reaches it, he finds nothing there. But he finds Allah there, who settles his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning. Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds—layers of darkness, one above another. When he stretches out his hand, he can scarcely see it. Whoever Allah grants no light has no light.”

The first is a likeness of corrupt beliefs and the deeds that follow from them. The person holding those beliefs imagines that they will benefit him, but when he comes to them, he finds nothing that benefits him. Allah then settles his account in full for those deeds.

And (the second: a likeness of simple ignorance and the absence of faith and knowledge. Someone in this condition is amid layers of darkness, one above another, unable to see anything; for it is only through the light of faith and knowledge that one sees. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, when those who fear Allah are touched by a prompting from Satan, they remember, and at once they see clearly.”

Allah Most High also says:

“She certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord.”

This was the proof of faith established in his heart, through which Allah turned him away from what he had intended, credited him with a full good deed, and did not record

a sin against him, for he had done good and had committed no evil.

Allah Most High says:

“So that you may bring people out of darkness into light.”

He also says:

“Allah is the Protector of those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light. As for those who disbelieve, their allies are the powers of evil, who bring them out of light into darkness.”

And He says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger. He will grant you a double share of His mercy and give you a light by which to walk.”

For this reason, Allah sets forth “two likenesses” of faith: one involving water, which gives life, and the froth that accompanies it; and another involving fire, which gives light, and the dross that accompanies what is heated in it. Likewise, Allah sets forth “two likenesses” of hypocrisy. Allah Most High says:

“He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity. The torrent carries swelling froth, and a similar froth rises from what people heat in the fire to make ornaments or useful goods. Thus Allah illustrates truth and falsehood. As for the froth, it is cast away, while what benefits people remains on the earth. Thus Allah sets forth likenesses.”

Allah Most High says of the hypocrites:

“Their likeness is that of someone who kindled a fire. When it lit up everything around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.”

“Deaf, dumb and blind, they will not return.”

“Or like a rainstorm from the sky, bringing darkness, thunder and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, fearing death. But Allah encompasses the disbelievers.”

“The lightning almost snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights the way for them, they walk in it; but when darkness falls over them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah has power over all things.”

Thus He likened them to someone who kindled a fire: whenever it gave light, Allah extinguished it. The water-based likeness concerns what descends from the sky, accompanied by darkness, thunder, and visible lightning. A fuller discussion of these likenesses belongs elsewhere. The purpose here is simply to discuss the life and illumination of hearts. A transmitted supplication says:

“Make the Quran the life-giving rain of our hearts and the light of our breasts.”

The word rabīʿ refers to rain that descends from the sky and causes vegetation to grow. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Among the plants brought forth by the rain are those that cause fatal bloating, or nearly so.”

The Arabs call the season in which the first rains fall rabīʿ, because that is when the rain falls that brings forth vegetation. Others use rabīʿ for the season following winter, since it is then that blossoms appear from which fruits develop, and leaves grow on trees.

Through the light within it, the living, illuminated heart hears, sees, and understands. The dead heart, however, neither hears nor sees. Allah Most High says:

“The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of someone calling to creatures that hear nothing but cries and calls. Deaf, dumb, and blind, they do not understand.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Among them are those who listen to you. But can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?”

“And among them are those who look at you. But can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?”

And Allah Most High says:

“Among them are those who listen to you

and We have placed coverings over their hearts so that they do not understand it, and deafness in their ears. Even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. When they come to you arguing with you, those who disbelieve say, ‘This is nothing but tales of the ancients.’”—and the subsequent verses.

He thus states that they do not understand with their hearts, do not hear with their ears, and do not believe in what they have seen of the fire. Likewise, He reports that they said:

“Our hearts are covered against what you call us to, there is deafness in our ears, and between us and you is a barrier.”

They thus mentioned the barriers affecting their hearts, hearing, and sight, although their bodies are alive, hearing sounds and seeing people. Yet bodily life without life in the heart is like the life of animals: they have hearing and sight, and they eat, drink, and mate. Hence Allah Most High says:

“The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of someone calling to creatures that hear nothing but cries and calls.”

He likens them to sheep that hear nothing but the shepherd’s calls, as He says in another verse:

“Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; indeed, they are even further astray from the path.”

Allah Most High also says:

“We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. They are like livestock; indeed, they are even further astray.”

translated_text:
Some commentators, when discussing these verses and similar passages—such as His saying:

“When adversity touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We remove his adversity, he goes on as though he had never called upon Us concerning the adversity that touched him”—

and other passages in which Allah mentions and condemns human failings, say: “This verse concerns the disbelievers; ‘man’ here means the disbeliever.” Those who hear this are then left thinking that none of this condemnation or warning applies to anyone who outwardly professes Islam. Rather, their thoughts turn to those Arabs who openly professed polytheism, or to those they know who openly profess disbelief, such as Jews, Christians, and polytheists among the Turks and Indians, and others like them. Thus, they derive no benefit from these verses, which Allah revealed to guide His servants.

The response is, first: those who outwardly profess Islam include both believers and hypocrites. Hypocrites are numerous in every age, and the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire.

Second: a person may have an element of hypocrisy and disbelief while also possessing faith, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in a hadith reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Whoever possesses four traits is a pure hypocrite, and whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he acts wickedly.”

He thus stated that whoever possesses one of these traits has a trait of hypocrisy.

It is also established in an authentic hadith that he said to Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him:

“There is some pre-Islamic ignorance in you.”

Yet Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the most sincere people in faith. He also said in an authentic hadith:

“Four practices in my community belong to the ways of pre-Islamic ignorance: boasting of ancestral distinction, disparaging people’s lineage, wailing over the dead, and seeking rain through the stars.”

He said in another authentic hadith:

“You will surely follow the ways of those before you, matching them as precisely as one arrow feather matches another, until, even if they entered a lizard’s hole, you would enter it.”

They asked, “The Jews and Christians?” He replied, “Who else?”

He also said in an authentic hadith:

“My community will surely follow the course taken by the nations before it, handspan for handspan and cubit for cubit.”

They asked, “Persia and Rome?” He replied, “Who else among the nations could it be?”

Ibn Abī Mulaykah said: “I met thirty of the Companions of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves.”

They raise this question only because they have not properly understood the straight path to which the servant seeks guidance. What is meant is to do whatever Allah has commanded and refrain from whatever He has forbidden in all matters. Although a person may acknowledge in general terms that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and that the Quran is true, he remains unaware of most of what he needs to know about what benefits and harms him, and what Allah has commanded and forbidden in specific matters and their particulars. Even much of what he does know, he has not put into practice. Even supposing that every command and prohibition in the Quran and Sunnah had reached him, the Quran and Sunnah state only general, universal matters—it could not be otherwise—and do not specify what pertains individually to each servant. This is why a person is commanded to ask for guidance to the straight path in such matters.

Guidance to the straight path encompasses all of this: being taught in detail what the Messenger brought, being shown what falls under his universal commands, and being inspired to act upon what one knows. Merely knowing the truth does not make a person rightly guided unless he acts upon his knowledge. This is why Allah said to His Prophet after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah:

Muslims have disagreed, as Allah has willed, over matters concerning reports, knowledge, belief, and practice, even though they all agree that Muhammad is truly Allah’s Messenger and that the Quran is true. As for those of this community whom Allah has guided until they became His pious allies, one of the greatest means of attaining this was their supplicating to Allah with this prayer in every prayer, while recognizing their constant need of Allah and their utter dependence upon Him to guide them to the straight path. Through continually making this supplication and acknowledging their need, they became Allah’s pious allies.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said, “No path brings a servant closer to his Lord than his need of Him.”

Whatever a person was guided in previously, he still needs guidance in it in the future. This is the true meaning of the interpretation:

the future; rather, it may disappear from the heart. Even when knowledge is present, action may not follow. Thus everyone is utterly dependent upon this supplication. This is why Allah has made it obligatory upon them in every prayer: there is no supplication they need more. When guidance to the straight path is attained, victory, provision, and everything else that souls seek for their happiness follow. Allah knows best.

Know that the life of the heart, and life in other things, does not consist merely in sensation and voluntary movement, or merely in knowledge and power, as some speculative thinkers who discuss Allah’s knowledge and power, such as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī, suppose. They say, “His life consists in His being such that He knows and has power.” Rather, life is an attribute subsisting in its subject. It is a prerequisite for knowledge, will, and the power to perform voluntary actions, and it also necessarily entails these. Every living being has awareness, will, and voluntary action exercised through its power; and whatever possesses knowledge, will, and voluntary action is alive.

Hayā’ (modesty) is derived from hayāh (life). A person whose heart is alive is himself alive and possesses modesty that restrains him from ugly deeds. It is the heart’s life that prevents the ugly deeds that corrupt it. This is why the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Modesty is part of faith.”

He also said:

“Modesty and reticence are two branches of faith, while obscene speech and ostentatious eloquence are two branches of hypocrisy.”

For the living repel whatever harms them, unlike the dead, who have no life. Such a person is called shameless. Shamelessness denotes hardness: the dryness that contrasts with the moisture of life. When someone is shameless, dry, and brazen-faced, his heart has no life to inspire modesty and restrain him from ugly deeds; he is like the earth

that is dry and unaffected by the tread of feet, unlike verdant earth. This is why a living person is visibly affected by what is shameful and has a will that prevents him from doing it, unlike the shameless person who is not alive and has neither modesty nor faith to deter him.

Thus, if the heart is alive and a person dies through his spirit’s departure from his body, the soul’s death consists in its separation from the body; the soul itself is not dead in the sense of having lost its life. This is why Allah Most High says:

“Do not say of those killed in the cause of Allah, ‘They are dead.’ Rather, they are alive.”

And He says:

“Never think of those killed in the cause of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive.”

Yet they are dead and are included in His words:

“Every soul will taste death,”

and His words:

“You will surely die, and they too will surely die,”

and His words:

“He is the One who gave you life, then will cause you to die, then will bring you back to life.”

The death affirmed here is therefore different from the death denied. What is affirmed is the spirit’s separation from the body; what is denied is the complete cessation of life in the spirit and the body. Similarly, sleep is the brother of death: it is called a taking of the soul and is also called death, although life remains in both.

Allah Most High says:

“Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. He then retains those for whom He has decreed death and releases the others until an appointed time.”

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, awoke from sleep, he would say:

“Praise be to Allah, who has brought us to life after causing us to die, and to Him is the resurrection.”

“Praise be to Allah, who has restored my spirit to me, granted me bodily well-being, permitted me to remember Him, and greatly favored me above many of those He has created.”

When he went to bed, he would say:

“O Allah, You created my soul, and You are the One who takes it. Its death and its life belong to You. If You retain it, have mercy upon it; and if You release it, protect it as You protect Your righteous servants.”

He would also say:

“In Your name, O Allah, I die and live.”

Section

Among the diseases of the heart is envy. Some have defined it as the pain one experiences upon learning of the prosperous condition of the wealthy. Thus, a virtuous person cannot be envious, for a virtuous person acts in accordance with what is good.

Some people have said that envy is wishing for a blessing to be taken away from the person envied, even if the envious person does not obtain its like. This differs from emulation, which is wishing for a similar blessing without wanting the person who enjoys it to lose it.

More precisely, envy is hatred and aversion toward the favorable condition one sees the envied person enjoying. It is of two kinds:

The first is an unqualified aversion to that person’s enjoyment of a blessing. This is blameworthy envy. When someone hates this, the existence of what he hates causes him pain and distress, becoming a disease in his heart. He takes pleasure in the other person’s loss of the blessing, even if he gains no benefit from its loss; rather, the benefit he derives is

translated_text:
the disappearance of the pain he felt within himself. Yet that pain subsides only through action on his part. This brings relief; at its most severe, his condition resembles that of a sick person treated with something that soothes his pain while the illness remains. His hatred of Allah’s blessing upon His servant is itself a disease, for that blessing may return to the envied person, and he may receive something greater still. A similar blessing may also be granted to someone like the person he envies. The envious person is not concerned with any particular thing; rather, he resents the blessings bestowed upon people of that kind.

This is why some have defined envy as wishing for a blessing to disappear: whoever resents another person’s blessing wishes in his heart for its disappearance.

The second kind is to resent another person’s superiority over oneself and therefore wish to be his equal or better than him. This too is envy, though it is what they have called emulation. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called it envy in the hadith reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. He said:

“There is no envy except in two cases: a man whom Allah has granted wisdom, by which he judges and which he teaches; and a man whom Allah has granted wealth and enabled to expend it in the cause of truth.”

This is Ibn Masʿūd’s wording. Ibn ʿUmar’s wording is:

“A man whom Allah has granted the Quran, who stands in prayer reciting it at various hours of the night and day; and a man whom Allah has granted wealth, who spends from it in the cause of truth at various hours of the night and day.”

Al-Bukhārī also narrated it from Abū Hurayra, with the wording:

“There is no envy except in two cases: a man whom Allah has granted the Quran, who recites it night and day. Another man hears him and says, ‘If only I had been given the like of what this man has been given

so that I could do with it what he does.’ And a man whom Allah has granted wealth, which he expends in the cause of truth. Another man says, ‘If only I had been given the like of what this man has been given, so that I could do with it what he does.’”

This envy, which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade except in two cases, is what those scholars called emulation: wishing to enjoy the same circumstances as another while resenting being surpassed by him.

If it is asked, “Why, then, is it called envy when he merely wishes Allah to bestow His favour upon him?” the answer is that this desire originates in his observing Allah’s favour upon another and resenting being surpassed by him. Were it not for that other person, he would not have desired it. Since it originates in his resentment at another’s superiority over him, it is envy: an aversion followed by a desire. As for someone who wishes Allah to bestow His favour upon him without looking at other people’s circumstances, he has no envy at all.

Most people are tested with this second kind, which may also be called competition. Two people compete for something desirable that they both seek, each wanting to obtain it because he resents being surpassed by the other, just as each of two racers dislikes being outpaced by the other. Competition is not blameworthy in every case; rather, competing in goodness is praiseworthy.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss,
looking on from adorned couches.
You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.
They will be given pure wine to drink, sealed,
its seal being musk. So for this let the competitors compete.”

He thus commanded those who compete to compete for this bliss, not for the pleasures of this world

which are fleeting. This accords with the hadith of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for he forbade envy except toward someone granted knowledge who acts upon it and teaches it, and someone granted wealth who spends it. As for someone granted knowledge who neither acts upon it nor teaches it, or someone granted wealth who does not spend it in obedience to Allah, one does not envy such a person or wish to be in his position. His circumstances offer nothing desirable; rather, he is exposed to punishment.

Anyone entrusted with authority who exercises it with knowledge and justice, renders trusts to their rightful owners, and judges between people according to the Book and the Sunnah has an exalted rank. Yet he is engaged in a tremendous struggle, as is the one who fights in Allah’s cause. People do not envy someone enduring great hardship. This is why the Prophet did not mention him, even though someone who fights in Allah’s cause is superior to someone who spends wealth. Those who spend and those who teach, by contrast, ordinarily have no external enemy. If they should have an enemy against whom they struggle, that further elevates their rank.

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not mention those who pray, fast, or perform Hajj, because these deeds do not ordinarily benefit people in the way that teaching and spending do—benefits for which people esteem a person and make him their leader. Envy arises primarily because of the honour and leadership another person attains. Otherwise, a worker is not ordinarily envied, even if his enjoyment of food, drink, and marital relations exceeds that of others. These two types, however, are frequently envied. This is why one finds among the people of

knowledge who have followers a degree of envy not found among those without followers. The same applies to those who have followers because they spend their wealth. The former benefit people by nourishing their hearts, and the latter by nourishing their bodies. Everyone needs what sustains both.

For this reason, Allah, glorified is He, sets forth “two parables,” one concerning each of these. He says:

“Allah presents a parable: a slave owned by another, unable to do anything, and someone whom We have granted good provision from Us, who spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? All praise belongs to Allah, but most of them do not know.”

“And Allah presents a parable of two men: one is mute, unable to do anything, and a burden to his master; wherever he sends him, he brings back no good. Is he equal to someone who commands justice and follows a straight path?”

And (Allah, glorified is He, sets forth these two parables concerning His own holy Self and what is worshipped besides Him. Idols are incapable of either beneficial action or beneficial speech. Suppose there is a slave owned by another, unable to do anything, and another person whom Allah has granted good provision, who spends from it secretly and openly. Is this slave, incapable of doing good, equal to the person who can do good and does so for people, secretly and openly? He, glorified is He, is able to bestow goodness upon His servants and constantly does so. How, then, can a powerless, owned slave, unable to do anything, be likened to Him and thus made a partner with Him in worship? This is the likeness of the person whom Allah has granted wealth and who spends from it by night and day.

{إنَّ رَبِّي عَلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ}
 . وَلِهَذَا كَانَ النَّاسُ يُعَظِّمُونَ دَارَ الْعَبَّاسِ كَانَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ يُعَلِّمُ النَّاسَ وَأَخُوهُ يُطْعِمُ النَّاسَ فَكَانُوا يُعَظِّمُونَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ.
 وَرَأَى مُعَاوِيَةُ النَّاسَ يَسْأَلُونَ ابْنَ عُمَرَ عَنْ الْمَنَاسِكِ وَهُوَ يُفْتِيهِمْ فَقَالَ:
 هَذَا وَاَللَّهِ الشَّرَفُ أَوْ نَحْوُ ذَلِكَ. هَذَا وَعُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ نَافَسَ أَبَا بَكْرٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ الْإِنْفَاقَ كَمَا ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -
 قَالَ:
 {أَمَرَنَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنْ نَتَصَدَّقَ فَوَافَقَ ذَلِكَ مَالًا عِنْدِي فَقُلْت الْيَوْمَ أَسْبِقُ أَبَا بَكْرٍ إنْ سَبَقْته يَوْمًا.
 قَالَ:
 فَجِئْت بِنِصْفِ مَالِي قَالَ: فَقَالَ لِي رَسُولُ
translated_text:
In the second parable, suppose there are two people: one is mute, unable to understand, speak, or do anything. Moreover, he is a burden to his master; wherever he sends him, he brings back no good. He is of no benefit whatsoever, but is instead a burden to whoever looks after him. The other is knowledgeable and just: he commands justice and acts justly, following a straight path. This is like the person whom Allah has granted wisdom, who acts upon it and teaches it to others. Allah has set this forth as a parable concerning Himself, for He, glorified is He, is All-Knowing, Just, and All-Powerful. He commands justice and upholds equity, following a straight path.

As He, Exalted is He, says:

“Allah bears witness—as do the angels and those endowed with knowledge—that there is no deity except Him, the One who upholds justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And Hūd said:

“Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.”

For this reason, people held the house of al-‘Abbās in high esteem: Abd Allāh taught people, while his brother fed them, and they were honoured for this.

Mu‘āwiyah saw people asking Ibn Umar about the pilgrimage rites while he gave them religious rulings. He said, “This, by Allah, is true honour,” or words to that effect.

Now Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, competed with Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, in charitable spending, as is established in an authentic report from Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed us to give charity. I happened to have some wealth at the time, so I said, ‘Today I shall outdo Abū Bakr, if ever I am to outdo him.’”

translated_text:
Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to me, ‘What have you left for your family?’ I replied, ‘As much again.’ Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, brought everything he had. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked him, ‘What have you left for your family?’ He replied, ‘I have left them Allah and His Messenger.’ I then said, ‘I shall never compete with you in anything again.’”

What Umar did was permissible rivalry and emulation. Yet the state of al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, was better: he was entirely free of rivalry, paying no attention to the circumstances of others.

Likewise, “Moses, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, felt rivalry with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and wished for a blessing like his, as related in the hadith of the Ascension. He even wept when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed beyond him. He was asked, ‘What makes you weep?’ He replied, ‘I weep because a young man was sent after me, yet more people from his community will enter Paradise than from mine.’”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. Another reported wording, other than the authentic account, states:

“We passed a man who was raising his voice and saying, ‘You have honoured him and favoured him!’ He continued: ‘We then raised him up to him and greeted him. He returned the greeting and asked, “Who is this with you, Gabriel?” He replied, “This is Ahmad.” He said, “Welcome to the unlettered Prophet who conveyed his Lord’s message and sincerely counselled his community.”’

“He continued: ‘Then we went on, and I asked, “Who is this, Gabriel?” He replied, “This is Moses son of Imrān.” I asked, “With whom is he remonstrating?” He replied, “He is remonstrating with his Lord concerning you.” I asked, “And he raises his voice at his Lord?” He replied, “Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows his sincerity.”’”

translated_text:
Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was likened to Moses. Our Prophet’s state was superior to that of Moses, for he had none of this. Likewise, among the Companions were Abū Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrāh and others who were free of all these things. They therefore held a higher rank than those who felt rivalry and wished for blessings like those of others, even when this was permissible. This is why Abū Ubaydah, may Allah be pleased with him, deserved to be the trusted man of this community. Someone entrusted with a responsibility who has no desire to compete for anything placed in his care is more worthy of that trust than someone whose competing ambitions are feared.

This is why eunuchs are entrusted with the care of women and children; lesser authority is entrusted to someone known not to compete for higher authority; and wealth is entrusted to someone known to have no desire to take any of it. Entrusting someone who harbours treachery is like entrusting a wolf with sheep: he cannot discharge that trust because he covets what has been placed in his care.

In the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“One day we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he said, ‘A man destined for Paradise will now appear before you from this mountain pass.’ Then a man from the Ansār appeared, his beard dripping with water from his ablution and his sandals hanging from his left hand, and offered his greeting. The next day, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said the same thing, and that man appeared in the same condition. On the third day, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, repeated his words, and that man appeared in the same condition. When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose, Abdullāh ibn Amr ibn al-Ās followed the man—may Allah be pleased

translated_text:
with him—and said, ‘I have quarrelled with my father and sworn not to visit him for three days. If you would be willing to let me stay with you until the three days have passed, please do so.’ He replied, ‘Yes.’

Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Abdullāh used to relate that he spent three nights with the man but did not see him rise for any night prayer. However, whenever he awoke and turned over in bed, he would remember Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and proclaim His greatness, until he rose for the dawn prayer.

Abdullāh said, ‘Yet I never heard him say anything but good. When the three days had passed, and I had almost come to regard his deeds as insignificant, I said, “O servant of Allah, there was neither anger nor estrangement between my father and me. Rather, I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say three times, ‘A man destined for Paradise will now appear before you,’ and each time it was you who appeared. I wanted to stay with you to see what deeds you performed so that I could follow your example. But I have not seen you perform many deeds. What, then, has brought you to the rank spoken of by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?”’

He replied, ‘It is nothing beyond what you have seen, except that I harbour no ill will towards any Muslim, nor any envy of any good that Allah has bestowed upon him.’

Abdullāh said, ‘That is what has brought you to this rank, and that is what we cannot manage.’”

Abdullāh ibn Amr’s words to him, “That is what has brought you to this rank, and that is what we cannot manage,” point to his complete freedom from every kind of envy.

It was for this that Allah Most High praised the Ansār, saying:

“And they harbour no desire in their hearts for what the others have been given, and give them preference over themselves, even though they themselves are in need.”

That is, what their brothers, the Emigrants, had been given. The Quran commentators explained that “they harbour no desire in their hearts” means no envy or resentment over what the Emigrants had been given. Some specified that this referred to fay revenues; others said it referred to distinction and precedence.

Thus, they harbour no resentment over either the wealth or the status others have been given; envy may concern either of these.

The Aws and the Khazraj used to compete in religious devotion. Whenever one group did something that earned them distinction before Allah and His Messenger, the other wished to do likewise. This was competition in what would bring them closer to Allah, as He says:

“So let those who compete compete for this.”

As for envy in its wholly blameworthy form, Allah Most High says concerning the Jews:

“Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed, out of envy arising within themselves, after the truth has become clear to them.”

“They wish” means that they desire your return to disbelief out of envy. He thus identifies envy as the cause of that desire, after the truth had become clear to them. For when they saw the blessings you had received—indeed, blessings the like of which they had not received—they envied you. Likewise, in the other passage:

“Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We have certainly given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom. Some of them believed in him, while others turned away from him. Sufficient is Hell as a blazing fire.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak,
from the evil of what He has created,
and from the evil of darkness when it settles,
and from the evil of those who blow on knots,
and from the evil of an envier when he envies.”

A number of Quran commentators have mentioned that it (was revealed because of the Jews’ envy of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which led them to bewitch him: Labīd ibn al-Asam, the Jew, bewitched him. Thus, the envious person

who resents the blessing Allah has bestowed upon another is an unjust aggressor. Whoever dislikes another being favoured over him and wishes to be his equal is forbidden to do so, except in matters that bring him closer to Allah. If he wishes to receive the same as another has received of what brings him closer to Allah, there is nothing wrong with that. Yet it is better for his heart to turn away from such comparisons altogether, without looking at the circumstances of others.

If an envious person acts upon his envy, he becomes an unjust aggressor deserving punishment unless he repents. The person envied is then wronged and is commanded to remain patient and mindful of Allah: he should patiently endure the envious person’s harm, forgive him, and overlook his offences. As Allah Most High says:

“Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed, out of envy arising within themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So forgive and overlook until Allah brings His command.”

Joseph was tried by his brothers’ envy when they said:

“Joseph and his brother are certainly dearer to our father than we are, though we are a strong group. Our father is clearly mistaken.”

They envied the two because their father favoured them. This is why Jacob said to Joseph:

“Do not tell your brothers your dream, lest they devise a plot against you. Surely Satan is a clear enemy to humankind.”

Then they wronged him by discussing killing him, casting him into the well, and selling him as a slave to someone who took him to a land of disbelief. Thus he became the slave of disbelieving people. After suffering this injustice, Joseph was then tried by someone who called him to sexual immorality, sought to seduce him, and enlisted others to help overcome his resistance. But he stood firm, choosing prison over sexual immorality, and preferred the torment of

For someone who suffers affliction and harm through his choice to obey Allah is rewarded for the afflictions themselves, and a righteous deed is recorded for him on their account.

This is unlike calamities that occur without a person’s choice, such as illness, the death of someone dear to him, or thieves taking his property. In such cases, he is rewarded only for bearing them patiently, not for the calamity itself, though it does expiate his sins. Reward is only for voluntary deeds and their consequences.

Those who are harmed because of their faith and obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and consequently suffer hardship, illness, imprisonment, separation from their homeland, loss of property and family, beatings, insults, or diminished authority and wealth, are following the path of the prophets and their followers, such as the earliest emigrants. They are rewarded for the harm they suffer, and a righteous deed is recorded for them on its account, just as someone striving in Allah’s cause is rewarded for the hunger, thirst, and fatigue he suffers, and for enraging the disbelievers. Although these effects are not themselves acts that he performs, they arise from his voluntary action; they are what are called resultant effects. People have differed over whether these should be considered the acts of the person who brings about their cause, the acts of Allah, or effects with no agent. The correct view is that they are jointly produced by the person who brings about the cause and all the other causes involved. This is why a righteous deed is recorded for him on their account.

Al-Hasan al-Basrī was asked, “Does a believer feel envy?” He replied, “How could you forget Joseph’s brothers, man? But it is a blindness within your heart; it will not harm you so long as you do not let it lead you to transgress with hand or tongue.”

Whoever finds himself envying another must counter it with mindfulness of Allah and patience, and dislike this feeling within himself. Many people who have religious commitment do not wrong the person they envy or help anyone who wrongs him. Yet neither do they fulfil their obligations towards him. If someone disparages him, they do not join in, but neither do they mention his praiseworthy qualities. Likewise, if someone praises him, they remain silent. Such people are culpable for neglecting what they have been commanded to do concerning his rights. They have failed in their duty, though they have not committed aggression against him. Their recompense is that they, too, are denied their rights: in some situations they are not treated fairly or supported against those who wrong them, just as they failed to support the person they envied. As for anyone who transgresses in word or deed, he is punished for that.

Whoever is mindful of Allah and patient, and thus does not join the wrongdoers, will benefit from his mindfulness through Allah’s help. This is what happened to Zaynab bint Jahsh—may Allah be pleased with her. Among the Prophet’s wives—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—she was the one who rivalled ‘Ā’ishah in standing. Envy among women is common and widespread, particularly among those married to the same man. A woman is jealous over her husband because of her own share in him, for sharing him means losing part of that share.

Likewise, envy frequently arises among those who share authority or wealth, when some receive a portion while another misses out. It also arises among peers because one dislikes the other being preferred over him, as with Joseph’s brothers, or with one of Adam’s two sons towards his brother. He envied him because Allah accepted his brother’s offering but did not accept his own. He envied the faith and piety with which Allah had favoured his brother—just as the Jews envy the Muslims—and killed him on that account.

Hence it has been said that the first sins through which Allah was disobeyed were three: greed, arrogance, and envy. Greed came from Adam, arrogance from Satan, and envy from Cain, when he killed Abel. A hadith states:

“No one escapes three things: envy, suspicion, and apprehension over ill omens. I shall tell you how to escape them: when you feel envy, do not hate; when you suspect, do not treat your suspicion as established fact; and when you fear an ill omen, proceed.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā narrated it from Abū Hurayrah. In the Sunan collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“The disease of the nations before you has crept among you: envy and hatred. It is the shaver. I do not say that it shaves the hair; rather, it shaves away religion.”

He thus called it a disease, just as he called miserliness a disease when he said:

“What disease is worse than miserliness?”

It is therefore clear that this is an illness. Another hadith states:

“I seek refuge in You from reprehensible traits of character, desires, and diseases.”

Thus he mentioned diseases alongside traits of character and desires.

For “character” is what has become habitual and ingrained in the soul. Allah Most High says:

“And indeed, you are of a great moral character.”

Ibn ‘Abbās, Ibn ‘Uyaynah, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with them—explained this as adherence to a great religion. In another wording, Ibn ‘Abbās said: “The religion of Islam.” Likewise, ‘Ā’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—said: “His character was the Quran.” Al-Hasan al-Basrī similarly said: “The conduct taught by the Quran is the exalted character.”

As for “desire,” it may be transient. An “ailment” is a disease: pain in the heart and corruption within it. In the first hadith, he paired envy with hatred because the envious person first resents Allah’s favour upon another, then comes to hate that person. Hatred of an inseparable attribute entails hatred of its bearer. Thus, if Allah’s blessing is inseparable from someone, and the envious person wishes it to disappear, but it can disappear only with that person’s disappearance, he hates him and wishes that he no longer existed.

Envy gives rise to wrongdoing, as Allah Most High tells us concerning those before us: they differed after knowledge had come to them, transgressing against one another. Their disagreement was not due to a lack of knowledge. Rather, they knew the truth, but wronged one another, just as the envious person wrongs the one he envies.

The two Sahīh collections report from Anas ibn Mālik—may Allah be pleased with him—that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Do not envy one another, hate one another, turn your backs on one another, or sever ties with one another. Be brothers, O servants of Allah. It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three nights: they meet, and each turns away from the other. The better of the two is the one who first offers the greeting of peace.”

He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—also said in a hadith recorded in both collections, likewise narrated by Anas: “By Him who

holds my soul in His hand, none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, among you is one who lingers behind. If a calamity befalls you, he says, ‘Allah has favoured me, for I was not present with them.’

“But if bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say—as though there had never been any affection between you and him—‘If only I had been with them, I would have attained a great triumph!’”

Those who linger behind do not love for their believing brothers what they love for themselves. Rather, if a calamity befalls their brothers, they rejoice that it has struck them alone. If a blessing comes to them, they do not rejoice for them, but wish to have a share of it themselves. Thus, when they have no love for Allah, His Messenger, or the Hereafter, they rejoice only in worldly gain that comes their way or worldly harm that is averted from them. If they did have such love, they would love their brothers, rejoice in the bounty He bestows upon them, and feel pain at the calamities that befall them. Whoever does not rejoice at what brings joy to the believers and grieve at what brings them grief is not one of them.

The two Sahīh collections report from ‘Āmir that he heard al-Nu‘mān ibn Bashīr delivering a sermon and saying:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—say: ‘The believers, in their mutual love, mercy, and compassion, are like a single body: when any part of it suffers, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness.’”

The two Sahīh collections also report from Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī—may Allah be pleased with him—who said:

“The Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said: ‘One believer is to another like a building whose parts strengthen one another,’ and he interlaced his fingers.”

Avarice is a disease, and miserliness is a disease; envy is worse than miserliness, as in the hadith

which Abū Dāwūd narrated from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“Envy consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood, and charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire.”

This is because the miser refrains from giving, whereas the envious person resents Allah’s blessings upon His servants. A man may give to those who help him achieve his aims while envying his peers; or he may be miserly without envying others. Avarice lies at the root of this.

Allah Most High says:

“And whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul—it is they who will be successful.”

The two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Beware of avarice, for it destroyed those before you. It commanded them to be miserly, so they were miserly; it commanded them to commit injustice, so they committed injustice; and it commanded them to sever ties, so they severed them.”

While circumambulating the Kaaba, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf would frequently supplicate, saying, “O Allah, protect me from the avarice of my own soul.” A man said to him, “How often you make this supplication!” He replied, “If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I am protected from avarice, injustice, and severing ties.” Envy gives rise to injustice.

Section

Miserliness and envy constitute a disease that causes the soul to hate what benefits it—indeed, to love what harms it. This is why envy is coupled with rancour and anger. As for the disease of desire and passionate love, it is the soul’s love for what harms it, which may also be accompanied by hatred of what benefits it. Passionate love is a psychological illness. It is related in a hadith:

“I keep those close to Me away from the pleasures and ease of this world, just as a caring herdsman keeps his camels away from deadly pastures. I keep them away from its comforts and easy living, just as a caring herdsman keeps his camels away from resting places where they would be caught unawares. This is not because they are insignificant to Me, but so that they may receive their full share of My honour, intact and undiminished, unscarred by the world and undimmed by desire.”

The sick person is cured only when his illness disappears—or rather, when that blameworthy love is removed from his heart.

translated_text:
Some say that it belongs to the realm of volition; this is the prevalent view. Others say that it belongs to the realm of mental representations and is a distortion of the imagination, whereby the beloved is conceived as he or she actually is. Those who hold the latter view say: “For this reason, Allah is not described as experiencing passionate love or as loving passionately, for He is exalted above that. Nor is anyone who entertains a distorted conception of Him to be praised.”

Among those who hold the first view, some say: “He may be described in terms of passionate love, for it is perfect love, and Allah is loved and He loves.” A report transmitted from ʿAbd al-Wāhid ibn Zayd states:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me, loving Me passionately, and I love him passionately.”

This is the view of some Sufis. The majority, however, do not use this expression with reference to Allah, because passionate love is excessive love that exceeds its proper bounds. Love for Allah Most High, however, has no limit: it does not reach a boundary beyond which one ought not to go.

They say: “Passionate love is blameworthy without qualification. It is not praiseworthy in love for either the Creator or created beings, because it is excessive love that goes beyond praiseworthy bounds. Moreover, in customary usage, the expression ‘passionate love’ is used only for a person’s love for a woman or a boy. It is not used for such things as love of family, wealth, homeland, status, or love for the prophets and the righteous. It is also frequently accompanied by forbidden conduct: love for a woman to whom one is not married, or for a boy, may be accompanied by forbidden looking, forbidden touching, and other forbidden acts. As for

translated_text:
a man’s love for his wife or concubine, it may be so intense that it leads him to act unjustly, doing what is unlawful for her sake and neglecting his duties—as happens so often. He may even wrong his son by his earlier wife because of his love for his new wife, and comply with her blameworthy demands in ways that harm his religious and worldly affairs. For example, he may single her out for an inheritance to which she is not entitled, give her family positions of authority and wealth in ways that transgress Allah’s limits, spend extravagantly on her, or grant her control over forbidden matters that harm his religious and worldly affairs. All this concerns passionate love for a woman with whom intercourse is lawful for him. What, then, of passionate love for a woman to whom he is not married, or for males among mankind? It entails evils that none but the Lord of all servants can count. It is among the diseases that corrupt a person’s religion and honour, and may then corrupt his mind and, thereafter, his body.

Allah Most High says:

“So do not be soft in speech, lest he in whose heart is disease should be moved with desire.”

When someone whose heart is afflicted with the disease of lust and desire for a person’s physical form hears the person he desires speaking softly, his hopes are aroused. Such hope strengthens his desire and pursuit, thereby intensifying the disease. The opposite happens when he has no hope of attaining the person he desires: hopelessness removes expectation, so desire weakens, and love consequently weakens. A person has no wish to pursue what he has no hope of attaining. Thus, no action at all accompanies his desire; it remains merely an inward thought—unless accompanied by speech, looking, or the like, in which case he sins thereby.

But if a person is afflicted with passionate love, remains chaste, and is patient, he is rewarded for his fear of Allah. It has been related in a hadith:

“Whoever falls passionately in love, remains chaste, conceals it, and is patient, then dies, is a martyr.”

This is known through the narration of Yahyā al-Qattāt, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ‘Abbās, as a report traced back to the Prophet. However, it is open to question and cannot be used as evidence. Nevertheless, the evidence of the revealed law establishes that if a person refrains from forbidden looks, words, and deeds, conceals his passion and does not speak of it, thereby avoiding unlawful speech—whether complaining to a created being, publicizing indecency, or making some overture to the beloved—and patiently perseveres in obedience to Allah, refrains from disobeying Him, and bears the pain of passionate love in his heart as an afflicted person bears the pain of his affliction, then he is among those who fear Allah and are patient:

“Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient—Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

The same applies to the disease of envy and other diseases of the soul. When the soul seeks what Allah hates, and a person restrains it out of fear of Allah, he is among those included in His words:

“But as for the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire, Paradise will be his refuge.”

When the soul loves something, it strives to obtain it by whatever means it can, even undertaking many things that are all steps toward that end. Whoever harbours blameworthy love or hatred and acts upon it is sinful. For example, a person may hate someone out of envy and consequently harm those connected to him, either by withholding their rights or by committing aggression against them; or out of love

translated_text:
for someone towards whom his desires draw him, he may do something forbidden for that person’s sake, or perform something he is commanded to do for Allah, but do it to satisfy his desires rather than for Allah. Such diseases abound in souls. A person may hate something and consequently hate many other things merely through illusion and imagination. Likewise, he may love something and consequently love many other things through illusion and imagination, as their poet said:

Out of love for her, I love black people—
So much that, for love of her, I even love black dogs.

He loved a black woman, and so came to love blackness itself, even in dogs. All of this is a disease of the heart affecting its perception and its will. We therefore ask Allah Most High to grant our hearts freedom from every disease, and we seek refuge in Allah from reprehensible character traits, desires, and diseases.

The heart was created solely for “love of Allah Most High.” This is the innate disposition upon which Allah created His servants, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born with the innate disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to an animal whole and sound: do you see any mutilation in it?”

Then Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, would say: “Recite, if you wish: ‘The natural disposition Allah has instilled in mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation.’”

Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
