 وَأَمَّا امْرَأَةُ الْعَزِيزِ فَكَانَتْ مُشْرِكَةً هِيَ وَقَوْمُهَا فَلِهَذَا اُبْتُلِيَتْ بِالْعِشْقِ وَمَا يُبْتَلَى بِالْعِشْقِ أَحَدٌ إلَّا لِنَقْصِ تَوْحِيدِهِ وَإِيمَانِهِ وَإِلَّا فَالْقَلْبُ الْمُنِيبُ إلَى اللَّهِ الْخَائِفُ مِنْهُ فِيهِ صَارِفَانِ يَصْرِفَانِ عَنْ الْعِشْقِ:
 (أَحَدُهُمَا إنَابَتُهُ إلَى اللَّهِ وَمَحَبَّتُهُ لَهُ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ أَلَذُّ وَأَطْيَبُ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ فَلَا تَبْقَى مَعَ مَحَبَّةِ اللَّهِ مَحَبَّةُ مَخْلُوقٍ تُزَاحِمُهُ.
translated_text:
Thus Allah, glorified be He, created His servants with an innate disposition to love and worship Him alone. If that disposition remains uncorrupted, the heart knows Allah, loves Him, and worships Him alone. Yet a person’s innate disposition becomes corrupted through the sickness afflicting him—as when his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. All these things alter the innate disposition with which he was created, even though they occur by Allah’s decree and predestination—just as the body is altered by mutilation. He may then return to his innate disposition if Allah Most High provides someone who strives to restore him to it. The messengers, may Allah bless them and grant them peace, were sent to affirm and perfect the innate disposition, not to change or transform it. When the heart loves Allah alone and devotes its religion sincerely to Him, it is not afflicted with love for anyone else at all, let alone passionate infatuation. Whenever it is afflicted with infatuation, this is due to its deficient love for Allah alone.

Thus Joseph, who loved Allah and devoted his religion sincerely to Him, was not afflicted with this. Rather, Allah Most High said:

“Thus We turned evil and indecency away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

The minister’s wife, however, was a polytheist, as were her people; hence she was afflicted with infatuation. No one is afflicted with infatuation except because of a deficiency in his affirmation of Allah’s oneness and his faith. By contrast, the heart that turns to Allah and fears Him has two things that turn it away from infatuation:

(The first is its turning to Allah and its love for Him. This is sweeter and more delightful than anything else, so alongside love for Allah, no love for a created being remains to compete with it.

translated_text:
And the second is its fear of Allah, for fear, which opposes infatuation, dispels it. Whoever loves something, whether with passionate infatuation or otherwise, is turned away from loving it by love for something dearer to him, when the two compete. He is also turned away from loving it by fear of suffering harm that he finds more hateful than relinquishing that love. Thus, when Allah is dearer to a servant than everything else, and feared by him more than anything else, neither infatuation nor any competing love arises, except during heedlessness or when this love and fear weaken through neglecting some obligations and committing some forbidden acts. For faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience. Whenever a servant obeys Allah out of love and fear of Him, and refrains from disobedience out of love and fear of Him, his love and fear of Allah grow stronger, removing from his heart love and fear of others.

The same applies to bodily illnesses. Health is preserved by what is like it, and illness is repelled by its opposite. Likewise, the heart’s health through faith is preserved by what is like it: beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds that bring faith to the heart. These nourish it, as in the report of Ibn Mas‘ūd, transmitted both as a saying traced back to the Prophet and as a statement of Ibn Mas‘ūd himself:

“Every host loves to have people attend his banquet, and Allah’s banquet is the Quran.”

The word ādib means a host; thus, the Quran is Allah’s hospitality to His servants . . . (1).

such as the latter part of the night, the times of the call to prayer and the call announcing its commencement, during one’s prostration, and at the close of the prayers. Seeking forgiveness should be added to this, for whoever seeks Allah’s forgiveness and then repents to Him, He will grant him a good enjoyment of life until an appointed term.

translated_text:
And let him adopt a regular portion of “words of remembrance” to recite during the day and at bedtime. Let him patiently endure whatever obstacles and distractions arise, for before long Allah will strengthen him with a spirit from Him and inscribe faith in his heart. Let him strive to perform the five obligatory prayers fully, inwardly and outwardly, for they are the pillar of religion. Let his constant refrain be, “There is no might nor power except with Allah,” for through it burdens are borne, terrors endured, and lofty spiritual states attained.

Let him never tire of supplication and asking, for a servant’s supplication is answered so long as he does not grow impatient and say, “I have supplicated again and again, but I have received no answer.” Let him know that victory comes with patience, relief with distress, and ease with hardship. No one, whether a prophet or anyone below him, has ever attained any share in the culmination of goodness except through patience.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. To Him belong all praise and gratitude for Islam and the Sunnah—praise commensurate with His outward and inward blessings, and befitting His noble Face and His sublime majesty. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, his Companions, his wives—the Mothers of the Believers—and those who follow them in righteousness until the Day of Judgment, and grant them abundant peace.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah bless our Prophet Muhammad and his Companions and grant them peace.

Section: The Heart’s Illness and Its Cure

We have explained in several places that human well-being lies in justice, just as human corruption lies in injustice. Allah, glorified be He, gave man balance and proportion when He created him. His bodily health and well-being arise from the balance of his humours and organs, whereas illness consists in deviation and imbalance. Likewise, the heart’s uprightness, balance, moderation, health, well-being, and soundness are inseparable.

Allah has mentioned “the illness of hearts and their healing” in several places in His Book, and this also appears in the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For example, Allah Most High says of the hypocrites:

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease.”

He says:

“So you see those in whose hearts is a disease rushing to join them.”

Allah Most High says:

“And heal the hearts of a believing people,”

“And remove the anger from their hearts.”

He says:

“There has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the hearts.”

Allah Most High says:

“We send down of the Quran that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers.”

Allah Most High says:

“Say: For those who believe, it is guidance and healing.”

Allah Most High says:

“Do not be soft in speech, lest someone whose heart is diseased should desire you.”

He says:

“If the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and those who spread rumours in Medina do not desist, We will surely incite you against them.”

He says:

“And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said: ‘Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for ignorance is simply to ask.”

Al-Rashīd said: “Now you have cured me, Mālik.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said:

“A person continues to fare well so long as he fears Allah and, whenever he is unsure about the meaning of something, asks someone who dispels his uncertainty. Yet soon he will find no such person—by Him besides whom there is no god.”

What Allah mentions concerning the illness of hearts and their healing is comparable to what He mentions concerning their death

translated_text:
and their life, hearing, sight, understanding, deafness, muteness, and blindness.

But our purpose here is to understand the illness of the heart. We therefore say:

Illness is of two kinds: impairment of sensation, and impairment of natural movement and the voluntary movement associated with it. The loss of either faculty brings pain and suffering. Just as sound sensation and sound voluntary and natural movement bring pleasure and well-being, their impairment brings pain and suffering.

Thus, blessings are a form of bliss: they are the favors Allah bestows upon His servants that bring pleasure and bliss. He says:

“On that Day you will surely be questioned about your blessings.”

That is, about showing gratitude for them. Pleasure arises from sensing what is agreeable, and pain arises from sensing what is disagreeable. Pleasure and pain are not sensation and perception themselves; rather, they are their result and fruit, their purpose and ultimate end.

Illness inevitably involves pain, even though that pain may sometimes subside because of a stronger counteracting factor. Its underlying cause remains present, and the slightest trigger can stir it. Thus, illness necessarily involves the presence of a cause of pain; the pain subsides only when a stronger counteracting factor is present. The heart’s pleasure and pain are greater than the body’s pleasure and pain—I mean its psychological pain and pleasure

although it may also experience the kind of pain that physical illness causes in the rest of the body—that, however, is a separate matter. Thus, the heart’s illness and its healing are of greater consequence than bodily illness and its healing. At times, its illness consists of doubts.

As He says:

“so that one in whose heart is disease is moved to desire.”

Likewise, al-Kharā’itī composed The Book of Hearts Afflicted by Passions. The hearts of the hypocrites suffer illness in both respects: corruption of beliefs and corruption of desires.

The person who has been wronged also has an illness in his heart: the pain caused by another’s injustice toward him. When he receives his due in full, his heart is healed, as Allah Most High says:

“and heal the hearts of a believing people”

“and remove the anger from their hearts.”

The heart’s anger serves to repel harm and pain. Once the harm has been repelled and the person has received his due in full, his anger subsides.

When a person can no longer hear with his ears, see with his eyes, or speak with his tongue, this is a painful illness that deprives him of benefits and exposes him to harm. Likewise, when he cannot hear or see with his heart, distinguish truth from falsehood, or discern good from evil and error from right guidance, this is among the gravest illnesses and pains of his heart.

Similarly, when he craves something harmful, such as excessive food through an all-consuming appetite, or eating clay and the like, this is an illness. He suffers until his pain is relieved

abstain from harmful things or persevere with unpleasant medicines, because this affords them some immediate relief and pleasure. Yet it brings them immense pain afterward or hastens their death.

So too are the children of Adam ignorant, wronging themselves. Each hastens toward what pleasure makes enticing and shuns what his soul dislikes, in ways that are not good for him. This brings them pain and punishment, either in this world or in the Hereafter, involving terrible torment and the greatest ruin.

“Piety” means protecting oneself from what is harmful by doing what is beneficial. Abstaining from harm necessarily entails making use of what is beneficial. Yet someone may make use of what is beneficial while also making use of what is harmful, and thus not be among the pious. As for dispensing with both the harmful and the beneficial, this is impossible: when a person cannot take nourishment, his body feeds on the substances already within it, which harm him until he perishes.

This is why the good outcome belongs to piety and the pious: they protect themselves from what harms them, so their ultimate outcome is Islam and honor. They may initially experience pain from taking the medicine and abstaining from harm, as when performing righteous deeds they find disagreeable. As He, Most High, says:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate something that is good for you, and perhaps you love something that is bad for you.”

And because there are so many wrongful deeds that are desired, as He, Most High, says:

“But as for the one who feared standing before

his Lord and restrained his soul from desire, Paradise will indeed be his refuge.”

And as He says:

“You wished that the unarmed group would be yours.”

As for someone who does not abstain from harmful things, this will cause him harm in the end. Someone who takes what benefits him, despite some dietary indiscretion, is better off than someone who observes complete abstinence and consumes nothing in secret. Complete abstinence without nourishment causes illness. The same applies to someone who abandons bad deeds but does no good deeds.

We have already explained in a “comprehensive discussion” that good deeds, as a whole, are more beneficial than refraining from bad deeds, as is likewise the case with nourishment and abstinence. We explained that the former is sought for its own sake, whereas the latter is sought for the sake of something else, in conjunction with it.

Just as one must avoid the cause of illness before it occurs and remove it once it has occurred, so too, with illnesses of the heart, one must preserve health from the outset and continue restoring it whenever illness arises. Health is maintained through what resembles it, while illness is removed through its opposite. Thus, the heart’s health is preserved by employing things akin to what it already contains, or whatever strengthens knowledge and faith, such as remembrance, reflection, and prescribed acts of worship. It is lost through their opposites. Thus, doubts are removed by clear proofs, and love of falsehood is removed by hatred of it and love of the truth.

For this reason, Yahyā ibn ‘Ammār said:

“Knowledge is of five kinds. One kind gives life to this world: knowledge of Allah’s oneness. Another nourishes religion: knowledge concerned with recalling the meanings of the Quran and hadith. Another is a remedy for religion: knowledge of issuing religious rulings. When a person faces a difficult case, he needs someone who

can cure him of it, as Ibn Mas‘ūd said. Another kind is a disease of religion: newly introduced speculative theology. Another brings about the destruction of religion: knowledge of sorcery and the like.”

Thus, health is preserved through what is akin to it, and illness is removed through its opposite. This applies both to physical ailments of the body and to ailments of the heart concerning the soul, religion, and the revealed Law. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to an animal with all its limbs intact. Do you see any among them born mutilated?”

Abū Hurayra would then say: “Recite, if you wish: ‘The natural disposition Allah has instilled in mankind.’”

It is recorded in the two Sahīh collections. Allah Most High says:

“To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.”

“And He is the One who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him. His is the highest description in the heavens and the earth.”

Further on, He says:

“Rather, the wrongdoers follow their desires without knowledge.”

And further on:

“So set your face towards the religion, inclining to truth—the natural disposition Allah has instilled in mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.”

He thus tells us that He created His servants with an innate disposition to turn their faces towards the religion, inclining to truth—that is, to worship Allah alone, without any partner. This is among the heart’s innate, natural, upright, and balanced inclinations. Abandoning it is a tremendous wrong, whose perpetrators follow their desires without knowledge. This innate disposition and constitution—which is a sound constitution—must have sustenance and nourishment to replenish it with knowledge and action akin to those with which it was naturally endowed.

Thus, religion reaches completion through the innate disposition being perfected by the revealed Law. This Law is Allah’s banquet, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith of Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“Indeed, every host wishes that

his banquet be attended, and Allah’s banquet is the Quran.” It is like water that Allah sends down from heaven, as it is portrayed in the Book and the Sunnah. Those who distort the natural disposition and turn the heart away from its uprightness cause hearts to become sick and diseased. Allah has sent down His Book as a healing for what is in the hearts.

The calamities that befall the believer in this world are like the pains that afflict the body, through which it regains health and is rid of its corrupt humours. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No illness, fatigue, worry, sorrow, distress, or harm befalls a believer—even the prick of a thorn—without Allah expiating his sins thereby.”

This is a fulfilment of His words:

“Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it.”

If a person is not purified of these diseases in this world so as to return in sound health, he will need to be purified of them in the Hereafter, and Allah will punish him. He is like someone whose corrupt humours have accumulated within him and who has taken no medicine to reduce them: they continue to accumulate until they destroy him. Hence the report:

“When people say of a sick person, ‘O Allah, have mercy on him,’ Allah says, ‘How am I to have mercy on him by removing the very thing through which I show him mercy?’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Illness is an expiation: it sheds the sins of the afflicted person just as a dry tree sheds its leaves.”

Just as there are bodily illnesses from which a person may die as a martyr—as in the case of someone who dies of plague, an abdominal disease, or pleurisy, and likewise someone who dies by drowning, burning, or a collapsing building—so too among

illnesses of the soul are some whose sufferer, if he fears his Lord and patiently endures them until death, is a martyr. Such is the coward who fears Allah and remains steadfast in battle until he is killed. Miserliness and cowardice are illnesses of the soul: yielding to either brings a person pain, while resisting it also causes him pain, as with bodily illnesses.

The same applies to passionate love, for it has been related:

“Whoever falls passionately in love, remains chaste, conceals his love, and patiently endures, then dies, dies a martyr.”

It is an illness of the soul that urges a person toward what harms his soul, just as illness urges a sick person to consume what harms him. If he yields to his desire, his torment increases greatly in the Hereafter and in this world as well. But if he resists his desire by remaining chaste and concealing his love, his soul suffers pain and sickness. If he dies from that illness, he is a martyr. This passion urges him toward the Fire, but he restrains it, just as the coward’s soul holds him back from Paradise, yet he drives it forward.

When accompanied by faith and fear of Allah, these illnesses are as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described:

“Allah decrees nothing for the believer but that it is good for him. If prosperity comes to him and he gives thanks, it is good for him; and if adversity befalls him and he remains patient, it is good for him.”

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon our master Muhammad, all his family, and all his Companions.

The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

“O mankind, worship your Lord.”

What is worship, and what are its branches? Does it encompass the whole religion or not? What is the true nature of servitude to Allah? Is it the highest spiritual station in this world and the Hereafter, or is there any station above it? Please explain this to us in detail.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

“Worship” is a comprehensive term for everything Allah loves and is pleased with, whether words or deeds, inward or outward. Thus, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, truthful speech, fulfilling trusts, dutifulness to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, honouring covenants, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, striving against the disbelievers and hypocrites, kindness to neighbours, orphans, the needy, travellers, and the slaves and animals one owns, supplication, remembrance of Allah, recitation of the Quran, and similar acts are all forms of worship.

Likewise, love for Allah and His Messenger, reverent fear of Allah, turning to Him in repentance, sincere devotion to Him alone, patiently submitting to His judgement, gratitude for His blessings, contentment with His decree, and reliance upon Him;

and hope for His mercy, fear of His punishment, and the like are all forms of worship of Allah.

This is because worshipping Allah is the purpose He loves and is pleased with, for which He created all beings. As He, Most High, said:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

With this message He sent all the messengers, as Noah said to his people:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

Hūd, Sālih, Shuʿayb and others likewise addressed their peoples. Allah, Most High, said:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying, ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’ Among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom misguidance became established.”

And He, Most High, said:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no god but Me, so worship Me.’”

And He, Most High, said:

“Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.”

As He said in the other verse:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I know well what you do.”

He made this binding upon His Messenger until death, saying:

“Worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.”

He also described His angels and prophets as worshippers, saying:

“To Him belong all who are in the heavens and the earth. Those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they grow weary.”

“They glorify Him night and day, without ceasing.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Indeed, those who are near your Lord are not too proud to worship Him. They glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.”

He condemned those too proud to worship Him, saying: “And said

your Lord: ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated.’”

He described the choicest of His creation as His servants, saying, Most High:

“A spring from which Allah’s servants drink, causing it to flow abundantly.”

And He said:

“The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk humbly upon the earth,”

and the subsequent verses.

When Satan said:

“He said, ‘My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil alluring to them on earth and mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them,’”

Allah, Most High, said:

“Indeed, you will have no authority over My servants, except those of the misguided who follow you.”

He described the angels in the same terms, saying:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a child.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants. They do not speak before He speaks, and they act at His command,”

up to His words:

“And they stand in awe of Him.”

And He, Most High, said:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a child.’ You have indeed made a monstrous claim. The heavens almost rupture at it, the earth splits apart, and the mountains collapse in devastation, because they attribute a child to the Most Merciful. It is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a child. There is no one in the heavens and the earth who will not come to the Most Merciful as a servant. “Do not lavish excessive praise on me as the Christians did on Jesus

“Glory be to Him who took His servant by night.”

Thus, Allah’s religion consists of worshipping Him, obeying Him and submitting to Him.

translated_text:
And the basic meaning of “worship” is likewise humility. A path is called mu‘abbad (well-trodden) when it has been worn smooth underfoot. Yet the worship that is commanded encompasses both humility and love: it entails the utmost humility before Allah together with the utmost love for Him. The final degree of love is “consummation.” Its first degree is “attachment,” because the heart becomes attached to the beloved; then comes “yearning,” because the heart pours itself towards the beloved; then “abiding love,” which remains firmly in the heart; then “passionate love”; and finally “consummation.” The expression Taym Allāh means “Allah’s servant”; thus, one utterly enamoured is enslaved to his beloved.

Whoever submits to someone while hating him is not worshipping him. Likewise, someone who loves something without submitting to it is not worshipping it, as with the love one may have for one’s child or friend. Hence, neither love nor humility alone suffices in worshipping Allah Most High. Rather, Allah must be dearer to His servant than everything else, and greater in his estimation than everything else. Indeed, none but Allah deserves perfect love and utter humility. Whatever is loved for other than Allah’s sake is loved in a corrupt manner, and whatever is venerated without Allah’s command is venerated falsely.

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your clan, wealth you have acquired, trade whose decline you fear, and homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.’”

Love, in its general sense, may therefore be directed to Allah and His Messenger, as may obedience; for obedience is due to Allah and His Messenger

and Allah and His Messenger are to be pleased:

“Allah and His Messenger have a greater right that they should seek His pleasure.”

Giving, too, is attributed to Allah and His Messenger:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them.”

As for “worship” and related acts, such as reliance, fear, and the like, these are for Allah alone, as He Most High says:

“Say, ‘O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is common between us and you: that we worship none but Allah and associate nothing with Him’”—up to His words: “But if they turn away, then say, ‘Bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

He Most High also says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn with longing.’”

Thus, giving is attributed to Allah and the Messenger, as in His words:

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.”

As for sufficiency, it is Allah alone who suffices, as He Most High says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

He Most High also says:

“O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for those believers who follow you.”

That is, Allah is sufficient for you and sufficient for those who follow you. Whoever supposes that the meaning is, “Allah, together with the believers, is sufficient for you,” has made a grave error, as we have explained at length elsewhere. He Most High also says:

“Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?”

To explain this precisely: the word “servant” may mean “one brought into subjection”—one whom Allah has subjected and humbled, and whose affairs He has governed

and whose course He has directed. In this sense, all created beings are Allah’s servants: the righteous and the wicked, the believers and the disbelievers, and the people of Paradise and the people of Hell. For He is the Lord and Sovereign of them all. They cannot escape His will, His power, or His perfect words, which neither the righteous nor the wicked can overstep. Whatever He wills comes to pass, even if they do not will it; and whatever they will, if He does not will it, does not come to pass. As He Most High says:

“Do they seek a religion other than Allah’s, when all those in the heavens and the earth have submitted to Him, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?”

He, glorified is He, is the Lord of all worlds, their Creator and Provider, the One who gives them life and causes them to die, turns their hearts, and directs their affairs. They have no Lord but Him, no Owner besides Him, and no Creator except Him, whether they acknowledge this or deny it, and whether they know it or are ignorant of it. The believers among them, however, know and acknowledge this, unlike those who are ignorant of it, or who deny it and arrogantly defy their Lord, neither acknowledging nor submitting to Him, despite knowing that Allah is their Lord and Creator.

Knowledge of the truth, when accompanied by an arrogant refusal to accept it and by denial of it, becomes a source of torment for the one who possesses it. As He Most High says:

“They denied them, though their souls were certain of them, out of injustice and arrogance. So see what was the end of those who spread corruption.”

He Most High also says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their own sons. Yet a group of them knowingly conceal the truth.”

He Most High also says:

“It is not you they disbelieve; rather, it is Allah’s signs that the wrongdoers reject.”

Thus, if a servant acknowledges that Allah is his Lord and Creator, and that he is dependent upon Him and in need of Him, he understands servitude as it relates to Allah’s lordship. This servant asks his Lord, humbly implores Him, and relies upon Him. Yet he may obey His command or disobey it; despite this acknowledgment, he may worship Him, or he may worship Satan and idols. Such servitude does not distinguish the people of Paradise from the people of Hell, nor does it make a person a believer. As He Most High says:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating partners with Him.”

The polytheists acknowledged that Allah was their Creator and Provider, yet they worshipped others besides Him. He Most High says:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’”

He Most High also says:

“Say, ‘To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?’ They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then take heed?’”

And so on, until His words:

“Say, ‘How, then, are you deluded?’”

Many of those who speak of reality and witness it are witnessing this reality, namely the “reality of the created order.” Believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, alike share in this reality, in witnessing it, and in knowing it. And he said:

Had they been guided, they would have known that we are commanded to be content with divine decree and patiently endure its consequences in the calamities that befall us, such as poverty, illness, and fear. Allah Most High says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

One of the early Muslims said: “This is a man whom calamity strikes, who knows that it is from Allah and so is content and submits.” Allah Most High also says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves without being recorded in a Book before We bring it into being. That is certainly easy for Allah.”

“So that you neither grieve over what you have missed nor exult over what He has given you.”

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said, ‘You are Adam, whom Allah created with His hand, into whom He breathed of His spirit, before whom He made His angels prostrate, and whom He taught the names of all things. Why, then, did you bring us and yourself out of Paradise?’

“Adam said, ‘You are Moses, whom Allah chose to bear His message and to whom He spoke. Did you find that this had been written concerning me before I was created?’

“He replied, ‘Yes.’”

The Prophet said, “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in the argument.”

Adam, peace be upon him, did not appeal to divine decree in his argument with Moses on the assumption that a sinner may plead divine decree as an excuse. No Muslim or rational person would say this. Were it an excuse, it would also excuse Satan, the people of Noah, the people of Hūd, and every disbeliever. Nor did Moses blame Adam for the sin itself, for Adam had repented to his Lord, who then chose him and guided him. Rather, he blamed him for the calamity that had befallen them because of that sin. This is why he said, “Why, then, did you bring us and yourself out of Paradise?” Adam answered that this had been written before he was created. Thus, both the deed and the calamity resulting from it had been decreed. One must submit to whatever calamities have been decreed, for this is part of being fully content with Allah as one’s Lord.

As for sins, Allah’s servant has no right to commit them. If he does sin, he must seek forgiveness and repent. Thus, he repents of his faults and patiently endures calamities. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient. Surely Allah’s promise is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin.”

Allah Most High also says:

“If you are patient and mindful of Allah, their schemes will not harm you at all.”

And He says:

“If you are patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed a matter requiring firm resolve.”

Joseph said:

“Indeed, whoever is mindful of Allah and patient—Allah never lets the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

Likewise, regarding the sins of others, a person must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong—to the best of his ability—strive in Allah’s cause against the disbelievers and hypocrites, be loyal to Allah’s allies and oppose Allah’s enemies, and love for Allah’s sake and hate for Allah’s sake. “O you who believe, do not take My enemies and your enemies

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.”

“Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

“Shall We then treat those who submit to Us like the criminals?”

He is therefore told: If divine decree is a valid excuse, then let everyone do whatever they wish to you and to others. If it is not an excuse, your fundamental claim that it is an excuse collapses.

Those who hold this view and invoke the “reality of the created order” do not apply their position consistently or abide by it. Rather, they follow their own opinions and desires. As one scholar said of them: “When it comes to obedience, you are a Qadarī (advocate of free will), and when it comes to sin, you are a Jabrī (advocate of compulsion). Whichever doctrine suits your desires, you adopt it.”

Among them is a “group” who claim spiritual realization and gnosis. They allege that commands and prohibitions bind only those who perceive themselves as acting and attribute deeds to themselves. As for someone who witnesses that his actions are created, or that he is compelled to perform them, and that Allah directs him just as all other moving things are moved, commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment no longer apply to him.

They may also say that whoever witnesses “the divine will” is no longer subject to religious obligation. One of them claims that al-Khidr was released from religious obligation because he witnessed the divine will. Thus, these people make no distinction between ordinary people and the elect who have witnessed the reality of the created order, witnessing that Allah creates His servants’ actions and governs all existing things. They may distinguish between someone who knows this intellectually and someone who perceives it through direct witnessing. They therefore do not regard religious obligation as lifted from someone who merely believes and knows this, but only from someone who

witnesses it directly and therefore sees no action as his own whatsoever. These people do not regard compulsion and the affirmation of divine decree, as such, as precluding religious obligation. Groups claiming spiritual realization, gnosis, and affirmation of Allah’s oneness have fallen into this error.

The reason is that they could not accommodate the notion that a servant may be commanded to do something while its opposite is decreed for him, just as the Muʿtazilah and similar Qadarī groups could not accommodate it. The Muʿtazilah affirmed religious commands and prohibitions but denied divine ordainment and decree—that is, Allah’s all-encompassing will and His creation of His servants’ actions. These people, by contrast, affirmed divine ordainment and decree but denied that commands and prohibitions apply to those who witness divine decree, since they could not deny them altogether.

Their position is worse than that of the Muʿtazilah; hence none of the early generations held it. These people consider commands and prohibitions applicable to those who remain veiled and have not witnessed this reality of the created order. They therefore hold that whoever attains the witnessing of this reality is no longer bound by commands and prohibitions and has become one of the elect. They sometimes interpret the words of the Most High accordingly:

“And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.”

They take certainty to mean knowledge of this reality. Their position is explicit disbelief, even though some groups have fallen into it without knowing that it is disbelief. For it is necessarily known in the religion of Islam that commands and prohibitions remain binding upon every servant as long as he retains his reason

Such doctrines have become widespread among later generations, whereas they were not known among the earlier generations of this community. In this respect, he is like someone who believes that prayer is not obligatory for him because the spiritual states he has attained in his heart make him independent of it; or that wine is lawful for him because he belongs to the elect, whom drinking wine does not harm; or that sexual immorality is lawful for him because he has become like the sea, which sins cannot sully; and other such beliefs.

There is no doubt that the polytheists who rejected the messengers waver between innovations contrary to Allah’s revealed law and invoking divine decree to justify disobeying Allah’s commands. Thus, these groups

resemble the polytheists: they either introduce religious innovations, invoke divine decree to justify their actions, or combine the two.

As Allah Most High says of the polytheists:

“When they commit an indecency, they say, ‘We found our fathers doing this, and Allah has commanded us to do it.’ Say, ‘Allah does not command indecency. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?’”

And as He, Most High, says of them:

“Those who associate partners with Allah will say, ‘Had Allah willed, neither we nor our fathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.’”

translated_text:
These people may call the religious innovations they have introduced “reality,” just as they call what they witness of divine decree “reality.” For them, the path of reality is a spiritual course whose follower is governed not by the Lawgiver’s commands and prohibitions, but by what he perceives, tastes inwardly, feels, and the like. These people do not invoke divine decree without qualification; rather, their mainstay is following their own opinions and desires. They designate what they perceive and desire as reality and command others to follow it instead of following the commands of Allah and His Messenger. This resembles the innovations of the speculative theologians—the Jahmiyyah and others—who treat the doctrines they have invented, contrary to the Quran and Sunnah, as rational truths that must be believed rather than what the revealed texts indicate.

They then either distort the Quran and Sunnah from their proper meaning or turn away from them altogether, neither reflecting upon them nor understanding them. Instead, they say, “We consign their meaning to Allah,” while believing the opposite of what they signify. When their supposed rational truths that contradict the Quran and Sunnah are subjected to scrutiny, they prove to be ignorant notions and corrupt beliefs. Likewise, when the others’ supposed realities of Allah’s friends, which contradict the Quran and Sunnah, are scrutinized, they prove to be desires followed by Allah’s enemies, not His friends.

The root of anyone’s misguidance lies in giving precedence to his own analogical reasoning over the text revealed by Allah, and in choosing desire over obedience to Allah’s commands. For inward taste, feeling, and similar experiences correspond to what a person loves: everyone who loves something has a taste and feeling proportionate to that love.

Thus, the people of faith experience inward taste and feeling of the kind explained by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the authentic hadith:

“Three qualities—whoever possesses them will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than

anyone else; that he loves a person only for Allah’s sake; and that he would hate to return to disbelief after Allah has saved him from it as much as he would hate to be cast into the Fire.” He, peace and blessings be upon him, also said in an authentic hadith:

“He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet.”

As for the people of disbelief, religious innovation, and lust, each experiences this according to his own condition. Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah was asked, “Why are people who follow deviant inclinations so deeply attached to them?” He replied, “Have you forgotten His words, Most High: ‘Because of their disbelief, their hearts were steeped in love of the calf’?”—or words to that effect.

Idol worshippers love their gods, as Allah Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

He also says:

“If they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desires without guidance from Allah?”

And He says:

“They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, although guidance has come to them from their Lord.”

This is why these people are drawn to listening to poetry and vocal performances that stir love in general—a love not exclusive to the people of faith, but shared by those who love the Most Merciful, idols, crosses, homelands, companions, beardless youths, or women. These are the people who follow their inward tastes and feelings without assessing them against the Quran, the Sunnah, and the way of the early generations of the Muslim community.

Anyone who departs from what Allah sent His Messenger with—worshipping and obeying Him and obeying His Messenger—is not following a religion prescribed by Allah. As He, Most High, says:

“Then We set you upon a clear way in matters of religion, so follow it

and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.”

“They will be of no avail to you against Allah,” up to His words: “And Allah is the Protector of the righteous.”

Rather, such a person follows his own desires without guidance from Allah. Allah Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

In this, they sometimes follow an innovation that they call a spiritual reality, giving it precedence over what Allah has prescribed. At other times, they invoke Allah’s decree governing creation to oppose His revealed law, as Allah has related concerning the polytheists, as mentioned earlier.

Among these people is a group who rank highest among them. They adhere to the religion by performing its well-known obligations and avoiding its well-known prohibitions. Yet they err by abandoning the means they have been commanded to pursue that are themselves acts of worship. They suppose that once a person of spiritual knowledge witnesses “the divine decree,” he turns away from such things. For example, some of them regard reliance upon Allah, supplication, and similar practices as spiritual stations for ordinary people, not the elect. This rests on the notion that whoever witnesses the divine decree knows that whatever has been decreed will come to pass, so there is no need for such practices. This is a grave error.

Allah has decreed things together with the means that bring them about, just as He has decreed felicity and wretchedness together with their means. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah created people for Paradise. He created it for them while they were still in their fathers’ loins, and they perform the deeds of the people of Paradise.”

Likewise, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed them that Allah had written down all that was decreed, they asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, should we not then abandon deeds and rely on what has been written?”

He replied:

“No. Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Whoever is among the people of felicity will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of felicity, and whoever is among the people of wretchedness will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of wretchedness.”

Thus, the means that Allah has commanded His servants to pursue are themselves acts of worship. Reliance upon Allah is coupled with worship, as in His words:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And His words:

“Say, ‘He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.’”

And the words of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him:

“In Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn.”

Among them are some who may abandon recommended deeds, though not obligatory ones, and thus fall short to that extent. Others are deluded by extraordinary occurrences they experience, such as spiritual unveilings, prayers answered in ways that depart from the ordinary course of events, and similar things. These distract them from the worship, gratitude, and other duties they have been commanded to observe. Such things frequently befall those pursuing the spiritual path and turning towards Allah. A servant escapes them only by adhering at all times to Allah’s command, with which He sent His Messenger.

As al-Zuhrī said:

“Those of our predecessors who came before us used to say, ‘Holding fast to the Sunnah is salvation.’”

For the Sunnah—as Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said—is like Noah’s ark: whoever boards it is saved, and whoever stays behind drowns.

Worship, obedience, uprightness, adherence to the straight path, and similar expressions all convey the same meaning, and they have two foundations:

{وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ دِينًا مِمَّنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ وَاتَّبَعَ مِلَّةَ إبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفًا وَاتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ إبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا}
 فَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ هُوَ الْإِحْسَانُ وَهُوَ فِعْلُ الْحَسَنَاتِ. و 
" الْحَسَنَاتُ "
 هِيَ مَا أَحَبَّهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَهُوَ مَا أَمَرَ بِهِ أَمْرَ إيجَابٍ أَوْ اسْتِحْبَابٍ فَمَا كَانَ مِنْ الْبِدَعِ فِي الدِّينِ الَّتِي لَيْسَتْ مَشْرُوعَةً فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّهَا وَلَا رَسُولُهُ فَلَا تَكُونُ مِنْ الْحَسَنَاتِ وَلَا مِنْ الْعَمَلِ الصَّالِحِ كَمَا أَنَّ مَنْ يَعْمَلُ مَا لَا يَجُوزُ كَالْفَوَاحِشِ وَالظُّلْمِ لَيْسَ مِنْ الْحَسَنَاتِ وَلَا مِنْ الْعَمَلِ الصَّالِحِ. وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُ. 
{وَلَا يُشْرِكْ بِعِبَادَةِ رَبِّهِ أَحَدًا}
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ}
 فَهُوَ إخْلَاصُ الدِّينِ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ وَكَانَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ يَقُولُ: اللَّهُمَّ اجْعَلْ عَمَلِي كُلَّهُ صَالِحًا وَاجْعَلْهُ لِوَجْهِكَ خَالِصًا وَلَا تَجْعَلْ لِأَحَدِ فِيهِ شَيْئًا.
 وَقَالَ الْفُضَيْل بْنُ عِيَاضٍ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{لِيَبْلُوَكُمْ أَيُّكُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا}
 قَالَ: أَخْلَصُهُ وَأَصْوَبُهُ قَالُوا: يَا أَبَا عَلِيٍّ مَا أَخْلَصُهُ وَأَصْوَبُهُ؟
 قَالَ:
translated_text:
the first is that none but Allah should be worshipped; the second is that He should be worshipped through what He has commanded and prescribed, not through innovations.

Allah Most High says:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

And He says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

And He says:

“And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while doing good and follows the religion of Abraham, upright in faith? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

Righteous action means doing good—that is, performing good deeds. “Good deeds” are those that Allah and His Messenger love: whatever He has commanded as obligatory or recommended. Religious innovations that have not been prescribed are loved neither by Allah nor by His Messenger, so they are neither good deeds nor righteous actions. Likewise, committing forbidden acts, such as indecencies and injustice, is neither a good deed nor a righteous action.

As for His words:

“And associate no one in the worship of his Lord,”

and His words:

“Submits himself to Allah,”

these mean devoting one’s religion sincerely to Allah alone. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to say: “O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your sake, and give no one else any share in them.”

Regarding His words:

“To test you as to which of you is best in deeds,”

al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said: “The most sincere and the most correct.” They asked: “Abū ‘Alī, what does ‘the most sincere and the most correct’ mean?” He replied:

“If a deed is sincere but not correct, it will not be accepted. If it is correct but not sincere, it will not be accepted, until it is both sincere and correct. Sincerity means that it is done for Allah, and correctness means that it accords with the Sunnah.”

If it is asked: Since everything Allah loves falls within the meaning of worship, why are other things mentioned alongside it, as in His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

and His words:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him,”

and the words of Noah:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me,”

and similar statements by other messengers?

The answer is that there are parallels to this, as in His words:

“Indeed, prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing.”

Indecency is itself a form of wrongdoing. Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, doing good, and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

Giving to relatives is part of justice and doing good, just as indecency and oppression are forms of wrongdoing.

Likewise, He says:

“And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer.”

Establishing prayer is among the greatest ways of holding fast to the Book.

Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear.”

Their calling upon Him in hope and fear is itself among those good deeds. There are many such examples in the Quran.

Sometimes, in this type of expression, one thing is included within the other but is mentioned alongside it to single it out for special mention, since it is required both under the general meaning and in its own specific capacity. At other times, a term’s scope varies depending on whether it occurs alone or alongside another term: when used alone, its meaning is general; when paired with another, its meaning is specific. Examples are the terms “poor” and “needy”: when

either is used alone, as in His words:

“For the poor who are restricted in the cause of Allah,”

and His words:

“Its expiation is to feed ten needy people,”

the other is included within its meaning. But when they are mentioned together in His words:

“Alms are only for the poor and the needy,”

they denote two distinct categories.

It has been said that when a specific term is mentioned alongside a general term, it is not included within the general term in that context; rather, this falls into the category just described. The correct view, however, is that this is not necessarily so. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael,”

and He says:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

A specific term may be mentioned alongside a general term for various reasons. Sometimes it possesses a distinctive quality not shared by the other members of the general category, as with Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. At other times, the general term is expressed without qualification, so its comprehensive scope may not be understood, as in His words:

“A guidance for the Allah-fearing,”

“Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them,”

“And who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you.”

His words, “believe in the unseen,” encompass the unseen matters in which belief is obligatory. Yet the expression is general and does not itself indicate that what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you are included among those unseen matters. The intended meaning may also be that they believe both in what is conveyed—the unseen—and in the revelation conveying news of the unseen, namely, what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you.

This category also includes His words, Most High:

“Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish prayer.”

And His words:

“And those who hold firmly to the Book and establish prayer.”

“Reciting the Book” means following it. Thus, concerning His words, Most High:

“Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited,”

Ibn Masʿūd said: “They regard as lawful what it declares lawful, regard as forbidden what it forbids, believe in its ambiguous passages, and act upon its clear passages.” Following the Book therefore encompasses prayer and other acts, but prayer is singled out for mention because of its special merit. Likewise, He said to Moses:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

Establishing prayer in remembrance of Him is among the greatest forms of worshipping Him. The same applies to His words, Most High:

“Fear Allah and speak words that are right.”

And His words:

“Fear Allah and seek the means of drawing near to Him.”

And His words:

“Fear Allah and be with the truthful.”

These things, too, are part of fully observing the fear of Allah. Likewise, He says:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

Reliance upon Allah and seeking His help are themselves part of worshipping Him. Yet they are singled out for mention so that the worshipper makes a deliberate point of practising them, for they provide help in all other forms of worship: He, glorified is He, can only be worshipped with His help.

Once this is clear, a created being’s perfection lies in fully realizing its servitude to Allah. The more fully a servant realizes this servitude, the greater his perfection and the higher his rank. Anyone who imagines that a created being can escape servitude in any respect, or that leaving it behind is a more perfect state, is among the most ignorant and misguided of all creatures.

Allah Most High says:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants.”

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act at His command.”

up to His words:

“and they stand in awe of Him.”

And He, Most High, says:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’”

“You have certainly said a monstrous thing,”

up to His words:

“There is no one in the heavens and the earth who will not come to the Most Merciful as a servant.”

“He has counted them and numbered them precisely.”

“And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone.”

He, Most High, says concerning the Messiah:

“He was only a servant whom We blessed and made an example for the Children of Israel.”

And He, Most High, says:

“To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. Those in His presence are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they grow weary.”

“They glorify Him night and day, never slackening.”

And He, Most High, says:

“The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near to Him. Whoever disdains to worship Him and grows arrogant—He will gather them all to Himself,”

up to His words:

“and they will find no protector or helper besides Allah.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated.’”

And He, Most High, says:

“Among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them, if it is Him that you worship.”

“But if they are too proud, those in the presence of your Lord glorify Him night and day, and never grow weary.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and fearfully,”

up to His words:

“Indeed, those in the presence of your Lord are not too proud to worship Him. They glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.”

These and similar passages, which describe the greatest of created beings as worshipping Him and condemn those who depart from this, occur frequently in the Quran. He has also stated that He sent all the messengers with this message.

Thus He, Most High, says:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no god but Me, so worship Me.’”

And He says:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying: ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’”

He, Most High, says to the Children of Israel:

“O My servants who believe, My earth is spacious, so worship Me alone.”

“And fear Me alone.”

And He says:

“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may become righteous.”

And He says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

He, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘I have been commanded to worship Allah, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.’”

“And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.”

“Say, ‘I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.’”

“Say, ‘It is Allah I worship, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.’”

“So worship whatever you wish besides Him.”

Every messenger began his call by inviting people to worship Allah, as Noah and those who came after him—peace be upon them—said:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

In the Musnad, Ibn ‘Umar reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I was sent with the sword ahead of the Hour, so that Allah alone would be worshipped, with no partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been laid upon whoever opposes my command.”

He has also made it clear that His servants are those who are saved from evil. Satan said:

“My Lord, because You have caused me to go astray, I will surely make evil seem appealing to them on earth, and I will lead them all astray,”

“except Your chosen servants among them.”

He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants, except

those of the misguided who follow you.”

And he said:

“By Your might, I will surely lead them all astray,
except Your chosen servants among them.”

Concerning Joseph, He said:

“Thus it was, so that We might turn evil and indecency away from him. He was indeed one of Our chosen servants.”

And He said:

“Glory be to Allah, far above what they ascribe to Him—except Allah’s chosen servants.”

And He said:

“Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.
His authority is only over those who take him as their ally and those who associate partners with Allah.”

It is as servants that He has described all those He has chosen from His creation, as in His words:

“Remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men of strength and insight.
We distinguished them with a special quality: remembrance of the Hereafter.
Indeed, in Our sight they are among the chosen, the truly good.”

And His words:

“Remember Our servant David, a man of strength; indeed, he constantly turned to Us.”

Of Solomon, He said:

“What an excellent servant! Indeed, he constantly turned to Us.”

And of Job:

“What an excellent servant!”

And He said:

“Remember Our servant Job, when he called upon his Lord.”

And Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“O descendants of those We carried with Noah! Indeed, he was a grateful servant.”

And He said:

“Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.”

And He said:

“When the servant of Allah stood up, calling upon Him.”

And He said:

“If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to Our servant.”

And He said:

“Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed.”

And He said:

“A spring from which the servants of Allah will drink.”

And He said:

“The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk humbly upon the earth.”

There are many such examples throughout the Quran.

Section

Now that this is clear, it is evident that people differ greatly in this regard, reflecting their differing degrees in the reality of faith. In this respect, they fall into general and special categories. Accordingly, the Lord’s lordship over them has both a general and a special aspect. This is why associating partners with Allah within this community is subtler than the creeping of ants.

It is related in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May the slave of the dirham come to ruin! May the slave of the dinar come to ruin! May the slave of plush fabric come to ruin! May the slave of the patterned cloak come to ruin! May he come to ruin and be cast down! If a thorn pricks him, may it not be removed! If he is given something, he is pleased; if he is denied it, he is displeased.”

Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, called him the slave of the dirham, the slave of the dinar, the slave of plush fabric, and the slave of the patterned cloak. He also spoke words containing both an imprecation and a statement:

“May he come to ruin and be cast down! If a thorn pricks him, may it not be removed!”

Naqsh means removing a thorn from the foot, and a minqāsh is the instrument used to remove it. Such is the condition of someone who, when afflicted by harm, neither escapes it nor prospers, having come to ruin and been cast down. He neither attains what he seeks nor escapes what he dislikes. This is the condition of one who worships wealth. He is described as follows:

“When he is given something, he is pleased; when he is denied it, he is displeased.”

As Allah Most High says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the distribution of alms. If

translated_text:
they are given some of it, they are pleased; but if they are given none, they become displeased.” Their pleasure and displeasure are thus for something other than Allah. Such is also the condition of someone attached to a position of authority, an outward form, or any similar object of his own desire: if he obtains it, he is pleased; if he does not, he is displeased. He is therefore the slave of whatever he desires, held in bondage to it. For slavery and servitude are, in reality, the slavery and servitude of the heart. Whatever enslaves and subjugates his heart makes him its slave.

Hence the saying:

“The slave is free so long as he is content, and the free man is a slave so long as he covets.”

A poet said:

“I obeyed my cravings, and they enslaved me;
Had I been content, I would have been free.”

It is also said: “Covetousness is a shackle around the neck and a fetter on the foot. When the shackle leaves the neck, the fetter leaves the foot.”

It is related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Covetousness is poverty, and giving up hope is freedom from need. When any of you gives up hope of something, he no longer needs it.”

A person can recognize this within himself. When he gives up hope of something, he neither seeks nor covets it, nor does he keep his heart dependent upon it or upon whoever might bring it about. But when he covets something and hopes for it, his heart becomes attached to it. He then becomes dependent on obtaining it and on anyone he believes instrumental in securing it. This applies to wealth, prestige, outward forms, and other things. Allah’s close friend, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“So seek provision from Allah, worship Him, and be grateful to Him. To Him you will be returned.”

A servant must have provision and is in need of it. If he seeks his provision from Allah, he becomes Allah’s servant, dependent upon Him; but if he seeks it from a created being, he becomes that being’s servant, dependent upon him. This is why “asking of created beings” is prohibited in principle and is permitted only out of necessity. Many hadiths prohibit it in the Sahīh, Sunan, and Musnad collections, such as the Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“One of you will persist in begging until he comes on the Day of Resurrection without a shred of flesh on his face.”

And his saying:

“Whoever asks people when he has enough to meet his needs will find his asking turned into scratches, claw marks, or gashes on his face on the Day of Resurrection.”

And his saying:

“Begging is not lawful except for someone burdened with an overwhelming debt, anguished weeping, or grinding poverty.”

This meaning is reported in the Sahīh collection. It also contains:

“For one of you to take his rope and go out to gather firewood is better for him than asking people, whether they give to him or refuse him.”

He also said:

“Whatever comes to you of this wealth without your asking for it or eagerly looking for it, take it. Whatever does not come to you, do not let your soul pursue it.”

He thus disapproved of taking it through verbal requests or inward longing. He said in an authentic hadith:

“Whoever seeks to be free of need, Allah will make him free of need; whoever seeks to refrain from asking, Allah will enable him to refrain; whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. No one has been given a gift better or more ample than patience.”

He instructed his closest Companions not to ask people for anything. It is reported in the Musnad:

“When Abū Bakr’s whip fell from his hand, he would not say to anyone, ‘Hand it to me.’ He would say, ‘My close friend instructed me not to ask people for anything.’”

the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, accepted his pledge of allegiance along with a group of others and quietly confided to them: ‘Do not ask people for anything.’ There were men among that group who, if their whip fell from their hand, would not say to anyone, ‘Hand it to me.’”

In numerous places, the scriptural texts command asking the Creator and prohibit asking created beings. For example, Allah Most High says:

“So when you are free, strive hard, and direct your longing to your Lord.”

And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Ibn ‘Abbās:

“When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

Another example is the statement of Abraham, Allah’s close friend:

“So seek from Allah your provision.”

He did not say, “So seek your provision from Allah,” because placing the adverbial phrase first suggests exclusivity and restriction. It is as though he said, “Seek provision from none but Allah.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And ask Allah of His bounty.”

A person must obtain the provision and other things he needs and ward off whatever harms him. In both matters, he is instructed to direct his supplication to Allah. He may ask Allah and bring his complaints to Him, as Jacob, peace be upon him, said:

“I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah.”

Allah Most High mentions in the Quran “gracious withdrawal,” “gracious forgiveness,” and “gracious patience.”

It has been said that gracious withdrawal is withdrawal without causing harm; gracious forgiveness is forgiveness without reproach; and gracious patience is patience without complaining to created beings. “So gracious patience is best.”

He also said:

“I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to recite the surahs Jonah, Joseph, and The Bee in the dawn prayer. When he came to this verse in his recitation, he wept until his sobbing could be heard from the back rows.

Among the supplications of Moses was:

“O Allah, to You belongs all praise; to You complaints are brought; You are the One whose help is sought; from You relief is sought; and upon You we rely. There is neither might nor power except through You.”

In the supplication the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, made after the people of Tāʾif treated him as they did, he said:

“O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources, and my low standing among people. You are the Lord of the oppressed, and You are my Lord. O Allah, to whom will You entrust me? To a stranger who receives me harshly, or to an enemy whom You have given power over me? If You are not angry with me, I do not mind, though Your protection from affliction would bring me greater ease. I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, through which darkness is dispelled and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right, lest Your displeasure descend upon me or Your anger fall upon me. It is for me to seek Your pleasure until You are pleased. For there is neither might nor power except through You.”

In some narrations: “And there is neither might nor power except through You.”

The stronger a servant’s longing for Allah’s bounty and mercy, and his hope that Allah will fulfil his needs and relieve his distress, the stronger his servitude to Him and his freedom from everything besides Him. Just as placing his hopes in a created being brings him into servitude to that being, giving up hope in him makes his heart independent of him.

Likewise, a servant’s longing for his Lord’s bounty and his hope in Him bring him into servitude to Him. His heart’s turning away from asking anyone other than Allah, and from placing hope in Him, causes his heart to turn away from servitude to Allah. This is especially so of someone who places his hopes in created beings rather than the Creator: his heart relies either on his authority, troops, followers, and slaves; on his family and friends; on his wealth and reserves; or on his masters and dignitaries—such as his owner, king, shaykh, patron, and others who have already died or will die.

Allah Most High says:

“And put your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die, and glorify Him with praise. Sufficient is He as One fully aware of His servants’ sins.”

Whoever attaches his heart to created beings, expecting them to help him, provide for him, or guide him, becomes inwardly submissive to them. His heart becomes enslaved to them in proportion to that attachment, even if outwardly he is their ruler, directing their affairs and exercising authority over them. A sensible person looks at realities, not appearances.

When a man’s heart becomes attached to a woman, even one lawful for him, his heart remains her captive: she rules it and controls it as she wishes. Outwardly, he is her master because he is her husband, but in reality he is her captive and slave. This is especially so if she knows how much he needs her, how passionately he loves her, and that he would accept no other woman in her place. She then rules him as an overpowering, unjust master rules his subjugated slave, who cannot escape

from him. Indeed, her domination is greater still, for captivity of the heart is more severe than captivity of the body, and enslavement of the heart is more severe than enslavement of the body. Someone whose body has been enslaved and reduced to bondage may be untroubled so long as his heart remains free of it and at peace. He may even devise a means of escape. But when the heart—which is the ruler—is itself in bondage, enslaved and enthralled by something other than Allah, this is utter humiliation and captivity, and servitude to whatever has enslaved the heart.

It is the heart’s servitude and captivity that entail reward and punishment. If a Muslim is captured by an unbeliever or wrongfully enslaved by an evildoer, that does not harm him so long as he fulfils whatever obligations he can. Someone lawfully enslaved receives two rewards if he fulfils his duties towards Allah and towards his masters. Even if he is compelled to utter words of unbelief and does so while his heart remains secure in faith, that does not harm him. But someone whose heart has become enslaved, making him a slave to something other than Allah, is harmed by this even if outwardly he is the king of all people.

True freedom is freedom of the heart, and true servitude is servitude of the heart, just as true wealth is wealth of the soul. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wealth does not consist in having many possessions; rather, true wealth is richness of the soul.”

All this, indeed, concerns someone whose heart has been enslaved by the beauty of a person lawful for him. But someone whose heart has been enslaved by the beauty of a person forbidden to him—a woman or a boy—experiences torment for which there is no recompense. Such people are among those who suffer the greatest torment and receive the least reward. For the heart’s persistent attachment to that person, even without committing sexual immorality, is more harmful to him than committing a sin and then repenting of it until its traces disappear from his heart. Such people are likened to the intoxicated and the insane.

As it has been said:

“Two intoxications: the intoxication of passion and that of wine—
When will someone gripped by both regain his senses?”

And it has been said:

“They said, ‘You have gone mad over the one you love.’ I replied,
‘Passion is worse than the madness of the insane.
One stricken by passion never regains his senses throughout his life,
Whereas the madman is seized only from time to time.’”

One of the greatest causes of this affliction is the heart’s turning away from Allah. Once the heart tastes the sweetness of worshipping Allah and being sincerely devoted to Him, nothing is ever sweeter, more delightful, or more pleasant to it. A person gives up something he loves only for something else he loves more, or out of fear of something unwelcome. Thus, the heart turns away from corrupt love only through wholesome love or fear of harm.

Allah Most High said concerning Joseph:

“Thus it was, that We might turn evil and immorality away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

Through His servant’s sincere devotion to Him, Allah turns away from him the harmful attraction and attachment to outward forms, and keeps him from sexual immorality. Thus, before a person tastes the sweetness of servitude to Allah and sincere devotion to Him, his soul overpowers him, making him follow its desires. But once he tastes sincere devotion and it grows strong in his heart, his desires yield to it without any need for remedial measures.

Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater.”

Prayer both wards off what is unwelcome—immorality and wrongdoing—and brings about what is beloved: the remembrance of Allah. Attaining what is beloved is greater than warding off what is unwelcome, for remembering Allah is worshipping Him, and the heart’s worship of Allah is sought for its own sake. By contrast, warding evil off from the heart is sought for a further purpose, as a subsidiary aim. The heart was created to love, desire, and seek the truth.

When the desire for evil arises within it, it seeks to repel that desire, for it corrupts the heart just as weeds growing among crops ruin them. Hence Allah Most High said:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it, and failed indeed is the one who corrupts it.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself, remembers the name of his Lord, and prays.”

And He said:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their chastity. That is purer for them.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Were it not for Allah’s bounty and mercy upon you, not one of you would ever have become pure.”

Thus He, glorified be He, has declared lowering the gaze and guarding chastity to be more purifying
