Likewise, one who seeks leadership and supremacy on earth is, at heart, enslaved to those who help him attain them. Although outwardly he may be their leader whom they obey, in reality he places his hopes in them and fears them. He lavishes wealth and positions of authority upon them and pardons them so that they will obey and support him. Outwardly, he is a leader who is obeyed; in reality, he is their obedient slave. The truth is that each party is, in some measure, enslaved to the other, and both have abandoned true worship of Allah. If they cooperate in seeking unjust supremacy on earth, they are like two people cooperating in sexual immorality or highway robbery. Each is enslaved by the other because of the desire that has enslaved and enthralled him.

The same applies to one who seeks wealth: it enslaves and enthralls him. These things are of two kinds:

(One kind)
comprises things a person needs, such as food, drink, housing, marriage, and the like. He seeks these from Allah and turns to Him in desire for them. Wealth is then something he uses to meet his needs, like the donkey he rides or the mat he sits upon—indeed, like the privy in which he relieves himself—without becoming enslaved to it and thus becoming fretful

—distressed when adversity befalls him, and withholding when good comes his way.

The other kind comprises things a person does not need. He should not attach his heart to these, for if he does, he becomes enslaved to them. He may even come to rely on other than Allah, so that he no longer truly worships Allah or truly relies upon Him. Rather, he has within him an element of worshipping other than Allah and an element of relying upon other than Allah. He is among those to whom the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, most aptly apply:

“May the slave of the dirham come to ruin! May the slave of the dinar come to ruin! May the slave of the plush cloak come to ruin! May the slave of the patterned cloak come to ruin!”

Such a person is enslaved to these things, even if he asks Allah for them: if Allah grants them to him, he is pleased; if He withholds them, he is displeased. The true servant of Allah, however, is one who is pleased by what pleases Allah and displeased by what displeases Allah; who loves what Allah and His Messenger love and hates what Allah and His Messenger hate; and who allies himself with Allah’s allies and opposes Allah’s enemies. Such a person has perfected his faith, as stated in the hadith:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

Allah Most High says:

“Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers.”

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.”

The Messenger commands what Allah loves, forbids what Allah hates, does what Allah loves, and conveys what Allah loves to be believed. Whoever loves Allah must therefore follow the Messenger: believing what he reports, obeying what he commands, and following his example in what he does. Whoever does this has done what Allah loves, and Allah will therefore love him.

Allah has thus given two signs by which those who love Him are known: following the Messenger and jihad in His cause. For jihad, in essence, consists in striving to bring about what Allah loves of faith and righteous deeds, and to repel what Allah hates of disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience.

Allah Most High says:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your clan”

“until Allah brings about His command.”

It is well known that what one loves generally cannot be attained without enduring what one dislikes, whether that love is sound or corrupt. Those who love wealth, authority, and physical beauty attain their goals only by suffering harm in this world, besides the harm that befalls them in this world and the Hereafter. Thus, if someone who loves Allah and His Messenger does not endure the hardships that discerning lovers of things other than Allah consider necessary and themselves endure to attain what they love, this indicates weakness in their love for Allah—provided that the course those others follow is one that reason recommends. It is well known that the believer is stronger in his love for Allah. As the Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah.”

Admittedly, a lover may, through poor judgment and a flawed understanding, follow a path that does not lead to the desired goal. Such a path is not commendable when the love itself is sound and praiseworthy; how much less so when the love is corrupt and the path does not lead to the goal! This is what reckless seekers of wealth, authority, and physical beauty do in loving things that bring them harm without securing what they seek. What is meant here is only the paths that reason follows to attain its goal.

Once this is clear, the more the heart grows in love for Allah, the more it grows in servitude to Him; and the more it grows in servitude to Him, the more it grows in love for Him and in freedom from everything besides Him. The heart is inherently in need

His deficiency and imperfection—indeed, his pain, regret, and torment—would be proportionate to that failure.

that He is the One petitioned, whose help is sought, and in whom trust is placed. He is his God, and he has no god besides Him; He is his Lord, and he has no lord besides Him. His servitude to Allah is complete only through these two aspects. Whenever he loves something other than Allah for its own sake, or looks to something other than Allah to help him, he becomes a servant of what he loves and of what he places his hope in, in proportion to his love and hope.

But if he loves none but Allah for His own sake, loves everything else only for His sake, and never places his hope in anything but Allah; and if, whatever means he employs or acquires, he remains conscious that Allah created and ordained them, and that Allah is the Lord, Sovereign, and Creator of everything in the heavens and the earth, all of which stands in need of Him—then he has attained completeness in his servitude to Allah in proportion to the share of this he has been granted.

People differ greatly in their degrees of attainment in this regard, across a range that only Allah can fully encompass. Those who are most perfect, best, highest in rank, closest to Allah, strongest, and best guided are those whose servitude to Allah is most complete in this respect.

This is the true essence of the religion of Islam with which He sent His messengers and revealed His Books: that the servant submit to Allah and to no other. Whoever submits to Him and to another associates partners with Him, while whoever refuses to submit to Him is arrogant. It is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“No one with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise, just as

no one with an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire.” He thus set arrogance in opposition to faith, for arrogance is incompatible with the true essence of servitude, as is established in an authentic report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Allah says: ‘Greatness is My lower garment and grandeur My upper garment. Whoever contests either of them with Me, I will punish him.’”

Greatness and grandeur belong exclusively to lordship, and grandeur is higher than greatness. Hence He likened grandeur to the upper garment and greatness to the lower garment. This is why the proclamation “Allah is the Greatest” is the hallmark of the prayers, the call to prayer, and the festivals. It is also recommended in elevated places such as al-Safā and al-Marwah, when one ascends a height or mounts a riding animal, and in similar circumstances. By it, a fire is extinguished, however great, and at the call to prayer Satan flees.

Allah Most High says:

“And your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation.’”

Everyone who is too arrogant to worship Allah must inevitably worship something else, for a human being is a sentient being who acts by will. It is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said:

“The most truthful names are Hārith and Hammām.”

Hārith means one who earns and acts, while Hammām is an intensive form derived from hamm (intention), and intention is the first stage of willing. A human being is always willing something, and every act of will must have an ultimate object. Every servant must therefore have a beloved object of desire that is the ultimate goal of his love and will. Whoever does not take Allah as the One he worships and the ultimate goal of his love and will, but is instead too arrogant to do so, must inevitably have a beloved object of desire

other than Allah that enslaves him. He thus becomes a slave to that beloved object of desire—whether wealth, prestige, physical beauty, or something he takes as a deity besides Allah, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, idols, or the graves of prophets and righteous people; or angels and prophets whom he takes as lords; or anything else worshipped besides Allah. If he is a slave to something other than Allah, he associates partners with Allah. Every arrogant person associates partners with Allah. Thus Pharaoh was among the most arrogant of all creatures in refusing to worship Allah, and he associated partners with Him.

Allah Most High says:

“And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh, Haman and Qārūn, but they said, ‘A magician and a liar.’”

Further on, He says:

“And Moses said, ‘Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account.’”

And further on:

“Thus does Allah seal the heart of every arrogant tyrant.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And Qārūn, Pharaoh and Haman—Moses had certainly come to them with clear proofs, but they were arrogant in the land, and they could not escape Us.”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was one of the corrupters.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran.

Pharaoh is also described as associating partners with Allah in His words:

“And the chiefs among Pharaoh’s people said, ‘Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?’”

Rather, examining the evidence shows that the more arrogantly a person refuses to worship Allah, the more he associates partners with Him. For the more arrogantly he refuses to worship Allah, the greater his dependence upon and need for the beloved object of his desire—the heart’s primary object of pursuit. He thus participates in such association through whatever of these things has enslaved him.

The heart can never become independent of all created beings unless Allah is its Master: it worships none but Him, seeks help from none but Him, relies upon none but Him, rejoices only in what He loves and approves, and dislikes only what the Lord hates and dislikes. It allies itself only with those whom Allah befriends and opposes only those whom Allah opposes. It loves only for Allah’s sake, hates anything only for Allah’s sake, gives only for Allah’s sake, and withholds only for Allah’s sake. The more sincerely a person devotes his religion to Allah alone, the more complete his servitude and independence of created beings become. Through complete servitude to Allah, he is freed from arrogance and associating partners with Him.

Associating partners with Allah predominates among Christians, while arrogance predominates among Jews. Allah Most High says concerning Christians:

“They have taken their scholars and monks as lords besides Allah, and also the Messiah, the son of Mary, although they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him.”

He says concerning Jews:

“Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you became arrogant? Some you denied, and others you killed.”

Allah Most High also says:

“I will turn away from My signs those who behave arrogantly on earth without right. And even if they see

every sign, they will not believe in it. And if they see the path of right guidance, they will not take it as their way; but if they see the path of error, they will take it as their way.”

Arrogance necessarily entails associating partners with Allah, which is the opposite of Islam and the sin that Allah does not forgive. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives whatever is less than that for whomever He wills. Whoever associates partners with Allah has indeed committed a tremendous sin.”

He also says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives whatever is less than that for whomever He wills. Whoever associates partners with Allah has indeed strayed far astray.”

Thus, all the prophets were sent with the religion of Islam. It is the religion besides which Allah accepts no other, whether from earlier or later generations.

Noah said:

“But if you turn away, I have asked you for no payment. My reward is only with Allah, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.”

Allah says concerning Abraham:

“And who would turn away from the faith of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We certainly chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.”

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

Then, further on, He says:

“So do not die except as Muslims.”

Joseph said:

“Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”

Moses said:

“O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.”

“They said, ‘In Allah we have put our trust.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We sent down the Torah, containing guidance and light. By it, the prophets who submitted to Allah judged for the Jews.”

Bilqīs said:

“My Lord, I have indeed wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds.”

And He says:

“And when I inspired the disciples, ‘Believe in Me and in My messenger,’ they said, ‘We believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

And He says:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

And He says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do they seek a religion other than Allah’s, when all those in the heavens and the earth have submitted to Him, willingly or unwillingly?”

He thus mentions the submission of all beings, willingly or unwillingly, because all creatures are His servants in the universal sense, whether they acknowledge this or deny it. They are subject to His authority and governance, submitting to Him willingly or unwillingly. No creature can escape what He has willed, ordained, and decreed, and there is no might or power except through Him. He is the Lord and Sovereign of all worlds, directing them however He wills. He is the Creator, Originator, and Fashioner of them all. Everything besides Him is subject to His lordship: made, brought into being, dependent, needy, enslaved, and subdued. He is the One, the Subduer, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner.

Although He has created what He has created through causes, He is the Creator of each cause and the One who ordains it; the cause is dependent upon Him just as its effect is. No created cause can independently bring anything about or ward off harm. Rather, every cause needs another cause to assist it, as well as something to repel whatever opposes and obstructs it. He alone—glory be to Him—is entirely free of need of everything besides Him. He has no partner to assist Him and no adversary to resist or oppose Him.

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides

Allah—if Allah intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’ Say, ‘Allah is sufficient for me; in Him let those who trust place their trust.’”

The Most High also says:

“If Allah touches you with harm, none can remove it except Him; and if He touches you with good, He has power over all things.”

The Most High also relates the words of His intimate friend, Abraham:

“O my people, I am free of whatever you associate with Allah.”

“Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, inclining to Him alone, and I am not one of the polytheists.”

“His people argued with him. He said, ‘Do you argue with me about Allah when He has guided me? I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord should will something.’”

And so on, up to His words:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and it is they who are rightly guided.”

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections from Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that when this verse was revealed, it troubled the Prophet’s Companions, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They said, “O Messenger of Allah, which of us has not mixed his faith with wrongdoing?” He replied, “It refers only to associating partners with Allah. Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: ‘Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong’?”

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, is the leader of the sincere monotheists. He was sent when the religion of the polytheists had spread throughout the earth. Allah Most High says:

“And when Abraham’s Lord tested him with commands, which he fulfilled, He said, ‘I will make you a leader for the people.’ Abraham said, ‘And from among my descendants?’ He said, ‘My covenant does not extend to the wrongdoers.’”

He thus made clear that His covenant concerning leadership does not extend to a wrongdoer. Allah, glory be to Him, therefore did not command that a wrongdoer be a leader. And the greatest wrongdoing is associating partners with Allah.

The Most High also says:

“Indeed, Abraham was a leader, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining to Him alone, and he was not one of the polytheists.”

A “leader” here is a teacher of good whom others follow, just as a “role model” is someone whose example others follow. Allah Most High placed prophethood and Scripture among his descendants, and the prophets He sent after him were sent with his religion. The Most High says:

“Then We revealed to you: Follow the religion of Abraham, inclining to Allah alone; he was not one of the polytheists.”

The Most High also says:

“Indeed, those with the greatest claim to Abraham are those who followed him, this Prophet, and those who believe. And Allah is the protector of the believers.”

The Most High also says:

“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but one inclining to Allah alone, submitting to Him; he was not one of the polytheists.”

It is authentically reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

translated_text:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware: do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

All of this is recorded in the Sahīh. It also states that he said this a few days before his death. This was part of completing his mission, for it affirms the perfection of his intimate friendship with Allah, founded upon Allah Most High’s love for His servant and the servant’s love for Allah, contrary to the Jahmiyyah. It also affirms Allah’s oneness and that none but Him should be worshipped, refuting those who resemble the polytheists. It further refutes the Rāfidah, who deny al-Siddīq his due and who, among those who profess allegiance to the qiblah, are the greatest in associating human beings with Allah.

Intimate friendship is perfect love, which entails, on the servant’s part, perfect servitude to Allah and, on the Lord’s part—glory be to Him—perfect lordship over His servants whom He loves and who love Him. The term “servitude” encompasses perfect humility and perfect love. The Arabs describe a heart as mutayyam (enthralled) when it is enslaved to the beloved. Mutayyam means “enslaved,” and Taym Allāh means “Allah’s servant.” Abraham and Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace, attained this in its perfection. This is why he had no intimate friend among the people of the earth: intimate friendship admits no sharing. As has been said on this subject:

“You have permeated the very course of my soul;
Thus is an intimate friend called khalīl.”

Love in the broader sense is different. In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning al-Hasan and Usāmah:

“O Allah, I love them both, so love them and love those who love them.”

Amr ibn al-Ās asked him, “Who is dearest to you?” He replied, “Ā’ishah.” He asked, “And among men?” He replied, “Her father.”

He also said to Alī, may Allah be pleased with him:

“I shall certainly give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.”

There are many similar examples. Allah Most High has stated that He loves the God-fearing, those who do good, those who act justly, those who repent, those who purify themselves, and those who fight in His cause in ranks as though they were a solidly joined structure. He also said:

“Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him.”

He has thus affirmed His love for His believing servants and the believers’ love for Him, even saying:

“But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah.”

Intimate friendship, however, is exclusive. Some people say, “Muhammad is Allah’s beloved, whereas Abraham is Allah’s intimate friend,” imagining that love is higher than intimate friendship. This is a weak view, for Muhammad is also Allah’s intimate friend, as established in widely transmitted authentic hadiths. As for the report that “al-Abbās will be gathered at the Resurrection between a beloved and an intimate friend,” and similar reports, these are fabricated hadiths that cannot be relied upon.

We have already explained that loving Allah Most High includes loving what He loves. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than all else; that he loves another person solely for Allah’s sake; and that he detests returning to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it just as he detests being cast into the Fire.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated that whoever possesses these three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith. This is because finding sweetness in something follows love for it. When someone loves or desires something and then obtains what he wants, he experiences sweetness, pleasure, and joy in it. Pleasure arises after perceiving what is congenial—that is, what is loved or desired.

Those who claim that pleasure is the perception of what is congenial, as some philosophers and physicians do, are clearly mistaken. Perception comes between love and pleasure. A person, for example, desires food; when he eats it, pleasure follows. Likewise, pleasure follows looking at something: when one looks at it, one experiences pleasure. Pleasure follows the act of looking; it is not the act of looking itself, nor is it the sight of the thing. Rather, it arises after seeing it. Allah Most High said:

“Therein is whatever souls desire and eyes delight in.”

Likewise, all the pleasures and pains the soul experiences—joy, sorrow, and the like—arise through awareness of what is loved or what is disliked. Yet awareness itself is not

and submission alone, unaccompanied by love; or that love entails indulgence in desires or an abasement incompatible with lordship. Thus, it is related that when people discussed love in the presence of Dhū al-Nūn, he said:

“Refrain from discussing this matter, lest souls hear of it and claim it for themselves.”

Some people of spiritual insight and knowledge disapproved of keeping company with those who spoke much about love without reverent fear. Some of the early generations said:

“Whoever worships Allah through love alone is a heretic; whoever worships Him through hope alone is a Murji’ite; whoever worships Him through fear alone is a Harūrī (Kharijite); and whoever worships Him through love, fear, and hope is a believer who affirms His oneness.”

Thus, among later generations, some became so unrestrained in their claims of love that this led them into a kind of folly and pretension incompatible with servitude, involving the servant in a kind of lordship befitting Allah alone. One of them makes claims exceeding the bounds of prophets and messengers, or they ask Allah for what belongs exclusively to Allah in every respect and is not fitting even for prophets and messengers. Many spiritual masters have fallen into this.

Its cause is a failure to fully realize the servitude explained by the messengers and precisely defined by the commands and prohibitions they brought—indeed, a weakness of the reason through which the servant recognizes his own true nature. When reason is weak, knowledge of religion is scant, and love is present in the soul, the soul foolishly gives itself free rein in that love, just as someone foolish and ignorant gives himself free rein in loving another person, saying:

“I am a lover, so I am not to be held accountable for the various things I do that involve transgression and ignorance.”

This is

sheer misguidance. It resembles the claim of the Jews and Christians:

“We are the children of Allah and His beloved.”

Allah Most High said:

“Say, ‘Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are human beings among those He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.’”

His punishing them for their sins entails that they are neither beloved nor related to Him as children; rather, they are created beings subject to His lordship. When Allah loves someone, He sets him to doing what his Beloved loves; that person does not commit the disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience that the True One hates and is displeased with. Whoever commits major sins, persists in them, and does not repent of them—Allah hates those deeds of his, just as He loves the good that he does. For His love for a servant is proportionate to that servant’s faith and mindfulness of Him.

Anyone who thinks that sins will not harm him because Allah loves him, despite his persistence in them, is like someone who claims that taking poison will not harm him because he has a healthy constitution, even though he continues taking it and seeks no treatment for it. If this fool reflected on the accounts Allah relates in His Book concerning His prophets—their repentance and seeking forgiveness, and the various trials that befell them, through which they were refined and purified according to their circumstances—he would understand something of the harm sins cause those who commit them, even those of the highest standing.

Someone who loves a created being but neither knows nor seeks that being’s best interests, acting instead merely on the impulse of love—even when this involves ignorance and wrongdoing—thereby gives the beloved cause to hate him and turn away from him, indeed, even to punish him.

translated_text:
Many seekers on the spiritual path, in professing love for Allah, have pursued various courses born of ignorance of religion: transgressing Allah’s limits, neglecting His rights, or making groundless claims with no basis in reality. One of them said:

“I disown any disciple of mine who leaves anyone in the Fire.”

Another said:

“I disown any disciple of mine who allows any believer to enter the Fire.”

The first credited his disciple with bringing everyone out of the Fire; the second credited his disciple with preventing those guilty of major sins from entering it. Some of them say:

“On the Day of Resurrection, I shall pitch my tent over Hell so that no one enters it.”

Such statements, and others like them, are reported from certain well-known spiritual masters. They are either falsely attributed to them or errors on their part. Such words may be uttered in a state of spiritual intoxication, overpowering emotion, and loss of self-awareness, in which a person’s discernment disappears or becomes so impaired that he does not know what he has said. “Intoxication” is pleasure accompanied by a lack of discernment. Thus, some among them would seek forgiveness for such words upon recovering their sobriety. This was the principal aim of those masters who indulged extensively in listening to poems of love, longing, blame, reproach, and consuming passion.

For this reason, Allah revealed a test of love by which He tests the one who professes it. He said:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

No one truly loves Allah unless he follows His Messenger. Obeying and following the Messenger brings true servitude to Allah into being. Yet many who profess love depart from his law and Sunnah and make claims involving

Yet Allah has made jihad in His cause an expression of love for Him and His Messenger. “Jihad” entails complete love for what Allah has commanded and complete hatred of what He has forbidden. For this reason, this community’s love for Allah is more complete than that of earlier communities, and their servitude to Allah is more complete than that of their predecessors. The most perfect members of this community in this respect are the Companions of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. The more closely someone resembles them, the more complete these qualities are in him. How far removed this is from people who merely profess love!

Among the sayings of certain spiritual masters is:

“Love is a fire that burns away from the heart everything other than what the Beloved wills.”

They meant that Allah has willed the existence of the entire universe, and so they supposed that perfect love requires the servant to love everything—even disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. Yet no one can love everything that exists. Rather, a person loves what suits and benefits him, and hates what is incompatible with him and harms him. Through this error, however, they found a means of following their own desires. They love whatever they desire, such as physical forms, leadership, surplus wealth, and misleading innovations, claiming that this is part of loving Allah. Yet loving Allah includes hating what Allah and His Messenger hate, and waging jihad against those who engage in it with one’s life and wealth.

Their fundamental error is that the person who said,

“Love is a fire that burns away everything other than what the Beloved wills,”

meant by Allah’s will His religious, legislative will, which signifies His love and pleasure. It is as though he had said, “It burns away from the heart everything other than what Allah loves.” This meaning is sound. Perfect love entails loving only what Allah loves; if you love what He does not love, your love is deficient. As for His decreeing and ordaining such a thing, He hates and detests it, is angered by it, and forbids it. If I do not share His hatred, aversion, and anger toward it, then I do not love Him; rather, I love what He hates.

Following the revealed law and undertaking jihad are therefore among the greatest distinctions between those who love Allah and His allies, whom He loves and who love Him, and those who claim to love Allah while considering only His all-encompassing lordship or following innovations contrary to His law. Such claims to love Allah are of the same kind as the claims of Jews and Christians to love Him. Indeed, these people’s claims may be worse than those of Jews and Christians because of their hypocrisy, which places them in the lowest depths of the Fire. Conversely, the claims of Jews and Christians may be worse than theirs if these people have not reached the same degree of disbelief. The Torah and the Gospel contain teachings about loving Allah on which they agree; indeed, they regard this as the greatest commandment of the Law.

Thus, the Gospel relates that the Messiah said:

“The greatest of the Messiah’s commandments is to love Allah with all your heart, mind, and soul.”

He, glorified is He, loves those who love Him. A servant cannot love Allah without Allah Most High loving him. Rather, Allah’s love for His servant corresponds to the servant’s love for his Lord, although Allah’s reward for His servant is greater.

As Allah Most High says in the authentic divine hadith:

“Whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him an arm’s length. Whoever draws near to Me an arm’s length, I draw near to him an armspan. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running.”

He, glorified is He, has declared that He loves the God-fearing, those who do good, the patient, those who repeatedly repent, and those who purify themselves. Indeed, He loves whoever fulfils His commands, whether obligatory or recommended, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears and his sight with which he sees”—to the end of the hadith.

Many of those who have erred by following spiritual teachers in “asceticism and worship” have fallen into some of the same errors as the Christians: claiming to love Allah while violating His law, neglecting to strive in His cause, and the like. In the religion through which they seek to draw near to Allah, they cling to things similar to those to which the Christians clung: ambiguous statements and accounts whose tellers’ truthfulness is unknown. Even if a teller were truthful, he would not be infallible. They attribute to this elite a share in divinity of the same kind that the Christians attribute to the Messiah and his mother. There are other such errors whose explanation would be too lengthy here.

The true religion consists only in fully realizing servitude to Allah in every respect, which means fully realizing love for Allah at every degree. As servitude becomes more complete, so too does the servant’s love for his Lord and the Lord’s love for His servant. As the former diminishes, so does the latter. Whenever the heart contains love for something other than Allah, it contains a corresponding degree of servitude to something other than Allah; and whenever it contains servitude to something other than Allah, it contains a corresponding degree of love for something other than Allah. Every love that is not for Allah’s sake is vain, and every deed through which Allah’s Face is not sought is vain. This world is accursed, and everything in it is accursed, except what is for Allah. Nothing is for Allah unless Allah and His Messenger love it—that is, unless it is prescribed in His religion.

Thus, any deed intended for someone other than Allah is not for Allah, and any deed that does not conform to Allah’s law is not for Allah. Rather, nothing is for Allah unless it combines both qualities: it must be for Allah’s sake, and it must accord with what Allah and His Messenger love—namely, what is obligatory or recommended.

As He says:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

Righteous deeds—those that are obligatory or recommended—are therefore indispensable, and they must be devoted sincerely to seeking the Face of Allah Most High. As He, Most High, says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.”

Another hadith relates:

their love for Allah, their servitude to Him, and their sincere religious devotion to Him alone. As Shaddād ibn Aws said:

“O remnant of the Arabs, what I fear most for you is showing off and hidden desire.”

Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī was asked, “What is hidden desire?” He replied, “Love of leadership.”

Kaʿb ibn Mālik reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two hungry wolves let loose in a sheepfold are no more destructive to it than a person’s eagerness for wealth and prestige is to his religion.”

Al-Tirmidhī said, “A good and authentic hadith.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus explained that eagerness for wealth and prestige is no less destructive to religion than two hungry wolves are to a sheepfold. This is clear, for sound religious devotion does not harbour such eagerness. Once the heart tastes the sweetness of servitude to Allah and love for Him, nothing becomes dearer to it such that it would give it precedence over that. Through this, evil and indecency are turned away from those sincerely devoted to Allah, as the Most High said:

“Thus it was, so that We might turn evil and indecency away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

One who is sincerely devoted to Allah has tasted a sweetness in serving Him that prevents him from serving anyone else, and a sweetness in loving Him that prevents him from loving anyone else. For the heart finds nothing sweeter, more delightful, more pleasant, gentler or more blissful than the sweetness of faith, which encompasses servitude to Allah, love for Him, and sincere religious devotion to Him alone. This draws the heart towards Allah, so that it turns to Him in repentance, fearing Him, filled with longing and awe. As the Most High said:

“One who feared the Most Merciful without seeing Him and came with a heart ever turning to Him.”

“Those whom they invoke seek a means of nearness to their Lord, striving to be closest to Him. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is ever to be feared.”

When a servant is sincerely devoted to Him, his Lord chooses him, revives his heart and draws him towards Himself. The evil and indecency that oppose this are thereby turned away from him, and he fears that the opposite might befall him. By contrast, a heart that is not sincerely devoted to Allah pursues, desires and loves without restraint. It craves whatever presents itself and clings to whatever it desires, like a branch that bends with every passing breeze.

At times, he is drawn to physical beauty, whether forbidden to him or not, and remains a captive and a slave to someone whom it would be shameful, demeaning and blameworthy for him to take as his own slave. At other times, he is drawn to prestige and leadership: a word pleases him, and a word angers him. Whoever praises him enslaves him, even through falsehood, while he becomes hostile towards whoever criticizes him, even truthfully. At still other times, he is enslaved by silver and gold, and by other such things that enslave hearts and that hearts desire. Thus he takes his own desire as his god and follows it without guidance from Allah.

Unless a person is sincerely devoted to Allah as His servant, with his heart wholly enslaved to his Lord alone, without partner—so that Allah is dearer to him than everything else, and he is humble and submissive before Him—created things will enslave him, and devils will take possession of his heart. He will be among the misguided, the brethren of the devils, and evil and indecency will arise within him to an extent known only to Allah. This is inevitable; there is no escaping it. Allah, glorified is He, made Abraham and the family of Abraham leaders of these sincere monotheists, who love Allah, worship Him and devote their religion sincerely to Him. Likewise, He made Pharaoh and the people of Pharaoh leaders of those who associate partners with Allah and follow their own desires.

The Most High said concerning Abraham:

“And We granted him Isaac, and Jacob as an additional gift, and made them all righteous.”

“And We made them leaders, guiding by Our command, and inspired them to do good deeds, establish prayer and give zakah. And they worshipped Us alone.”

He said concerning Pharaoh and his people:

“And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.”

“And We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.”

Thus, the followers of Pharaoh first come to make no distinction between what Allah loves and approves of and what He has decreed and ordained. Rather, they consider only His unrestricted, all-encompassing will. Eventually, they cease to distinguish between the Creator and creation, regarding the existence of the one as the very existence of the other. [Their leading exponents say: “In the revealed Law there is obedience and disobedience, while in spiritual reality there is disobedience without obedience”]; at the level of realization, there is neither obedience nor disobedience. This is the full realization of the doctrine of Pharaoh and his people, who denied the Creator, denied that He spoke to His servant Moses, and denied the commands and prohibitions with which He sent him.

As for Abraham and the family of Abraham—the sincere monotheists and prophets—they know that a distinction must be maintained between the Creator and creation, and between obedience and disobedience. They know that the more a servant advances in realization, the greater his love for Allah, his servitude and obedience to Him, and his turning away from worshipping, loving and obeying anyone other than Him.

These misguided polytheists equate Allah with His creation, whereas Allah’s intimate friend says:

you and your forefathers?

They cling to ambiguous statements made by the spiritual masters, just as the Christians did. An example is the term “fanā” (annihilation). There are three kinds of fanā: one belonging to those who have attained perfection among the prophets and Allah’s friends; another belonging to those striving among Allah’s friends and the righteous; and another belonging to the hypocrites who deviate from the truth and liken Allah to His creation.

(As for the first), it is “ceasing to desire anything other than Allah,” such that a person loves none but Allah, worships none but Him, relies on none but Him, and seeks none but Him. This is the meaning that must be intended by the words of Shaykh Abū Yazīd when he said: “I desire to desire only what He wills.” That is, what He wills in the sense of loving and approving of it—what is intended by His prescriptive will. The servant’s perfection lies in desiring, loving and approving only what Allah wills, approves of and loves: what He has commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation. He loves only what Allah loves, such as the angels, the prophets and the righteous.

This is the meaning of their explanation of His words:

“Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

As for the second kind, it is “ceasing to perceive anything other than Allah.” This happens to many who follow the spiritual path. Their hearts are so intensely drawn to remembering, worshipping and loving Allah, yet too weak to perceive anything besides the One they worship or behold anything besides the One they seek, that nothing other than Allah enters their hearts. Indeed, they are not even aware of anything else. Thus, concerning His words:

“The heart of Moses’ mother became empty. She almost disclosed his identity, had We not strengthened her heart.”

They said: “Empty of everything except the thought of Moses.”

This often happens to someone overwhelmed by a concern—whether love, fear or hope—which turns his heart away from everything except what he loves, fears or seeks. When entirely absorbed in it, he is unaware of anything else. If this state intensifies in someone experiencing annihilation, he becomes so absorbed in the One he finds that he loses awareness of his own existence; in the One he beholds, of his own beholding; in the One he remembers, of his own remembrance; and in the One he knows, of his own knowledge. Eventually, that which once did not exist—the created beings other than Him, all subject to Him—vanishes, and He who has always existed—the Lord Most High—remains. What is meant is that these beings vanish from the servant’s awareness and remembrance, and that he ceases to perceive or behold them.

When this intensifies, the lover grows weak until his discernment becomes impaired. He may then imagine that he himself is his beloved, as in the story related of a man who threw himself into the sea, whereupon the one who loved him threw himself in after him. The first said: “I fell in, but what made you fall in after me?” He replied: “I became so absorbed in you that I lost awareness of myself, and thought that you were me.”

translated_text:
And it is at “this point” that some people have gone astray, imagining that this is union, and that the lover becomes united with the beloved until there is no distinction between their very existences. This is an error, for nothing whatsoever can become united with the Creator. Indeed, nothing becomes united with anything else unless both are transformed and lose their original natures, their union producing a third thing that is neither the one nor the other—as when water and milk, or water and wine, are mixed together, and so forth. Rather, their objects of desire, love and aversion may be one and the same, and their willing and aversion may accord: one loves what the other loves, hates what the other hates, is pleased with what pleases the other, resents what the other resents, dislikes what the other dislikes, befriends those whom the other befriends, and opposes those whom the other opposes. All such annihilation involves some deficiency.

The greatest friends of Allah—such as Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers—did not experience this annihilation, let alone the Prophets, who rank above them. Something of this occurred only after the time of the Companions. The same applies to all experiences of this kind in which reason and discernment are lost because of states of faith that come upon the heart. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were too complete, strong and steadfast in their states of faith to lose their reason or experience fainting, swooning, intoxication, annihilation, bewilderment or madness. These phenomena first appeared among the devout worshippers of Basra belonging to the generation of the Successors. Some would faint upon hearing the Quran.

Some would even die, such as Abū Juhayr the Blind and Zurārah ibn Awfā, the judge of Basra. Likewise, some Sufi shaykhs later experienced annihilation and intoxication to such a degree that

their discernment weakened, until they uttered things in that state which, upon regaining sobriety, they recognized as mistaken. Such things are related of Abū Yazīd, Abū al-Husayn al-Nūrī, Abū Bakr al-Shiblī and others like them. This was unlike Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, Ma‘rūf al-Karkhī and al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād—indeed, unlike al-Junayd and others whose reason and discernment remained with them throughout their spiritual states, so that they did not fall into such annihilation, intoxication or similar experiences.

Rather, those who attain perfection have hearts filled with nothing but love for Allah, seeking Him and worshipping Him. Yet their knowledge and discernment are sufficiently broad to perceive things as they truly are. Indeed, they perceive created beings as sustained by Allah’s command, governed by His will, responsive to Him and humbly obedient to Him. In them they find insight and a reminder. What they witness thus reinforces and nourishes the sincere devotion, unalloyed monotheism and worship of Allah alone, without partner, that reside in their hearts.

This is the “reality” to which the Quran calls, and which is upheld by those who have truly realized faith and those perfected in spiritual knowledge. Our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is their leader and the most perfect of them. Thus, when he was taken up to the heavens, witnessed the signs there, and received the revelation conveyed to him in various forms of intimate discourse, he was among his people the next morning with his state unchanged and no outward sign of that experience upon him. This contrasts with the signs of being overcome that would appear in Moses—may Allah bless them all and grant them peace.

translated_text:
As for the third kind of what may be called annihilation, it consists in perceiving that nothing exists but Allah, and that the Creator and creation have one and the same existence, with no distinction between the Lord and the servant. This is the annihilation of those given to misguidance and heresy, who fall into indwelling and union.

When an upright spiritual master says, “I see none but Allah,” or “I look to none but Allah,” or something similar, he means: “I see no lord besides Him, no creator besides Him, no governor besides Him, and no deity besides Him. Nor do I look to anything else out of love for it, fear of it, or hope in it.” For the eye looks towards whatever occupies the heart. Whoever loves something, hopes in it, or fears it turns towards it. But when the heart has no love, hope, fear, hatred, or any other attachment to something, it does not deliberately turn towards it, look at it, or seek to see it. If one happens to see it, merely seeing it without any further involvement, it is like seeing a wall or anything else to which the heart has no attachment.

The righteous spiritual masters—may Allah be pleased with them—speak of aspects of pure monotheism and the realization of complete sincerity in all religious devotion, such that the servant neither turns towards nor looks to anything other than Allah out of love, fear, or hope. Rather, the heart is empty of created things, free of attachment to them, and looks upon them only by Allah’s light. Thus, through the True One he hears, through the True One he sees, through the True One he grasps, and through the True One he walks. Among created things, he loves what Allah loves and hates what Allah hates; he befriends those whom Allah befriends and is hostile to those opposed by

This is the sound heart: upright in faith, affirming Allah’s oneness, submitting to Him, believing in Him, knowing Him, realizing the truth, and affirming His oneness through the knowledge, spiritual realization, and monotheism of the prophets and messengers.

(As for the third kind)

It is annihilation in what exists: the realization, knowledge, and monotheism of Pharaoh’s people, such as the Qarmatians and their like. This kind, which the followers of the prophets adhere to, is “praiseworthy annihilation,” through which a person becomes one of those whom Allah has praised: His God-fearing allies, His successful party, and His victorious army.

By this statement, the spiritual masters and the righteous do not mean that the created things I see with my own eyes are the Lord of the earth and the heavens. Only someone steeped in utter misguidance and corruption would say this—whether corruption of reason or corruption of belief. His condition thus lies between madness and heresy.

All the spiritual masters who are followed as examples in religion agree with the consensus of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars: the Creator, glorified be He, is distinct and separate from created things. Nothing of His essence is within His creation, and nothing of His creation is within His essence. The Eternal must be distinguished from that which came into being, and the Creator from creation. They have discussed the diseases and misconceptions that afflict hearts, and how someone may behold the existence of created things and mistake it for the Creator of the earth and the heavens, because his heart lacks discernment and the ability to distinguish. He is like someone who sees the sun’s rays and imagines them to be the sun itself in the sky.

They also speak of “distinction and collectedness,” using striking expressions similar to those used in discussing annihilation. When a servant perceives the diversity and multiplicity of created things, his heart remains attached to them and scattered among them, attending to them and clinging to them through love, fear, or hope. When he moves to collectedness, his heart becomes wholly focused on affirming Allah’s oneness and worshipping Him alone, without partner. His heart turns to Allah after having turned to created beings: his love is now for his Lord, his fear is of his Lord, his hope rests in his Lord, and he seeks his Lord’s help. In this state, his heart may have no room to consider created beings so as to distinguish between the Creator and creation. He may thus be wholly focused on the Truth, turning away from creation in both attention and intention. This resembles the second kind of annihilation.

Beyond this, however, comes the “second distinction”: to perceive that created things are sustained by Allah and governed by His command, and to perceive their multiplicity as negated by the oneness of Allah, glorified and exalted be He; and that He, glorified be He, is the Lord, God, Creator, and Owner of all created things. and enmity for His sake, and the like—he remains mindful of the distinction between the Creator and creation, distinguishing one from the other. He perceives the diversity and multiplicity of created things while also perceiving that Allah is the Lord, Sovereign, and Creator of everything, and that He is Allah: there is no god worthy of worship except Him. This is sound and upright perception. This is required in the heart’s knowledge, perception, remembrance, and recognition, as well as in its state, worship, purpose, will, love, loyalty, and obedience.

This is the realization of “the testimony that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah.” He denies in his heart the divinity of anything other than the Truth and affirms in his heart the divinity of the Truth. Thus, he denies the divinity of every created thing and affirms the divinity of the Lord of all worlds, the Lord of the earth and the heavens. This entails the heart’s complete devotion to Allah and its turning away from everything besides Him. He therefore distinguishes between the Creator and creation in his knowledge and purpose, his perception and will, and his recognition and love. He knows Allah Most High, remembers Him, and recognizes Him, while also knowing that He is distinct from His creation, separate from them, and uniquely One.

He loves Allah, venerates Him, worships Him, places his hope in Him, fears Him, maintains loyalty and enmity for His sake, seeks His help, and places his trust in Him. He refrains from worshipping any other, placing his trust in any other, seeking help from any other, fearing any other, placing his hope in any other, maintaining loyalty or enmity for the sake of any other, or obeying the commands of any other, and from directing to any other such acts as belong exclusively to the divinity of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

His acknowledgment of the divinity of Allah Most High alone, to the exclusion of all others, entails his acknowledgment of His lordship: that He is the Lord, Sovereign, Creator, and Disposer of everything. Only then does he truly affirm Allah’s oneness.

This is further clarified by the fact that the best remembrance is “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah,” as narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Abī

al-Dunyā and others in a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“The best remembrance is ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

In al-Muwattaʾ and elsewhere, it is reported from Talhah ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best that I and the prophets before me have said is: ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner. His is the dominion and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

Those who claim that this is the remembrance of ordinary people, that the remembrance of the elite consists of the name alone, and that the remembrance of the elite of the elite consists of the pronoun are astray and mistaken.

Some of them cite His words as evidence for this:

“Say, ‘Allah,’ then leave them to amuse themselves in their vain discourse.”

This is among their most obvious errors, for the name is mentioned in a command to answer a question, namely His words:

“Say, ‘Who sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for mankind?’”

Through to His words:

“Say, ‘Allah.’”

That is: Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought. The name is therefore the subject of a nominal sentence, whose predicate is indicated by the question. This is like other such expressions: you ask, “Who is his neighbour?” and someone answers, “Zayd.”

As for the name on its own, whether expressed as a noun or a pronoun, it is neither a complete utterance nor a meaningful sentence. It conveys neither faith nor disbelief, neither a command nor a prohibition. None of the early generations of the Muslim community mentioned this practice, nor did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribe it. In itself, it gives the heart neither beneficial knowledge nor a beneficial spiritual state. It merely provides a bare conception, without affirming or denying anything about it. So if it is not accompanied by something in the heart’s knowledge and state that is beneficial in itself,

Some who have persevered in this form of remembrance have fallen into various forms of heresy and unionism, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

As for the statement attributed to one of the shaykhs, “I fear that I may die between the negation and the affirmation,” this is a state in which its possessor should not be followed, for the error involved is plain. If a servant were to die in that state, he would die only upon what he intended and meant, since deeds are judged by intentions. It is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed that the dying be prompted to say, “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah.” He also said:

“Whoever’s last words are ‘There is no god worthy of worship except Allah’ will enter Paradise.”

If what that shaykh mentioned were truly a danger, the Prophet would not have prompted the dying person with an utterance that might leave him dying in a blameworthy state before completing it. Rather, he would have prompted him with the remembrance that this shaykh preferred: the name alone.

Remembrance consisting of a pronoun alone is still further removed from the Sunnah, more deeply rooted in religious innovation, and more likely to lead to Satan’s misguidance. For when someone says, “Yā Hū, yā Hū” (“O He, O He”), or “Hū, Hū” (“He, He”), or the like, the pronoun refers only to what his heart conceives—and the heart may be rightly guided or may go astray. Some shaykhs frequently cite His words,

“Say, ‘Allah,’ then leave them,”

as evidence for saying “Allah” alone. They suppose that Allah commanded His Prophet to utter the name in isolation. This is an error by the agreement of the scholars, for His words, “Say, ‘Allah,’” mean: Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought.

This answers His words:

“Say, ‘Who sent down the Book that Moses brought as a light and guidance for people, which you make into sheets, displaying them while concealing much? You have been taught what neither you nor your forefathers knew.’ Say, ‘Allah.’”

That is, Allah is the One who sent down the Book that Moses brought. With this He refuted those who said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.” He said, “Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?” Then He said, “Say, ‘Allah’”—He sent it down—then leave these deniers “to amuse themselves in their vain discourse.”

Further clarification of the foregoing is found in what Sībawayh and other leading grammarians stated: the Arabs use the verb “to say” to quote complete speech, not merely an utterance. What follows this verb as a quotation must be complete speech: a nominal or verbal sentence. This is why they pronounce the particle as inna when it follows the verb “to say.” An isolated noun is not quoted in this way.

Whoever says a hundred times in a day, ‘Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Most Great,’ will have his sins erased, even if they are like the foam of the sea.”

In al-Muwatta’ and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The best words that I and the prophets before me have said are: ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs all dominion and all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

In Sunan Ibn Mājah and elsewhere, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The best remembrance is ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the best supplication is ‘Praise be to Allah.’”

There are many such hadiths concerning the various expressions of remembrance and supplication. Likewise, the words of Allah Most High in the Quran:

of the grammarians’ two views—or a verbal sentence. The implied wording is either “My slaughtering is in the name of Allah” or “I slaughter in the name of Allah.” The same applies when someone reciting the Quran says, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.” The implied wording is “My recitation is in the name of Allah” or “I recite in the name of Allah.” Some understand the implied wording in such cases to be “My beginning is in the name of Allah” or “I begin in the name of Allah.” The former interpretation is better, because the entire act is performed in the name of Allah, not merely its beginning. What is meant is to say, “In the name of Allah,” not to mention the name alone. The same applies to his words to ʿAdī ibn Hātim in an authentic hadith:

Likewise, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

[Al-Khalīl asked his companions to pronounce the letter zāy in Zayd. They replied, “Zāy.” He said, “You have given its name; the letter itself is ‘z’.”] (*)

The grammarians subsequently adopted the convention of calling what ordinary Arabic calls a harf a kalimah (word), and of reserving the term harf (particle) for something that conveys a meaning but is neither a noun nor a verb, such as prepositions and similar particles. As for the spoken letters of the alphabet, the term harf sometimes denotes the actual letter within an utterance and sometimes the name of that letter. When this convention became predominant, those accustomed to it began to imagine that this was also how these terms were used in ordinary Arabic. Some of them consider kalimah to have more than one meaning in Arabic, denoting, for example, both a noun and a sentence. Yet in unambiguous Arabic usage, kalimah is known only in the sense of a complete sentence.

The point here is that the prescribed remembrance of Allah, glorified is He, consists of remembering Him through “a complete sentence.” This is what is termed kalām (speech), an individual instance of which is called a kalimah. It is this that benefits hearts and brings reward and recompense, nearness to Allah, knowledge of Him, love for Him, fear of Him, and other lofty aims and noble objectives.

As for restricting oneself to “an isolated name,” whether stated explicitly or represented by a pronoun, this has no foundation, let alone being a form of remembrance particular to the spiritual elite and those who know Allah. Rather, it leads to various innovations and forms of misguidance, and opens the way to conceiving corrupt spiritual states of the kind found among those who deviate from the faith and those who profess divine union, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
Religion is summed up in “two principles”: that we worship none but Allah, and that we worship Him only as He has prescribed, not through innovations. As the Most High says:

“Whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

This is the realization of the “two testimonies of faith”: the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. The first requires that we worship none but Him; the second affirms that Muhammad is His Messenger, who conveys His message. We must therefore believe what he tells us and obey his commands. He has explained how we are to worship Allah, forbidden us from introducing innovations into religion, and told us that they are misguidance.

The Most High says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah and does good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

Just as we are commanded to fear none but Allah, to rely on none but Allah, to direct our hopes to none but Allah, to seek help from none but Allah, and to worship none but Allah, so too are we commanded to follow the Messenger, obey him, and take him as our example. What is lawful is what he has declared lawful; what is forbidden is what he has forbidden; and religion is what he has prescribed. The Most High says:

“If only they had been satisfied with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.’”

Thus, He attributes giving to both Allah and the Messenger, as He says:

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.”

But He makes reliance upon Allah alone, saying:

“And had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us.’”

He did not say, “and His Messenger.” Likewise, He says in (the other verse):

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

Similar to this is His saying:

“O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers who follow you.”

That is,

Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers, as He says:

“Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?”

Then He says:

“Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger.”

Thus, He attributes giving to both Allah and the Messenger, mentioning His bounty first, because bounty is in Allah’s hand: He grants it to whomever He wills, and Allah possesses immense bounty. His bounty extends to His Messenger and to the believers. He also says:

“Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.”

Thus, He makes Allah alone the object of hope, as in His words:

“So when you have finished, strive in worship, and to your Lord alone turn in hope.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Ibn ‘Abbās: “When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

The Quran teaches this in numerous places. Allah makes worship, reverent fear, and mindfulness of Him due to Him alone, while making obedience and love due to both Allah and His Messenger. Thus Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“Worship Allah, be mindful of Him, and obey me.”

And Allah says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah, and is mindful of Him—it is they who will triumph.”

There are many similar passages. The messengers were commanded that worship should be devoted to Him alone, that hope and reliance should be directed to Him, and that they themselves should be obeyed.

But Satan led the Christians and those like them astray, so they associated partners with Allah and disobeyed the Messenger:

“They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, as well as the Messiah, son of Mary.”

They began directing their hopes to them, relying upon them, and asking of them, despite disobeying their commands and departing from their way. Allah, however, guided the believers sincerely devoted to Him, the people of the straight path, who recognized the truth and followed it,

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked about the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The supplication of my brother Jonah, the Man of the Fish, is: ‘There is no deity except You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.’ No one in distress offers this supplication without Allah relieving his distress.”

What does this supplication mean? Why does it dispel distress? Are there inward conditions that must accompany its utterance? How must the heart’s conviction accord with its meaning for it to bring about relief from affliction?

What is the relevance of his saying, “Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers,” when affirming Allah’s oneness brings relief from affliction? Is his acknowledgment sufficient, or must there also be repentance and firm resolve for the future? What is the underlying reason that affliction is relieved and removed when one ceases to place hope in created beings and becomes detached from them? How can the heart turn away entirely from placing hope in created beings and being attached to them, and instead become attached to Allah Most High, place its hope in Him, and turn wholly to Him? What helps one achieve this?

He answered:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. In the Quran, the terms du‘ā and da‘wah (invocation) encompass two meanings: invocation as worship

and invocation as petition.

Allah Most High says:

“So do not invoke another deity alongside Allah, lest you be among those who are punished.”

He also says:

“Whoever invokes another deity alongside Allah, for which he has no proof, his reckoning rests only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will never prosper.”

And He says:

“Do not invoke another deity alongside Allah. There is no deity except Him.”

And He says:

“When the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him, they almost crowded around him in throngs.”

And He says:

“They invoke none besides Him but female deities, and they invoke none but a rebellious Satan.”

Allah Most High also says:

“To Him alone belongs the true invocation. Those whom they invoke besides Him do not respond to them at all. They are like someone stretching out his hands towards water for it to reach his mouth, but it will never reach it.”

And He says:

“Those who do not invoke another deity alongside Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse.”

At the end of the surah, He says:

“Say, ‘My Lord would not care for you were it not for your invocation.’”

This has been interpreted as: “Were it not for your calling upon Him,” and also as: “Were it not for His calling you.” A verbal noun may be attributed either to its subject or to its object. Attributing it to its subject, however, is stronger, because it must necessarily have a subject. This is therefore the stronger of the two interpretations. That is, He would not care for you were it not that you call upon Him, worshipping Him and asking of Him.

“But you have denied, so the punishment will be inescapable.”

That is, an inescapable punishment for those who deny the truth. The word salāh (prayer) originally means invocation in Arabic. Prayer is called invocation because it encompasses the meaning of invocation: worship and petition.

Allah Most High’s words,

“Call upon Me; I will answer you,”

have been interpreted in both senses. One interpretation is: “Worship Me and obey My command; I will answer you.” As Allah Most High says:

“He answers those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

That is, He responds to them. This usage is well established in Arabic: both istajābahu and istajāba lahu mean “he answered him.” As the poet said:

A caller cried, “O you who answer the call to generosity!”
Yet no one answered him then.

The other interpretation is: “Ask of Me; I will give to you.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is reported to have said:

“Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: ‘Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him? Who asks of Me, that I may give to him? Who seeks My forgiveness, that I may forgive him?’”

He first mentions calling upon Him, then asking and seeking forgiveness. The one who seeks forgiveness is asking, just as the one who asks is calling upon Him. However, mentioning the one who asks for harm to be averted after the one who asks for good, and mentioning both after the one who calls upon Him—a description encompassing them both and others besides—is an instance of mentioning the specific after the general.

Allah Most High says:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the invocation of the one who calls upon Me when he calls upon Me.”

Every petitioner has hope and fear, and thus worships the One he petitions; and everyone who worships Him

 وَلَا يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَخْلُوَ دَاعٍ لِلَّهِ - دُعَاءَ عِبَادَةٍ أَوْ دُعَاءَ مَسْأَلَةٍ - مِنْ الرَّغَبِ وَالرَّهَبِ مِنْ الْخَوْفِ وَالطَّمَعِ. وَمَا يُذْكَرُ عَنْ بَعْضِ الشُّيُوخِ أَنَّهُ جَعَلَ الْخَوْفَ وَالرَّجَاءَ مِنْ مَقَامَاتِ الْعَامَّةِ فَهَذَا قَدْ يُفَسَّرُ مُرَادُهُ بِأَنَّ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ اللَّهِ فَيَقْصِدُونَ التَّلَذُّذَ بِالنَّظَرِ إلَيْهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ هُنَاكَ مَخْلُوقٌ يَتَلَذَّذُونَ بِهِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَرْجُونَ حُصُولَ هَذَا الْمَطْلُوبِ وَيَخَافُونَ حِرْمَانَهُ فَلَمْ يَخْلُوا عَنْ الْخَوْفِ وَالرَّجَاءِ لَكِنَّ مَرْجُوَّهُمْ وَمَخُوفَهُمْ بِحَسَبِ مَطْلُوبِهِمْ.
 وَمَنْ قَالَ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ:
 لَمْ أَعْبُدْكَ شَوْقًا إلَى جَنَّتِكَ وَلَا خَوْفًا مِنْ نَارِكَ
translated_text:
likewise has hope and fear, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment. Thus every worshipper is a petitioner, and every petitioner is a worshipper.

Either term encompasses the other when used alone. When they are used together, however, “petitioner” means someone who seeks to obtain benefit and avert harm through expressions of request and petition, while “worshipper” means someone who seeks this by obeying the command, even without using expressions of petition.

The worshipper who seeks Allah’s Face and to look upon Him likewise has hope and fear, longing and dread: he longs to attain what he seeks and dreads missing it. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope.”

It is inconceivable that anyone who calls upon Allah—whether through worship or petition—should be without longing and dread, fear and hope. As for the reported statement of some spiritual masters that fear and hope belong to the spiritual stations of ordinary believers, their intention may be understood as follows: those brought near to Allah seek His Face, aiming to delight in looking upon Him, even if there is no created thing there from which they derive pleasure. These people hope to attain what they seek and fear being deprived of it. Thus they are not without fear and hope; rather, what they hope for and fear corresponds to what they seek.

As for anyone among them who says:

“I have not worshipped You out of longing for Your Paradise or fear of Your Fire,”

translated_text:
he assumes that Paradise denotes a place where one enjoys created things, and that the Fire denotes a place where there is no torment other than pain inflicted by created things. This reflects their deficient understanding of what Paradise encompasses. Rather, everything Allah has prepared for His allies belongs to Paradise, including looking upon Him. Hence, the best of creation used to ask Allah for Paradise and seek His protection from the Fire. When he asked one of his Companions what he said in his prayer, the man replied:

“I ask Allah for Paradise and seek Allah’s protection from the Fire. But I am not adept at your murmured supplications or those of Mu‘ādh.” He replied, “That is what our supplications revolve around.”

A group of speculative theologians objected to anyone who uttered these words—meaning, “I ask You for the pleasure of looking upon Your Face”—because they supposed that no pleasure could be taken in looking upon Allah, and that bliss could only come through something created. These people misunderstood the meaning of Paradise, just as the others did. Yet the others sought what deserves to be sought, whereas these people denied it.

As for suffering pain in the Fire, this is inevitable. Whoever says, “Were He to cast me into the Fire, I would be content,” is expressing his resolve to remain content. Yet resolves may crumble when confronted with reality. Statements of this kind occur in the words of various people, such as Sumnūn, who said:

“I have no wish for anything but You;
so test me however You will.”

He was then afflicted with difficulty urinating and began going around to schoolchildren, saying, “Pray for your lying uncle.”

Allah Most High says:

“You certainly longed for death before you encountered it. Now you have seen it with your own eyes.”

translated_text:
Some who have discussed the defects of spiritual stations have classified love, contentment, fear, and hope as stations belonging to ordinary people. They base this on witnessing divine decree, holding that whoever witnesses divine decree and the oneness of divine action—until that which once was not vanishes and He who has never ceased to exist remains—passes beyond these things. This claim is flawed both in reality and according to revealed law.

As for reality, it is inconceivable that a living being should lack sensation, love for what suits it, or aversion to what is disagreeable to it. Anyone who says that a living being is equally indifferent to everything decreed is one of two people: either he does not understand what he is saying and is simply ignorant, or he stubbornly denies what is evident.

Even supposing that someone experiences a state that deprives him of his reason—whether called istilām, effacement, annihilation, fainting, or weakness—this does not eliminate his capacity for sensation altogether. He still senses what suits him and what is disagreeable to him. Even if his awareness of some things disappears, his awareness of everything has not disappeared.

Thus, whoever claims that someone witnessing Allah’s oneness in lordship enters the station of undifferentiated awareness and annihilation, and consequently perceives no distinctions, is mistaken. Distinction is inevitable, for it is a necessary feature of human existence. But if he abandons the distinctions prescribed by revealed law, he remains subject to those dictated by his natural inclinations. He is then following his desires rather than obeying his Lord.
