translated_text:
divinity encompasses lordship, and lordship necessarily implies divinity, the fact that either term includes the other when used alone does not prevent each from bearing its distinct meaning when used alongside the other. Thus Allah says:

“Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,
the Sovereign of mankind,
the God of mankind.”

And He says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

He thus brings together the two names: God and Lord. “God” is the One who is worshipped and deserves to be worshipped, while “Lord” is the One who nurtures His servant and directs his affairs. Hence worship is associated with His name Allah, and supplication with His name Lord. Worship is the ultimate purpose for which creation was created. Divinity is the ultimate end, whereas lordship encompasses creating creatures and bringing them into being, and thus encompasses the beginning of their existence.

When someone praying says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

he places the intended purpose, which is the ultimate end, before the means, which is the starting point. Worship is the end sought, and seeking help is the means to it: the former is the underlying purpose, and the latter is the cause. The distinction between a final cause and an efficient cause is well known. Hence the saying: “What comes first in thought comes last in action, and what comes first in aspiration comes last in attainment.” The final cause therefore comes first in conception and intention, but last in actual existence.

The believer intends from the outset to worship Allah, knowing that this can only be accomplished with His help. He therefore says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Since worship is associated with the name Allah, Exalted is He, the prescribed words of remembrance employ this name, such as the words of the call to prayer:

“Allah is the Greatest, Allah is the Greatest.”

Likewise, the two testimonies of faith:

“I bear witness that there is no god but Allah. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

Likewise, the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer):

“All greetings of reverence belong to Allah.”

Likewise, the expressions of glorification, praise, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and proclamation of His greatness:

“Glory be to Allah; all praise is for Allah; there is no god but Allah; Allah is the Greatest.”

As for supplication, it frequently employs the name Lord, as in the words of Adam and Eve:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

And the words of Noah:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You for that of which I have no knowledge.”

And the words of Moses:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

And the words of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend:

“Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House, our Lord, so that they may establish prayer,”

and the rest of the verse. And his words together with Ishmael:

“Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

Likewise, the words of those who say:

“Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.”

There are many such examples.

It has been reported that Mālik said:

“I dislike a man saying in his supplication, ‘O my Master, O my Master! O Compassionate One, O Compassionate One!’ Rather, he should supplicate as the prophets did: ‘Our Lord, our Lord.’”

Al-Utbī transmitted this from him in al-Utbiyyah.

Allah Most High says concerning people of understanding:

“Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: ‘Our Lord, You have not created this in vain. Glory be to You! Protect us, then, from the punishment of the Fire,’”

and the verses that follow.

Thus, when the intention to petition first comes into a servant’s heart, it is fitting for him to ask Allah by His name “Lord.” If he asks Him by His name “Allah,” which encompasses the name “Lord,” that too is good. But when the intention to worship first comes into his heart, the name “Allah” is more appropriate.

When beginning with praise, he mentions the name “Allah”; when intending to supplicate, he invokes the name “Lord.” Thus Jonah said:

“There is no god but You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

And Adam said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Jonah, peace be upon him, departed in anger. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient with your Lord’s judgment, and do not be like the man of the fish.”

And He Most High says:

“Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy.”

He had done something for which he deserved blame. It was therefore fitting for his condition that he begin by praising his Lord and acknowledging that there is no god but Him. He alone deserves to be worshipped, to the exclusion of all others; personal desires must therefore not be obeyed, for following them weakens the worship of Allah alone. It has been reported that Jonah, peace be upon him, regretted that the punishment had been lifted from his people after it had loomed over them. He feared that they would accuse him of lying, and so he became angry.

He acted in a way that called for the words Allah Most High has related, and for the declaration:

“There is no god but You.”

These words entail denying divinity to anything other than Allah, whether its attribution arises from personal desire, obedience to created beings, or anything else. Thus he said:

“Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

A servant says words such as these concerning what he supposes when it does not accord with reality, and what he desires when it is not good.

As for Adam, peace be upon him, he first acknowledged his sin, saying:

“We have wronged ourselves.”

Adam had nothing within him that contested his desire to obey Allah’s command in a way that would rival Allah’s exclusive right to worship. Rather, he believed Satan to be truthful when he

“swore to them both, ‘I am indeed a sincere adviser to you.’”

“Thus he brought about their fall through deception.”

Satan deceived them both and presented himself as their sincere adviser. Having accepted his deception and apparent sincerity, their condition called for them to say:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

This was because of their negligence, not because of some desire or personal interest competing with Allah’s exclusive right to worship. They needed Him to nurture them as their Lord, perfecting their knowledge and intention so that they would not be deceived in such a way again. Thus they recognized their need for Allah, their Lord, whose place no one else could take in meeting their needs.

Jonah, the man of the fish, recognized that his departure in anger and his aversion to those people’s being saved had involved a failure to fulfil Allah’s exclusive right to worship. This involved a degree of opposition in action, arising from love for something else, which required him to devote his love and worship entirely to Allah and to say:

“There is no god but You.”

For when a servant says, “There is no god but You,” this eradicates his taking his own desire as a god. It has been reported:

“Beneath the vault of heaven, no object of worship is more grievous in Allah’s sight than desire that is followed.”

Thus Jonah, may Allah’s blessings be upon him, perfected his devotion to Allah as his only God and his rejection of desire taken as a god besides Him. When he fully realized the meaning of his words, “There is no god but You,” no desire remained in him—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him—that competed with the True One’s exclusive right to worship. Rather, he devoted his worship sincerely to Allah, for he was among the finest of Allah’s sincere servants.

And (also), such a state may befall someone, leaving within him

a measure of resentment towards the divine decree, opposition to Allah in His creation and commands, and troubling doubts about His wisdom and mercy. The servant therefore needs to rid himself of two things: corrupt opinions and corrupt desires. He must recognize that wisdom and justice lie in what Allah’s knowledge and wisdom dictate, not in what the servant’s own knowledge and wisdom dictate. His desires must follow what Allah has commanded, leaving him with no desire that opposes Allah’s command and judgment.

Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort over what you have judged and submit in full submission.”

It has been reported that the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until his desires accord with what I have brought.”

Abū Hātim narrated it in his Sahīh. In the Sahīh, it is reported that Umar said to him, “O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, you are dearer to me than my own self.” He replied, “Now, O Umar!”

Also in the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon him, is reported to have said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his children, his parents, and all mankind.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you delight in are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.’”

Thus, if faith is not attained until the servant accepts Allah’s Messenger as judge, submits to him, and brings his desires into accord with what he brought, and until love for the Messenger and striving in Allah’s cause takes precedence over his love for himself, his wealth, and his family, then how much more must he accept Allah Most High as judge and submit to Him?

translated_text:
So if someone believes that certain people deserve punishment, yet Allah has forgiven them and shown them mercy, and he resents this, his resentment stems either from a will that opposes Allah’s judgment or from an assumption that contradicts Allah’s knowledge. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. Once you know that He is All-Knowing and All-Wise, no grounds remain for resenting what He has done. This applies to what He has commanded and to what He has left, which He has not commanded us to hate or resent.

As for things that exist which He has commanded us to hate—such as disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience—we must obey His command. This is unlike His acceptance of His servants’ repentance and His deliverance of them from punishment. These are among His deeds that He has not commanded us to hate; rather, they are things He loves, for He loves those who repent and those who purify themselves. To resent this is a form of following a will that rivals His divinity.

Anyone harbouring such a will must therefore make his worship sincerely devoted to Allah alone, saying:

“None has the right to be worshipped but You.”

We must love what He loves, be pleased with what pleases Him, enjoin what He commands, and forbid what He prohibits. Since He “loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves,” we must love them, rather than make gods of our own wishes that conflict with what He loves.

The discussion here rests upon a “principle”: by the consensus of the Muslim community, the prophets, may Allah’s blessings be upon them, are protected from error in what they report about Allah, glorified be He, and in conveying His messages. Hence, it is obligatory to believe in everything they were given, as

He, the Exalted, said:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given, and what the prophets were given by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’”

“So if they believe as you believe, they are rightly guided. But if they turn away, they are only in opposition. Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

And He said:

“But righteousness is to believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture, and the prophets.”

And He said:

“The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ And they say, ‘We hear and obey. We seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.’”

Those who are not prophets, by contrast, are not protected from error as the prophets are, even if they are allies of Allah. Hence, whoever reviles any prophet is to be put to death, according to the consensus of the jurists, whereas whoever reviles anyone else is not to be put to death.

This protection from error established for the prophets is what ensures that the purpose of prophethood and messengership is fulfilled. A “prophet” is one who receives tidings from Allah, while a “messenger” is one whom Allah Most High has sent. Every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger. Their protection from error in what they convey from Allah is established; thus, by the consensus of the Muslims, no error is allowed to persist in it.

But can something occur that Allah then rectifies, removing what Satan casts and making His verses firm? There are two views on this. What is transmitted from the early generations accords with the Quran on this matter.

Those among the later scholars who ruled this out challenged the reported addition to Sūrat al-Najm:

“These are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for.”

They said that this had not been established. Those who knew it to be established said that Satan had cast these words into the listeners’ ears, but the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had not uttered them. Yet the question still arises on this understanding as well.

They also interpreted His words:

“…except that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation”

as referring to inner thoughts. Those who affirmed what was transmitted from the early generations, however, said that these reports were firmly established and could not be impugned, and that the Quran supported them in His words:

“We never sent a messenger or a prophet before you except that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation. But Allah removes what Satan casts; then Allah makes His verses firm. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“So that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those whose hearts are diseased and those whose hearts are hardened. Indeed, the wrongdoers are in profound opposition.”

“And so that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, believe in it, and have their hearts humbly submit to it. Indeed, Allah guides those who believe to a straight path.”

They said that the reports explaining this verse were well known and firmly established in the books of Quranic commentary and hadith, and that the Quran agreed with them. For Allah’s removal of what Satan casts and His making His verses firm serve precisely to remove what has intruded into His verses and to distinguish truth from falsehood, so that His verses are not confused

Thus, the Messenger’s explanation—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that Allah made His verses firm and removed what Satan had cast provides still stronger evidence of his scrupulous truthfulness and freedom from lying. Or is it obligatory to affirm such protection only in conveying the message? Must protection from disbelief and sins also be affirmed before the prophetic mission, or not? This question is discussed at length elsewhere.

The view held by the majority, which accords with the reports transmitted from the early generations, affirms that the prophets are protected from being allowed to persist in any sin whatsoever, and rejects the view that they may be allowed to persist in sins. When carefully examined, the arguments of those who affirm protection from sin establish only this position. Nor do the arguments of those who deny it establish any instance of a sin in which the prophets were allowed to persist.

Those who affirm protection from sin argue that following the prophets’ example is prescribed, and that this is permissible only if one allows that their actions may be sins. Yet it is well known that following their example is prescribed only in matters in which they were allowed to continue, not in matters which they were forbidden to do and from which they turned back. Likewise, obedience to their commands and prohibitions is obligatory only where these have not been abrogated. An abrogated command or prohibition may no longer be treated as prescribing or forbidding something, let alone as requiring compliance and obedience.

The same applies to their arguments that sins are incompatible with perfection, that they are more reprehensible when committed by someone who has received great blessings, that they cause people to turn away, and other such rational arguments. These apply only when someone persists in sin and does not turn back. Otherwise, through sincere repentance that He accepts, Allah raises the repentant person to a higher station than before, as stated by

some of the early generations:

“David, peace be upon him, was better after repentance than he had been before his sin.”

Another said: “Had repentance not been the most beloved of things to Him, He would not have tested those of His creation most honored in His sight with sin.” The authentic hadith collections record the hadith on repentance:

“Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than a man who stopped at a place,” and so on.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who constantly repent and loves those who purify themselves.”

He also says:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds: Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds.”

An authentic collection also records the hadith about:

“The man whose minor sins Allah lays before him while concealing his major sins from him. He fears that his major sins will be revealed, but Allah says to him: ‘I have forgiven them for you and replaced every evil deed with a good deed.’ He then says: ‘My Lord, I have other evil deeds that I have not seen.’”

When he sees evil deeds being replaced with good deeds, he asks to see the major sins whose disclosure he had feared. Clearly, his state with this replacement is better than it would have been had neither the evil deeds nor their replacement occurred.

translated_text:
and that Allah may turn in mercy to the believing men and believing women. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.”

Thus, every person’s ultimate aim is to be among the believing men and women to whom Allah has turned in mercy. The Quran, the authentic Sunnah, and the scriptures revealed before the Quran contain more support for this position than can be enumerated.

Those who reject this have interpreted these texts much as the Jahmiyyah, Qadariyyah, and Dahriyyah interpret the texts concerning “the divine names and attributes,” “divine decree,” and “the Hereafter.” Such interpretations are akin to those of the esotericist Qarmatians: they are self-evidently false and constitute a distortion of words from their proper meanings. One of these people intends to honor the prophets, yet ends up denying their truthfulness; he wishes to believe in them, yet falls into disbelief in them.

Moreover, they have derived no benefit from the infallibility established by revelation, reason, and scholarly consensus—namely, “infallibility in conveying the revelation”—since they do not acknowledge the implications of what the prophets conveyed. They acknowledge only wording whose meaning they have distorted, or approach it like the unlettered who know nothing of the Scripture beyond mere recitation.

As for the infallibility they have claimed, even if it were established, they would derive no benefit from it, nor, on their own terms, would they have any need of it. It concerns others, rather than what they themselves have been commanded to believe. Thus, one of them makes pronouncements about the prophets in this matter without any authority from Allah, while neglecting his own duty to believe the prophets and obey them. It is through this that happiness is attained, while its opposite brings misery. Allah Most High says:

“He is responsible only for what he has been charged with, and you are responsible for what you have been charged with”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High never mentions any such matter concerning a prophet in the Quran without accompanying it with repentance and seeking forgiveness. Thus, Adam and his wife said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Noah said:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. Unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.”

Abraham, Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him, said:

“Our Lord, forgive me, my parents, and the believers on the Day the Reckoning takes place.”

He also said:

“And who, I hope, will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.”

Moses said:

“You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us. You are the best of those who forgive. And ordain good for us in this world and in the Hereafter. Indeed, we have turned to You in repentance.”

He also said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

And:

“When he regained consciousness, he said, ‘Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers.’”

Allah Most High says of David:

“He sought his Lord’s forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned to Him in repentance. So We forgave him that. Indeed, he has nearness to Us and a good place of return.”

Allah Most High relates that Solomon said:

“Forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will belong to no one after me. Indeed, You are the Bestower.”

As for Joseph, the utterly truthful, Allah mentions no sin on his part. Accordingly, He does not mention him seeking forgiveness as would be appropriate following a sin. Rather, He says:

“Thus did We turn evil and indecency away from him. Indeed, he was one of Our chosen servants.”

He thus states that He turned evil and indecency away from Joseph. This indicates that no evil or indecency proceeded from him.

As for His words:

“She certainly desired him, and he felt an inclination toward her, which he would have acted on had he not seen the proof of his Lord.”

The point here is that everything blameworthy in the account of Jonah was forgiven: Allah replaced it with good deeds and raised his rank. After emerging from the fish’s belly and repenting, he held a higher rank than before those events occurred. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, and do not be like the man of the fish when he called out, filled with anguish.”

“Had grace from his Lord not reached him, he would have been cast onto barren ground, condemned.”

“But his Lord chose him and made him one of the righteous.”

This contrasts with his state when the fish swallowed him, for Allah says:

“Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy.”

He thus states that Jonah was blameworthy at that time. A blameworthy person is someone who has done something deserving of blame. The blame therefore applied to that state, not to his state when he was cast onto barren ground, ailing. Thus, after saying:

“There is no deity except You; glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers,”

his state was more exalted than it had been before those events occurred. What counts is the perfection attained at the end, not what happened at the beginning; deeds are judged by their endings. Allah Most High created the human being and brought him forth from his mother’s womb knowing nothing, then taught him, taking him from deficiency to perfection. It is therefore not permissible to judge a person’s worth by what he did before attaining perfection; rather, he must be judged by his perfected state. In their final state, Jonah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the other prophets are in the most perfect of states.

This is where those who preferred the angels over the prophets and the righteous went wrong: they compared the angels’ perfection with the righteous at their beginning, while they were still deficient. Had they instead considered the state of the prophets and the righteous after entering the Gardens and attaining the pleasure of the Most Merciful, when everything deficient and blameworthy has disappeared and everything bringing mercy and peace has been attained, until they are firmly settled in their abiding home—

“and the angels will enter upon them from every gate,”

“Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. How excellent is the final home!”—

then, with that state taken into account, its superiority over the state of other created beings would have become apparent. Otherwise, could any reasonable person judge one of them by his state before attaining perfection when discussing praise, superiority, and freedom from shortcomings and faults? If that were the basis of judgment, one would have to consider him when he was a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then when the spirit was breathed into him, then as a newborn, a nursing infant, a weaned child, and through further stages. Clearly, in these states he did not yet possess the qualities of perfection that would entitle him to the fullest praise and distinction, and to superiority over every kind and generation. His superiority is determined only by his ultimate state, when perfection has been attained.

Some people suppose that someone born into Islam who has never disbelieved is superior to someone who was a disbeliever and then embraced Islam. This is incorrect. Rather, what counts is the final outcome: whichever of them is more mindful of Allah in his final state is superior. It is well known that the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, who believed in Allah and His Messenger after having disbelieved, are superior to those born into Islam, whether their own children or others. may know and love good, and know and hate evil, more fully than someone who has not known and tasted both as he has. Indeed, someone who has known only good may encounter evil without recognizing it as such; he may then either fall into it or fail to condemn it as someone familiar with it would. For this reason, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “The bonds of Islam are undone, one by one, only when people grow up within Islam without knowing pre-Islamic ignorance.”

It is just as ʿUmar said. Islam is perfected through enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and this is brought to completion through striving in Allah’s cause. Someone raised among what is right, knowing nothing else, may lack the knowledge of wrongdoing and its harm possessed by someone familiar with it. Nor will he strive against its practitioners as someone well acquainted with them would. Thus, a person familiar with evil and its causes, if his intentions are sound, takes precautions against it, restrains its practitioners, and strives against them in ways that others do not.

For this reason, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, surpassed those who came after them in faith and striving: their knowledge of good and evil, their love of good, and their hatred of evil were more complete. They knew the goodness of Islam, faith, and righteous deeds, and the ugliness of disbelief and sins. Likewise, someone who has tasted poverty, illness, and fear is more eager for prosperity, health, and security than someone who has not experienced them.

Hence the saying:

“A thing’s beauty is revealed by its opposite.”

translated_text:
It is also said:

“Things become clear through their opposites.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say:

“I am no deceiver, nor can a deceiver fool me.”

The praiseworthy, sound heart is one that desires good, not evil. Its perfection lies in knowing both good and evil. As for someone who does not recognize evil, this is a deficiency in him, not something deserving praise.

This does not mean that everyone who has tasted disbelief and sins necessarily knows them better and hates them more than someone who has never tasted them. This is not invariably the case: a physician may know more about diseases than the patients themselves. The Prophets—may blessings and peace be upon them—are physicians of faith. They know better than anyone else what sets hearts right and what corrupts them, even though a Prophet may not have tasted the evil that others have tasted.

Rather, the point is that some people, through tasting evil, gain a knowledge of it, an aversion to it, and a love of good when they taste it, which some others do not attain. An example is someone who was a polytheist, a Jew, or a Christian, and came to know the specious arguments, corrupt doctrines, darkness, and evil found in disbelief. Then Allah opened his heart to Islam and acquainted him with its virtues. Such a person may have a greater desire for Islam and a stronger hatred of disbelief than some who have not understood the reality of disbelief and Islam, but instead turn away from aspects of both, or merely follow others in praising the one and condemning the other.

translated_text:
An example of this is someone who has tasted hunger and then the satisfaction of eating his fill, illness and then health, or fear and then security. His love and desire for health, security, and having enough to eat, and his aversion to hunger, fear, and illness, are greater than those of someone who has never suffered these afflictions or known their reality.

Likewise, someone who joined the people of religious innovation and wickedness, but to whom Allah then made the truth clear, granting him sincere repentance and enabling him to strive in His cause, may surpass others in explaining their condition, shunning their evil practices, and striving against them. Nuʿaym ibn Hammād al-Khuzāʿī, who was stern towards the Jahmiyyah, said: “I am stern towards them because I used to be one of them.”

Allah Most High has said:

“As for those who emigrated after being persecuted, then strove and remained steadfast—your Lord thereafter is surely All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

This verse was revealed concerning a group of the Companions whom the polytheists had persecuted into forsaking their religion. Then Allah turned to them in mercy, and they emigrated to Allah and His Messenger, strove, and remained steadfast.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb and Khālid ibn al-Walīd, may Allah be pleased with them both, were among the fiercest opponents of Islam. Yet when they embraced Islam, they surpassed people who had preceded them in accepting it. Some who had preceded them were below them in faith and righteous deeds because of the excellence of their striving against the disbelievers and their support for Allah and His Messenger. And ʿUmar, being more complete in faith, sincerity, truthfulness, knowledge, discernment, and light, further removed from the desires of the soul, and loftier in aspiration

in establishing Allah’s religion, ranked above all other Muslims except Abū Bakr—may Allah be pleased with them all. This and other examples show that what matters is the perfection attained at the end, not the shortcomings at the beginning.

As for the report found among the Israelite traditions:

“Allah said to David: ‘As for the sin, We have forgiven it; but as for love, it will not return.’”

Even if you knew this to be authentic, it would not constitute religious law for us, and we may not build our religion upon it. For the religion of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, brought teachings concerning repentance that no previous revealed law had brought. Hence he said:

“I am the Prophet of mercy, and I am the Prophet of repentance.”

Through him, burdens and shackles imposed upon those before us were lifted.

Allah Most High has said in His Book:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves.”

We are also told that He, Most High, rejoices at His servant’s repentance more than someone who has lost the food, drink, and mount he needs rejoices upon finding them after losing all hope. If such is the Lord’s joy at the repentance of one who repents, and such is His love, how can it be said that He will not love him again?

“And He is the All-Forgiving, the All-Loving, Lord of the Throne, the All-Glorious, Doer of whatever He wills.”

His affection and love, however, are proportionate to how the servant draws near to Him after repentance. If what he does after repentance of the things Allah loves is better than what he did before, then His love for him after repentance is greater than His love for him before repentance. But if it is less,

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him. My servant draws near to Me through nothing like fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I do not hesitate over anything I am to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet he must undergo it.’”

It is well known that the best of Allah’s friends after the prophets are the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers. The Lord’s love and affection for them after they repented of unbelief, transgression, and disobedience were of the highest degree. The more they drew near to Him through voluntary acts of worship after fulfilling their obligations, the more He loved them and bestowed His affection upon them.

Allah Most High has said:

“Perhaps Allah will bring about affection between you and those of them whom you have treated as enemies. Allah is All-Powerful, and Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

translated_text:
Allah brought about affection between them and the messengers and believers. They differed in the degree of that affection: ‘Ikrimah, Suhayl, and al-Hārith ibn Hishām had greater affection than Abū Sufyān ibn Harb and others like him. It is established in the Sahīh that Hind, the wife of Abū Sufyān and mother of Mu‘āwiyah, said:

“By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, there was no household on earth that I wished to see humiliated more than yours. Now there is no household on earth that I wish to see honored more than yours.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, expressed something similar to her.

It is well known that the love and affection between believers follow from their love for Allah Most High, for the firmest bond of faith is loving for Allah’s sake and hating for Allah’s sake. Loving for Allah’s sake is part of perfecting monotheism, whereas loving others as rivals to Allah is polytheism.

Allah Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Thus, the affection that developed between the Messenger and the believers, on the one hand, and the polytheists who had opposed them, on the other, was affection and love for Allah’s sake. Whoever loves Allah, Allah loves him; whoever holds Allah dear, Allah holds him dear. It is therefore clear that Allah loved them and held them dear after their repentance, just as they loved Him and held Him dear. How, then, can it be said that one who repents receives forgiveness but not affection?

If someone says:

“Those people were unbelievers who did not know that what they had done was forbidden; rather, they were ignorant, unlike someone who knows that an act is forbidden yet commits it.”

The response is twofold:

First, that is not the case. Rather, many unbelievers knew that Muhammad was the Messenger of Allah, yet opposed him out of envy and arrogance. Abū Sufyān had heard accounts confirming the Prophet’s prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him, that others had not heard, including what he heard from Umayyah ibn Abī al-Salt and from Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantines. He himself reported that he remained certain that the Prophet’s cause, peace and blessings be upon him, would prevail, until Allah brought him to Islam despite his aversion to it. Statements heard from him during the year of Yarmūk and at other times demonstrated the sincerity of his Islam and his love for Allah and His Messenger after that intense hostility.

Allah Most High says:

“Those who do not invoke another god besides Allah, nor kill a soul Allah has forbidden to be killed except by right, nor commit adultery. Whoever does these things will meet with punishment.”

“The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will remain in it forever, humiliated.”

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds: Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds.”

If Allah replaces their evil deeds with good deeds, then those good deeds bring them Allah’s affection. Nor is the replacement of evil deeds with good deeds restricted to those who were unbelievers. Allah Most High says:

“Allah accepts the repentance only of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterward. It is they whose repentance Allah accepts. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

(The second response):

The distinction mentioned between one repentant person and another regarding Allah Most High’s love for those who repent has no basis. Rather, the Quran and the Sunnah indicate that Allah loves those who repent and rejoices at their repentance, whether or not they knew that what they had done was a sin.

Anyone who knew that what he had done was a sin and then repented must replace his blameworthy qualities with praiseworthy ones. If he hated the truth, he must come to love it; and if he loved falsehood, he must come to hate it. The repentant person’s knowledge of the truth, his love for it and adherence to it, and his hatred and avoidance of falsehood are all things that Allah Most High loves and is pleased with. Likewise, Allah’s love corresponds to the extent to which His servant does what He loves. The more a person does what Allah loves, the greater Allah’s love for him.

When he turns from what Allah dislikes to what He loves, intensely hating the falsehood he formerly followed and intensely loving the truth to which he has turned, Allah’s love and affection for him must therefore increase. Indeed, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds: because he has replaced his blameworthy qualities with praiseworthy ones, Allah replaces his evil deeds with good deeds. For recompense is of the same nature as the deed.

Thus, if the repentant person does more of what Allah loves than someone else does, Allah’s love for him is greater. And if he does more of what Allah loves him to do than he did before repenting, then

Allah’s affection for him after repentance is greater than His affection for him before repentance. How, then, can it be said, “Affection does not return”?

This also clarifies the answer to the misconception of those who say, “Allah sends as a prophet only someone who was protected from sin before prophethood,” as a group among the Rāfidah and others maintain. The same applies to those who say, “He sends as a prophet only someone who was a believer before prophethood.” These people mistakenly suppose that sins remain a deficiency even after a person repents of them. This is the source of their error. Whoever thinks that a person who has sinned remains deficient despite sincere repentance is gravely mistaken. None of the blame or punishment that befalls sinners befalls the repentant person. If he repents promptly, none of it befalls him; if he delays repentance, then, between his sins and his repentance, he may incur blame and punishment appropriate to his circumstances.

The prophets—Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them—did not delay repentance. Rather, they hastened and raced towards it. They neither delayed nor persisted in sin; indeed, they were protected from doing so. If any of them delayed repentance briefly, Allah expiated that through the trials He subjected him to, as He did with Jonah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is according to the well-known view that he was cast overboard after receiving prophethood. Those who hold that he was cast overboard before prophethood have no need of this explanation.

A person who repents of disbelief and sins may be superior to someone who never fell into disbelief or sins. If he may be superior, then the superior person is more deserving of prophethood than someone who does not equal him in virtue. Allah has recounted the sins of Joseph’s brothers, yet they are the Asbāt (the Tribes) whom Allah Most High made prophets. Allah Most High also says:

“So Lot believed him, and he said, ‘I am emigrating to my Lord.’”

Lot thus believed Abraham, peace be upon him, and Allah Most High subsequently sent him to the people of Lot. Allah Most High says in the account of Shuʿayb:

“The arrogant chiefs among his people said, ‘We will certainly expel you, Shuʿayb, and those who believe with you from our town, unless you return to our religion.’ He said, ‘Even if we are unwilling? We would indeed be fabricating a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it. We cannot return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in His knowledge. In Allah we put our trust. Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of judges.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“Those who disbelieved said to their messengers, ‘We will certainly expel you from our land unless you return to our religion.’ Their Lord then revealed to them, ‘We will surely destroy the wrongdoers and settle you in the land after them. This is for whoever fears standing before Me and fears My warning.’”

Once it is understood that what counts is the perfection attained at the end, and that this perfection is attained only through repentance and seeking forgiveness, it follows that every servant must repent. Repentance is obligatory upon all, from the earliest generations to the latest. As Allah Most High says:

“So that Allah may punish the hypocritical men and women and the men and women who associate partners with Him, and turn in mercy to the believing men and women. Allah is ever All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Allah, glorified be He, has told us of the repentance of Adam, Noah, and those who came after them, down to the last of the messengers, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The last revelation he received—or among the last—was His saying, Most High:

“When Allah’s help comes and victory,
and you see people entering Allah’s religion in multitudes,
then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

In the two Sahīhs, ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would frequently say while bowing and prostrating: “Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me.” He was thereby putting the Quran into practice.

Before that, Allah had revealed to him:

“Allah has indeed turned in mercy to the Prophet, the Emigrants, and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of some of them had almost swerved. Then He turned to them in mercy. Indeed, He is Most Kind and Most Merciful to them.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O people, repent to your Lord. By Him in whose hand is my soul, I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.”

In Sahīh Muslim, al-Agharr al-Muzanī reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah’s forgiveness one hundred times a day.”

In the Sunan collections, Ibn ʿUmar said: We would count the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying one hundred times in a single gathering: “My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepter of repentance, the All-Forgiving.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Seek forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and women.”

“Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory, so that Allah may forgive your past and future sins.”

This concerns those who repent. That is why He states in general, unrestricted, and categorical terms that He forgives all sins. In the other verse, however, He says:

“But He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

He thus specifies what falls short of associating partners with Him and makes its forgiveness subject to His will. Given, then, that associating partners with Allah is forgiven only through repentance, whereas Allah forgives lesser sins for those who repent and may forgive them without repentance for whomever He wills, acknowledging one’s sin together with belief in Allah’s oneness ensures forgiveness if that acknowledgment includes repentance. Once a sin is forgiven, its punishment is removed, for forgiveness means protection from the harm of sin.

Some people say, “Forgiveness means concealment.” They maintain that maghfirah (forgiveness) and al-Ghaffār (the Oft-Forgiving) are so called because they convey the meaning of concealment, and interpret Allah’s name al-Ghaffār as “the Concealer.” This, however, falls short of the full meaning of forgiveness. Forgiveness means protection from the harm of sin, such that one is not punished for it. Whoever has had his sin forgiven is not punished for it. Mere concealment, however, does not preclude inward punishment. Anyone who is punished for a sin, inwardly or outwardly, has not been forgiven for it. A sin is forgiven only when the person is spared the punishment that the sin deserves. If, despite being forgiven, he is subjected to a trial that serves to increase his reward, this does not contradict forgiveness.

A person may think that he has repented when he has not; he may merely have stopped committing the sin. Merely stopping is not the same as repenting. “That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed,”

al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād said, “The most sincere and the most correct.” They asked, “Abū ‘Alī, what does ‘the most sincere and the most correct’ mean?”

He replied, “If a deed is sincere but not correct, it is not accepted; and if it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted. It must be both sincere and correct. To be sincere means that it is done for Allah, and to be correct means that it accords with the Sunnah.”

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say in his supplication:

“O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your Face alone, and give no one else any share in them.”

A detailed discussion of repentance belongs elsewhere. As for acknowledging one’s sin in humble submission to Allah without abandoning it, this amounts to merely seeking forgiveness without repentance. Such a person is like someone who asks

original_text:

 فَمِثْلُ هَذَا الدُّعَاءِ قَدْ تَحْصُلُ مَعَهُ الْمَغْفِرَةُ وَإِذَا لَمْ تَحْصُلْ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَحْصُلَ مَعَهُ صَرْفُ شَرٍّ آخَرَ أَوْ حُصُولُ خَيْرٍ آخَرَ فَهُوَ نَافِعٌ كَمَا يَنْفَعُ كُلُّ دُعَاءٍ.
 وَقَوْلُ مَنْ قَالَ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ:
 الِاسْتِغْفَارُ مَعَ الْإِصْرَارِ تَوْبَةُ الْكَذَّابِينَ،
 فَهَذَا إذَا كَانَ الْمُسْتَغْفِرُ يَقُولُهُ عَلَى وَجْهِ التَّوْبَةِ أَوْ يَدَّعِي أَنَّ اسْتِغْفَارَهُ تَوْبَةٌ وَأَنَّهُ تَائِبٌ بِهَذَا الِاسْتِغْفَارِ فَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُ مَعَ الْإِصْرَارِ لَا يَكُونُ تَائِبًا فَإِنَّ التَّوْبَةَ وَالْإِصْرَارَ ضِدَّانِ:
 الْإِصْرَارُ يُضَادُّ التَّوْبَةَ لَكِنْ لَا يُضَادُّ الِاسْتِغْفَارَ بِدُونِ التَّوْبَةِ.
وَقَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ:
 هَلْ الِاعْتِرَافُ بِالذَّنْبِ الْمُعَيَّنِ يُوجِبُ دَفْعَ مَا حَصَلَ بِذُنُوبِ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ أَمْ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ اسْتِحْضَارِ جَمِيعِ الذُّنُوبِ؟
 فَجَوَابُ هَذَا مَبْنِيٌّ عَلَى أُصُولٍ:
translated_text:
Allah Most High to forgive his sin even though he has not repented of it. This is despair of Allah’s mercy, and his forgiveness cannot be assured, for he is merely offering a supplication.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No one offers a supplication involving neither sin nor the severing of kinship ties without receiving one of three things: either Allah grants his request promptly, reserves an equivalent reward for him, or averts an equivalent evil from him.”

They said, “Messenger of Allah, then we shall supplicate abundantly!” He replied, “Allah has still more.”

Such a supplication may bring forgiveness. If it does not, it must bring either the averting of some other evil or the attainment of some other good. Thus, it is beneficial, as every supplication is beneficial.

As for the statement of some scholars, “Seeking forgiveness while persisting in sin is the repentance of liars,” this applies when the person seeks forgiveness as an act of repentance, or claims that his seeking forgiveness constitutes repentance and that he has thereby repented. There is no doubt that, while persisting in sin, he has not repented, for repentance and persistence in sin are opposites. Persistence in sin is incompatible with repentance, but not with seeking forgiveness without repentance.

As for the question, “Does acknowledging a particular sin necessarily avert the consequences of multiple sins, or must one call all one’s sins to mind?”—the answer rests on several principles:

original_text:
أَحَدُهَا:

{سَأَلْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَنْ نَظْرَةِ الْفَجْأَةِ فَقَالَ: اصْرِفْ بَصَرَك}

 وَأَحْمَد يَقُولُ:
translated_text:
First: Repentance from one sin is valid even while a person persists in another, if the motive for repenting of one is stronger than the motive for repenting of the other, or the deterrent to one is stronger. This is the well-known position among both the early and later scholars.

A group of speculative theologians, such as Abū Hāshim, held that repentance from one evil deed is invalid while a person persists in another. They argued: “Unless repentance is motivated by fear of Allah, it is not valid repentance; yet fear of Allah restrains a person from all sins, not merely some of them.”

Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and Ibn ‘Aqīl related this as a position reported from Ahmad, because al-Marwadhī reported that Ahmad was asked about someone who had repented of sexual immorality and said, “If I fell ill, I would not return to it,” but would not give up looking. Ahmad replied:

“What sort of repentance is this? Jarīr ibn ‘Abd Allāh said: ‘I asked the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, about an inadvertent glance, and he said: “Avert your gaze.”’”

The well-known position of Ahmad and the other imams, however, is that such repentance is valid. In this case, Ahmad meant only that this was not comprehensive repentance by which the person would be counted, without qualification, among the repentant. He did not mean that this person’s sin was equivalent to that of someone who persists in major sins. His statements transmitted through numerous independent reports, together with his firmly established pronouncements, contradict such an interpretation.

It is more appropriate to interpret an imam’s statements in a way that makes them mutually consistent than to interpret them as contradictory—especially when the alternative position is an innovation not known to have been held by any of the early scholars. Ahmad says:

original_text:

(أَيْضًا)

 بِحُبُوطِ جَمِيعِ الْحَسَنَاتِ بِالْكَبِيرَةِ. وَأَمَّا الصَّحَابَةُ وَأَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ فَعَلَى أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْكَبَائِرِ يَخْرُجُونَ
translated_text:
“Beware of speaking on a matter in which you have no imam to follow.” During the ordeal, he would say: “How can I say what has never been said before?” Ahmad’s adherence to the Sunnah and the transmitted reports, his eagerness to follow them, and his aversion to opposing them are established through numerous independent reports, known to scholars and ordinary people alike who are familiar with his life.

As for their assertion that fear of Allah necessarily restrains a person from all sins, the answer is that someone may recognize the wrongfulness of one sin but not another, and repent only of what he knows to be wrong. He may (also) know that both are wrong, yet his desires overpower him regarding one but not the other, so he repents of this one but not that one. This is like someone who fulfils some obligations but not others: what he fulfils is accepted from him.

The Mu‘tazilah, however, have a false principle in which they agree with the Khawārij in their judgment, although they differ from them in the designation they use. They say that those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever and will not leave it through intercession or anything else. In their view, it is impossible for Allah to punish a person and then reward that same person. Hence, they maintain that a major sin nullifies all good deeds.

The Companions and Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, however, hold that those who commit major sins will emerge

translated_text:
from the Fire and will receive intercession, and that a single major sin does not nullify all good deeds. According to most of Ahl al-Sunnah, however, an equivalent amount of good deeds may be nullified. Nothing nullifies all good deeds except disbelief, just as nothing wipes out all evil deeds except repentance. Thus, if someone who commits a major sin performs good deeds seeking Allah’s pleasure, Allah rewards him for them, even though he deserves punishment for his major sin. The Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguishes between a thief, a fornicator, and believers who fight one another, on the one hand, and disbelievers, on the other, in matters of “designations and rulings.” The Sunnah transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—through numerous independent chains, and the consensus of the Companions, establish this, as explained at length elsewhere.

Accordingly, people have differed over His words:

“Allah accepts only from the God-fearing.”

According to the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah, no good deed is accepted except from someone who is God-fearing without qualification and has committed no major sin. According to the Murji’ah, Allah accepts only from those who avoid associating partners with Him; they thus include those who commit major sins within the designation “the God-fearing.”

According to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, a deed is accepted from someone who fears Allah in performing it, doing it sincerely for Allah and in accordance with His command. The Third Principle

A person may call particular sins to mind and repent of them, or he may repent in general terms without calling his sins to mind. If, however, his intention is comprehensive repentance, it encompasses everything he regards as sinful. For comprehensive repentance includes a general resolve to do what is commanded and abandon what is forbidden, as well as general remorse for every forbidden act.

As for “remorse”—whether it is classified among beliefs, volitions, or the pains that afflict the soul because it has done something harmful to itself—when the heart becomes conscious that it has done something harmful to itself, it comes to recognize that what it did was evil. This belongs to the category of beliefs. It also feels an aversion to what it did, which belongs to the category of volitions, and experiences distress and grief over what it did. This belongs to the category of pains, such as sorrow and sadness, just as joy and happiness belong to the category of pleasures, not to that of beliefs or volitions.

There is no doubt that love presupposes awareness of the beloved, just as desire presupposes awareness on the part of the one who desires. translated_text:
at all, he experiences no pleasure, just like someone who craves food but has not tasted any of it. Likewise, if he tastes something he does not love, he experiences no pleasure, like someone who tastes what he does not want. When love for something and the tasting of it come together, pleasure follows. If, however, dislike of something is combined with experiencing that disliked thing, pain results. Thus, someone who hates a sin but does not commit it feels no remorse, while someone who does not hate it feels no remorse for committing it. But if he commits it and recognizes that it is something he hates and that harms him, he regrets having committed it.

In the Musnad, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Remorse is repentance.”

Once this is clear, whoever repents comprehensively has offered a repentance that entails forgiveness of all sins, even if he does not bring the individual sins to mind—unless something counters this general scope and requires it to be restricted. For example, there may be a sin from which he would not repent if he brought it to mind, because of his strong desire for it or his belief that it is good rather than evil. Any sin from which he would not repent if he brought it to mind is not included in his repentance. But any sin from which he would repent if it came specifically to mind is included in comprehensive repentance.

As for “unqualified repentance”—meaning that a person repents in general terms without this entailing repentance from every sin—it neither necessarily includes every individual sin nor precludes its inclusion, just like an unqualified expression. Such repentance may, however, serve as a cause for the forgiveness of a particular sin, just as it may serve as a cause for the forgiveness of all sins, in contrast to

comprehensive repentance, which entails forgiveness of all sins, since it encompasses them all.

Many people, when repenting, bring to mind only certain indecent acts or their preliminaries, or certain wrongs committed by word or deed. Yet their neglect of what Allah requires of them, inwardly and outwardly, among the branches and realities of faith may be more harmful to them than some of the indecent acts they have committed. For the realities of faith that Allah has commanded, through which a servant becomes a true believer, are more beneficial than abstaining from certain outward sins. One example is love for Allah and His Messenger, which is the greatest of positive good deeds. Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh:

“In the time of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), there was a man called Himār who used to drink wine. Whenever he was brought before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), he would administer the prescribed punishment of flogging. After this had happened repeatedly, the man was brought before him once more, and he ordered that he be flogged. A man cursed him, whereupon the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, ‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

Thus, he forbade cursing him despite his persistent drinking, because he loved Allah and His Messenger—even though the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) cursed ten in connection with wine:

“He cursed wine, the one who presses it, the one for whom it is pressed, the one who drinks it, the one who serves it, the one who carries it, the one to whom it is carried, the one who sells it, the one who buys it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

However, a curse pronounced in general terms does not necessarily entail cursing a particular individual in whom there is something that prevents the curse from applying to him.

translated_text:
The same applies to “general judgments of unbelief” and “general threats of punishment.” Thus, the general threats of punishment in the Quran and Sunnah apply only when the necessary conditions are met and no impediments are present. By agreement of the Muslims, they do not apply to someone who repents of the sin, nor to someone whose good deeds erase his evil deeds, nor to someone for whom intercession is accepted or who is forgiven.

For the punishment of sins—namely Hell—is averted through repentance, good deeds that erase sins, and afflictions that expiate them—though these are themselves punishments in this world—as well as through hardships experienced in the intermediate state after death and on the gathering grounds of the Day of Resurrection. It is also averted through the supplications of believers, such as their funeral prayer for a person, and through the intercession of an intercessor whose plea is accepted, as when the foremost of intercessors, “Muhammad”—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—intercedes for someone.

Accordingly, whatever sin a person repents of, its consequence is removed. Whatever he does not repent of remains subject to the ruling applicable to unrepented sins. If hardship befalls him because of sins and he repents of some of them, his hardship is alleviated in proportion to what he has repented of, but not in respect of what he has left unrepented. His case differs from that of someone who repents comprehensively.

People generally do not repent comprehensively, despite their need to do so. Repentance is obligatory upon every servant in every circumstance, for he continually becomes aware of duties he has neglected or prohibitions he has transgressed. He must therefore continually repent. And Allah knows best.

As for the questioner’s words:

“Why does relief come when hope in created beings is exhausted? How can one turn the heart away from attachment to them and attach it to Allah?”

The answer is:

This comes about through fully realizing Allah’s oneness: “oneness in lordship” and “oneness in worship.”

“Oneness in lordship” means that there is no creator but Allah, so nothing besides Him can independently bring anything about. Rather, whatever He wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. Anything besides Him, if considered a cause, necessarily has a cooperating factor that assists it and an opposing factor that impedes it. Thus, to ask anything besides Him to bring something about is to ask it for something it cannot accomplish independently or achieve on its own.

Even the voluntary actions asked of a servant cannot be performed without Allah’s assistance—for example, by making him perform them through the decisive will He creates within him and the complete ability He creates for him. When complete ability and decisive will are present, the act necessarily occurs.

Allah’s will alone necessarily brings about everything He wills. Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. The will of anything besides Him, however, does not by itself bring anything about. Rather, what it wills can come about only through factors beyond its power. Unless the Lord assists it through those factors, it will not attain what it seeks. Its very will cannot arise except by the will of Allah Most High.

As the Most High said:

“For whoever among you wills to take the straight path.”

“But you do not will unless Allah, Lord of all worlds, wills.”

And He said:

—exalted is He—:

“So whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.”

“But you do not will unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.”

And He said:

“So whoever wills may heed it.”

“But they will not heed it unless Allah wills. He is the One to be feared and the One who grants forgiveness.”

A person who places his hope in a created being seeks with his heart what he wants from that being, yet that being is powerless to provide it. Moreover, this is part of the association of partners with Allah that He does not forgive. Thus, among the manifestations of His perfect grace and kindness toward His believing servants is that He prevents them from attaining their aims through associating partners with Him, so that He may turn their hearts toward His oneness. Then, if the servant worships Him alone, he attains happiness in this world and the Hereafter.

But if he is among those described in His words:

“When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm, he carries on as though he had never called upon Us concerning the harm that afflicted him. Thus, what the transgressors used to do has been made appealing to them.”

And in His words:

“When harm befalls you at sea, those you invoke vanish from your thoughts, except Him. But when He delivers you safely to land, you turn away. Man is ever ungrateful.”

Then whatever realization of Allah’s oneness he had attained becomes evidence against him.

Likewise, Allah, glorified is He, established His case against the polytheists who acknowledge that He is the Creator of everything, yet associate partners with Him rather than worship Him alone, without partner. The Most High said:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and everyone upon it, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then take heed?’”

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then fear Him?’”

“Say, ‘In whose hand is the dominion of all things, who grants protection while none can protect against Him, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘How then are you deluded?’”

And the Most High said:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ How then are they turned away?”

This is mentioned in several places in the Quran. Among the manifestations of Allah’s perfect favor toward His believing servants is that He afflicts them with hardship, suffering, and circumstances that compel them to worship Him alone. They then call upon Him with sincere devotion, place their hope in Him alone, and attach their hearts to Him rather than anyone else. Through this, they attain such reliance upon Him, such turning to Him, such sweetness of faith and experience of its savor, and such freedom from associating partners with Him, that these are a greater blessing for them than relief from illness, fear, or drought, or the attainment of ease and relief from hardship in their livelihood. Those are bodily pleasures and worldly blessings, of which a disbeliever may receive more than a believer.

But what is attained by those who worship Allah alone with sincere devotion is too great for words to express its true nature or for the mind to encompass its details. Every believer has a share of this in proportion to his faith. Thus, one of the early Muslims said:

“O son of Adam, you have indeed been blessed through a need that has led you to knock often at your Master’s door.”

One of the spiritual teachers said:

“At times I have a need that I ask Allah to fulfill. As I call upon Him, He opens to me such delight in knowing Him and such sweetness in speaking intimately to Him that I do not wish Him to hasten the fulfillment of my need, for fear that my soul might turn away

Some reports from the Israelites contain the words: “O son of Adam, affliction brings you and Me together, while well-being brings you and your own self together.”

This theme occurs frequently. It is a reality that the believer tastes and perceives through his inner sense. Every believer has experienced enough of it to recognize what we have described, for it belongs to the realm of taste and perception, known only to those who have tasted and perceived it.

Although the word “taste” may be thought originally to refer exclusively to tasting with the tongue, its use in the Quran and Sunnah shows that its scope is broader: it is used for sensing both what is agreeable and what is disagreeable. Similarly, in customary usage, the word “perception” encompasses whatever is perceived through the five senses, and indeed inwardly as well. In its linguistic origin, however, it means “seeing,” as in His words:

“Do you perceive any one of them?”

(The point at issue) is the word “taste.” The Most High said:

“So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear.”

He thus described fear and hunger as things tasted, and associated the garment with them to indicate that it clothed the hungry and fearful person, enveloping and surrounding him just as a garment surrounds its wearer;

unlike someone whose pain does not encompass all his senses but is confined to particular parts of his body. The Most High said:

“So taste the painful punishment.”

The Most High also said:

“Taste! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble!”

And He said:

“Taste the touch of Hellfire.”

And He said:

“They will not taste death therein.”

The Most High also said:

“There they will taste neither coolness nor drink, except scalding water and foul discharge.”

And He said:

“We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet.”

Thus, the word “taste” is frequently used for perceiving both what is agreeable and what is disagreeable. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“There are three qualities which, if present in a person, enable him to experience the sweetness of faith.”

This hadith has already been mentioned. A believer’s experience of the sweetness of faith in his heart, and his tasting of faith, are known to those who have had this experience. Those who taste it do so in varying degrees.

Thus, what the people of faith experience when they devote their hearts exclusively to Allah and turn to Him rather than anything besides Him—as pure monotheists, sincerely devoting their religion to Him, loving nothing except for His sake, relying on none but Him, forming allegiances only for His sake, bearing enmity only for His sake, asking none but Him, hoping in none but Him, and fearing none but Him; worshipping Him and seeking His help for His sake, so that they are with the True One without distraction by creation, and with creation without being driven by personal desire; their desire for anything besides Him having faded away through their desire for Him, their love of anything besides Him through their love of Him, and their fear of

This is the very essence of Islam, with which Allah sent the messengers and revealed the Scriptures. It is the central axis around which the Quran revolves. And Allah, glorified be He, knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section: “Fanā” (Passing Away)

The term fanā, as it occurs in Sufi writings, is explained in three ways.

(The first): The heart’s ceasing to direct its desire, reliance, worship, and related acts toward anything besides the Lord. This is true and sound; it is pure monotheism and sincerity. In “reality,” it is the heart’s worship, reliance, seeking help, adoration, repentant return, and turning toward Allah alone, without partner, together with the knowledge and spiritual states that follow from this. No one is exempt from this.

This is the “sound heart” of which Allah says:

“Except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

It means the heart’s freedom from corrupt beliefs, corrupt desires, and all that follows from them.

translated_text:
This “passing away” does not conflict with “subsistence”; rather, the two coexist. The servant’s desire for anything besides Allah passes away, even while he remains aware of Allah and of other things. This is expressed by the declaration, “There is no god worthy of worship but Allah.” The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“There is no god worthy of worship but Allah, and we worship none but Him. His are all blessings and bounty, and to Him belongs all good praise.”

This, in broad terms, is the beginning and end of religion.

(The second): The heart’s losing awareness of everything besides the Lord. The former concerns the passing away of desire for anything else; this concerns the passing away of awareness of anything else. The former means ceasing to worship or rely upon another; this means ceasing to be conscious of another or to attend to it.

This kind of passing away involves a deficiency. For perceiving realities as they truly are—that is, perceiving the Lord as governing His servants and commanding His revealed laws—is more complete than perceiving His existence, one of His attributes, or one of His names, and thereby losing awareness of everything else. The Companions’ perception was therefore too complete for a general awareness of Allah to diminish their detailed awareness of Him. Nevertheless, much of this occurred among many later members of this community.

Likewise, when certain realities became manifest to them, they experienced death, fainting, cries, and agitation. This was because their hearts were too weak to perceive realities as they truly are, and to perceive distinction within unity and multiplicity within oneness. They even disagreed over whether this was possible. Many of them believe that no other state is possible, having found that remembering creation or the divine command distracts them from the Creator who issues the command. Thus, some of them say that when the Real manifests Himself, it is impossible to hear His speech. It is related that when Ibn Arabī was told that Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī considered both experiences possible together, he said: “We are speaking to him about perceiving the Essence, while he is telling us about perceiving the attributes.”

Shihāb al-Dīn was correct, for his belief concerning the distinction between the Lord and the servant was sound. Ibn Arabī merely based his view on his premise, which constitutes disbelief, that the Real is the existence flowing into contingent beings. It is evident that perceiving this involves no speech addressed to the perceiver; such speech occurs only at the station of the intellect (1).

In this state of passing away, a person may say, “I am the Real,” “Glory be to me,” or “There is nothing within this robe but Allah.” This happens when absorption in the One he perceives makes him lose awareness of his own perception; absorption in the One whose existence he apprehends, of his own existence; absorption in the One he remembers, of his own remembrance; and absorption in the One he knows, of his own knowing.

They relate, for example, that a man was so absorbed in his love for another that, when his beloved fell into the sea, he threw himself in after him. The beloved asked, “What made you throw yourself in after me?” He replied, “I was so lost in you that I forgot myself and thought that you were me.”
