 كَقَوْلِ بَعْضِهِمْ: أَنْصِبُ خَيْمَتِي عَلَى جَهَنَّمَ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَقْوَالِ وَالْأَعْمَالِ الْمُخَالِفَةِ لِلشَّرْعِ؛ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ صَاحِبُهَا غَيْرَ مَأْثُومٍ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ فَيُشْبِهُ هَذَا الْبَابُ أَمْرَ خُفَرَاءِ الْعَدُوِّ وَمَنْ يُعِينُ كَافِرًا أَوْ ظَالِمًا بِحَالِ وَيَزْعُمُ أَنَّهُ مَغْلُوبٌ عَلَيْهِ. وَيَحْكُمُ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ أَنَّ أَحَدَهُمْ إذَا زَالَ عَقْلُهُ بِسَبَبِ غَيْرِ مُحَرَّمٍ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمْ فِيمَا يَصْدُرُ عَنْهُمْ مِنْ الْأَقْوَالِ وَالْأَفْعَالِ الْمُحَرَّمَةِ بِخِلَافِ مَا إذَا كَانَ سَبَبُ زَوَالِ الْعَقْلِ وَالْغَلَبَةِ أَمْرًا مُحَرَّمًا. وَهَذَا كَمَا قُلْنَا فِي عُقَلَاءِ الْمَجَانِينِ والمولهين الَّذِينَ صَارَ ذَلِكَ لَهُمْ مَقَامًا دَائِمًا كَمَا أَنَّهُ يَعْرِضُ لِهَؤُلَاءِ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَوْقَاتِ كَمَا قَالَ بَعْضُ الْعُلَمَاءِ ذَلِكَ فِي مَنْ زَالَ عَقْلُهُ حَتَّى تَرَكَ شَيْئًا مِنْ الْوَاجِبَاتِ. إنْ كَانَ زَوَالُهُ بِسَبَبِ غَيْرِ مُحَرَّمٍ مِثْلِ الْإِغْمَاءِ بِالْمَرَضِ أَوْ أُسْقِيَ مُكْرَهًا شَيْئًا يُزِيلُ عَقْلَهُ فَلَا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ وَإِنْ زَالَ بِشُرْبِ الْخَمْرِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَحْوَالِ الْمُحَرَّمَةِ أَثِمَ بِتَرْكِ الْوَاجِبِ وَكَذَلِكَ الْأَمْرُ فِي فِعْلِ الْمُحَرَّمِ. وَكَمَا أَنَّهُ لَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمْ فَلَا يَجُوزُ الِاقْتِدَاءُ بِهِمْ وَلَا حَمْلُ كَلَامِهِمْ وَفِعَالِهِمْ عَلَى الصِّحَّةِ بَلْ هُمْ فِي الْخَاصَّةِ مِثْلُ الْغَافِلِ وَالْمَجْنُونِ فِي التَّكَالِيفِ
translated_text:
the sweetness of faith, just as happens with the intoxication of wine or of one infatuated with physical beauty.

Likewise, passing away may result from a state of fear or hope, just as it may result from a state of love. The heart then loses awareness of certain realities, and the person says or does things resembling the behaviour of the intoxicated. Such are the ecstatic excesses of certain shaykhs—for example, one of them saying, “I shall pitch my tent over Hell,” and similar statements and actions contrary to the revealed Law.

The person responsible may be free of sin. If he is not, this category resembles the case of those who protect the enemy, or someone who assists an unbeliever or an oppressor through a spiritual state and claims to be overpowered by it. The ruling concerning such people is that, if someone loses his reason through a cause that is not forbidden, he incurs no blame for the forbidden statements or actions that proceed from him. This differs from the case in which his loss of reason and the state that overwhelms him arise from something forbidden.

This is as we have said concerning the “sane madmen” and those bewildered by ecstasy, for whom this has become a permanent condition, whereas it overtakes these others only at certain times. Some scholars have made the same distinction concerning someone whose loss of reason causes him to neglect an obligation: if he loses his reason through a cause that is not forbidden—such as fainting through illness, or being forcibly made to drink something that deprives him of his reason—he incurs no sin. But if he loses it through drinking wine or through similar forbidden states, he sins by neglecting the obligation. The same applies to committing a forbidden act.

Although they incur no blame, it is not permissible to follow their example or to construe their words and deeds as sound. Rather, in the sphere of the spiritual elite, they are like the heedless and the insane with respect to religious obligations

of outward observance; and one scholar said of them: “These are people whom Allah granted intellects and spiritual states. He then took away their intellects while leaving their spiritual states, and lifted the obligations He had imposed because of what He had taken away.”

For this reason, those who know Allah agree that the state of abiding is superior to this: it is witnessing realities through Allah’s enabling one to witness them. As Allah Most High said, according to what His Messenger related from Him:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely grant him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks.”

In another version:

“Through Me he speaks, and through Me he understands.”

Thus, when he hears through Allah and sees through Him, he hears things as they really are and witnesses the truth as it really is. Most of what you find concerning passing away in the writings of sound Sufis, such as Shaykh al-Islām and those before him, is of this kind. Nevertheless, some of them may err in certain judgments concerning it, as I have discussed elsewhere.

In sum, this passing away is valid and occurs among those of a Jesus-like disposition within the Muhammadan community. It resembles the fainting and cries that appeared among the Successors. Yet many of these people consequently fall into a kind of error, because passing away from witnessing realities ultimately amounts to an absence of knowledge and awareness. This is an attribute of deficiency, not perfection. It is praiseworthy only in respect of

Scholars of a “Moses-like disposition,” by contrast, generally possess knowledge of other things, desire them, and become infatuated with them, and are described as knowledgeable. Yet the former are characterized by ignorance and justice, while the latter are characterized by injustice (1). Both descriptions are accurate.

As for knowing the True One and creation while desiring Allah alone, without any partner, this characterizes those of a Muhammadan disposition who have attained perfection in knowledge and will. The soundness of heart that deserves praise is soundness . . . (2), for ignorance is not, in itself, a praiseworthy quality. It may, however, be praised because it keeps a person safe from evils. For most souls, upon learning of an evil they desire, follow it, become frightened of it, or are seduced by it.

This means that a person regards Allah as existence itself and holds that nothing else exists, whether through Him or through anything else. This doctrine and spiritual state belong to the heretical proponents of union among later figures, such as al-Balyānī, al-Tilimsānī, al-Qūnūnī, and others like them. “The truest words ever spoken by a poet are these words of Labīd:

And as has been said concerning His words:

“Everything will perish except His Face.”

Had they meant that, this would have been sound spiritual witnessing. But they mean that He is identical with existing things. This is disbelief and misguidance. Its adherents sometimes seize upon ambiguous expressions found in the words of certain spiritual masters, just as Christians seize upon ambiguous expressions reported from the Messiah. They rely on an unsound spiritual experience or faulty reasoning. Reflect, then, on this classification, for it makes the straight path clear.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

“Commands and prohibitions,” which some scholars call “obligation under the Sharia,” are conditional upon the capacity to know and to act. Thus, the obligations of the Sharia do not apply to those incapable of understanding, such as the insane and young children. Nor do particular obligations apply to those incapable of fulfilling them, as with the blind, the lame, and the sick in the case of jihad. Likewise, purification with water, praying while standing, fasting, and other such duties are not obligatory for those unable to perform them.

This holds whether imposing obligations beyond a person’s capacity is considered permissible or not, for there is no disagreement that imposing an obligation upon someone who has absolutely no capacity to perform the act does not occur in

the Sharia. Indeed, the Sharia may exempt those whose faculties of understanding and action are not yet fully developed, both to ease their burden and to establish a clear criterion for legal responsibility, even when imposing obligations upon them would be possible. Thus, the pen is lifted from a child until he reaches puberty, even though he possesses understanding and discernment. This is because his understanding is not yet complete, and because reason develops gradually in people, who differ in this respect. Since the underlying consideration is difficult to ascertain and varies widely, puberty was made the defining criterion.

Likewise, according to the majority of scholars, Hajj is obligatory only upon someone who possesses provisions and a mount, even if walking is possible, because of the hardship involved. Similarly, a traveller is not obliged to fast, even if able to do so, as a concession to ease his burden. Obligations are also waived because of an illness when performing them is feared to worsen the illness and delay recovery, even though their performance remains possible.

These, however, are matters in which revealed laws differ. In one revealed law, Allah may make obligatory something difficult and prohibit something that is difficult to forgo—as with the burdens and shackles imposed upon the Children of Israel—while granting relief in another revealed law. Thus the believers said:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

He Most High also said:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you.”

And He said:

“He has imposed no hardship upon you in religion.”

And He said:

“Allah intends to lighten your burden.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions concerning the incident involving the Bedouin:

“You were sent only to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”

He said to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā:

“Make things easy, and do not make them difficult.”

He also said:

“This religion is easy, and no one overburdens himself in practicing it without being overwhelmed by it.”

He said:

“Do not impose hardship upon yourselves, lest Allah impose hardship upon you. Some people imposed hardship upon themselves, so Allah imposed hardship upon them. Those who remain of them are there in hermitages and monasteries: ‘Monasticism which they invented—we did not prescribe it for them.’”

He said:

“There is no monasticism in Islam.”

He also said:

“But I fast and refrain from fasting; I pray at night and sleep; I marry women and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

He said:

“Allah loves that His concessions be accepted, just as He hates that He be disobeyed.”

It is also reported that he said:

“I was sent with the upright, accommodating faith.”

As for whether a person desires what he is commanded to do or dislikes it, revealed laws take no account of this; nor, indeed, do the commands of any rational person. Rather, a person is commanded to oppose his own whims. “Desire” is what distinguishes the people of Paradise from the people of Hell, as Allah Most High said:

“Whoever desires this fleeting life, We hasten for him therein whatever We will, for whomever We please. Then We assign Hell to him, where he will burn, condemned and banished. But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is they whose striving will be appreciated.”

Allah Most High also said:

“That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who desire neither supremacy on earth nor corruption.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We shall repay them in full

for their deeds therein,” and so on. Allah Most High also said:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

There are many similar passages. These principles are well established in the Quran, the Sunnah, and the words of scholars and those with spiritual insight. The purpose here is not to establish them.

Rather, the purpose is to address another matter: if religious accountability is conditional upon the ability to acquire knowledge, which rests upon reason, and upon the ability to act, then we say:

Either of these capacities may be lost through prohibited causes or through causes that are not prohibited. If someone deprives himself of his reason by drinking wine, taking henbane, or the like, this does not absolve him of sin for the obligations he neglects and the prohibited acts he commits, if intoxication leads to that conduct. This differs from losing his reason through a cause that is not prohibited, such as fainting from illness or fear, or becoming intoxicated through drinking that is not prohibited—for example, being compelled to swallow wine. Such a person incurs no sin.

As for his being required to make up the prayers according to Ahmad, and according to those who say that he must make up the prayers of one day and night, this is analogous to the obligation to make up prayers for someone who sleeps through them or forgets them, neither of whom incurs any sin. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is no negligence in sleep; negligence is only while awake.”

He also said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must pray it when he remembers it, for that is its appointed time. There is no expiation for it other than that.”

 إنْ كَانَ زَوَالُ ذَلِكَ بِسَبَبِ غَيْرِ مُحَرَّمٍ فَلَا حَرَجَ عَلَيْهِمْ فِيمَا يَتْرُكُونَهُ مِنْ الْوَاجِبَاتِ وَيَفْعَلُونَهُ مِنْ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ وَلَا يَجُوزُ أَيْضًا اتِّبَاعُهُمْ فِيمَا هُوَ خَارِجٌ عَنْ الشَّرِيعَةِ مِنْ أَقْوَالِهِمْ وَأَفْعَالِهِمْ وَلَا نَذُمُّهُمْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ بَلْ قَدْ يُمْدَحُونَ عَلَى مَا وَافَقُوا فِيهِ الشَّرِيعَةَ مِنْ
translated_text:
The same applies to “a person’s capacity to act”: if, after Hajj becomes obligatory for him, he is negligent and squanders his wealth, Hajj remains an obligation upon him. Likewise, regarding permission to do what is prohibited, Allah Most High said:

“But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limits, incurs no sin.”

Necessity arising from a prohibited act does not make prohibited things permissible, unlike necessity arising from a cause that is not prohibited. Scholars have differed over whether someone whose journey is itself sinful may avail himself of the concessions granted to travellers. The position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that he may not.

As for the states experienced by devoted worshippers, those with spiritual insight, ascetics, and others like them, these may deprive a person of his reason and awareness, leaving him like someone who is insane, distraught, intoxicated, or asleep. They may also deprive him of his capacity to act, leaving him helpless, or like someone compelled to act, whose words and deeds occur without his will or choice. Losing reason and capacity may render him unable to fulfil obligations and may cause him to commit prohibited acts.

Concerning such people, we say: if this loss results from a cause that is not prohibited, they incur no sin for the obligations they neglect or the prohibited acts they commit. Nor, however, is it permissible to follow them in any of their words or deeds that fall outside the Sharia. We do not blame them for that; rather, they may be praised for what accords with the Sharia in their

Indeed, such a scholar belongs to this category, since he is absolved of blame because he was unable to attain the requisite knowledge. If, however, their loss of reason or capacity results from a prohibited cause, they deserve blame and punishment for the obligations they neglect and the prohibited acts they commit.

An example of the “first” case is someone who listens to the Quran in the prescribed manner, whereupon a spiritual emotion that he cherishes, or fear or hope, surges within him. Unable to bear it, he dies, falls unconscious, cries out loudly, or becomes violently agitated. If this results in his missing an obligatory prayer or committing an aggression against someone, he is excused for that. In this state, he is like those distraught people described as the wise among the insane, who have lost their reason despite being righteous and possessing spiritual insight. This may be due to the intensity of the inward experience that comes upon them, their hearts’ inability to bear it, an imbalance in their bodily temperaments and the potency of a bodily humour, or an affliction caused by the jinn.

Their condition is as described in the report that has reached us from Imam Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī. When asked about them, he said:

[These are people whom Allah endowed with reason and spiritual states. He then took away their reason while leaving their spiritual states intact, and relieved them of the obligations He had imposed because of what He had taken away.] (*)

Among these people are also those so overwhelmed by remembrance of Allah, affirmation of His oneness, and love for Him that, absorbed in the One they remember, witness, love and worship, they lose awareness of everything else. Something similar happens to a lover who becomes oblivious to everything but his beloved. In this state, one of them may say, “I am the Truth,” “Glory be to me,” or “There is nothing in this robe but Allah.” Others are so overwhelmed by hope and mercy that they say, “I shall spread my prayer rug over Hell.” Whoever says this while deprived of his reason, so that he resembles someone drunk or distraught, incurs no sin, provided that the cause of his condition was not prohibited by Islamic law.

An example of the “second” case is what may happen to many who attend listening sessions when they hear whistling and clapping. Someone may recite poetry containing things contrary to Islamic law, using vocal sounds that also contravene it. If a listener is predisposed to such reactions, this may cause mental confusion and loss of reason, to the point that some kill others, either outwardly or inwardly through their wills and hearts. It also leads to neglect of the obligations of Islamic law and aggression against believers in their religious and worldly affairs, to an extent known to Allah.

translated_text:
Likewise, one of them may engage in forms of worship contrary to Islamic law, in both belief and practice. These acts of worship and practices produce powerful, overwhelming states in him, causing him to neglect obligations and commit prohibited acts against people’s lives and property more grievous than those committed by a tyrannical king intoxicated with wine.

When someone addresses him while he is sober and in possession of his reason, he says: “I was overpowered. A spiritual impulse came upon me and did this to me, and the spiritual impulse rules.” Such is the condition of many who protect the enemy, and of many among those who experience spiritual states who assist unbelievers and oppressors and commit aggression against Muslims and believers. Such a person says that he was overpowered in this, that a spiritual impulse came upon him and compelled it, and that he was instructed to perform that act.

He should be told:

“As for your loss of reason, to the point that you no longer understand Allah’s commands and prohibitions, and your loss of control, to the point that you are compelled to perform those acts—even if you are truthful about this, it results from your own initial negligence and transgression, which brought you into the condition of the insane and the intoxicated. You are therefore like someone who drinks wine and becomes intoxicated, or someone who exposes himself to passionate love until he falls in love and it wreaks havoc upon him. There is no difference between intoxication through sounds, beautiful forms, and drink: one is intoxication of the body, another intoxication of the soul, and another intoxication of the spirit. If its cause is prohibited, the intoxicated person is not excused in Islam.

They are comparable to the states experienced by people other than worshippers and ascetics: sanity and sobriety, fainting, intoxication and insanity, compulsion and free choice. The states of kings and rulers, guides and scholars, and shaykhs and the spiritual poor all fall under this noble principle, and Islamic law judges them by distinguishing between them.

If to this is added the fact that disclosures of knowledge or effects brought about under divine decree by those experiencing such states do not necessarily entail friendship with Allah—not even righteousness, nor indeed faith, since such things may occur in an unbeliever, a hypocrite, an evildoer or a sinner—and that the friends of Allah, who shall have no fear nor grieve, are only those who believe and are mindful of Him, then a distinction is drawn between friendship with Allah and these states, just as a distinction is drawn between the prophetic caliphate and kingship in general, and between the knowledge that is the prophets’ legacy and discourse in general.

These two categories overlap without coinciding. A man may be a friend of Allah who experiences a state involving extraordinary effects and disclosure, or he may be a friend of Allah without possessing that state in its fullness. Conversely, he may possess something of these states without being a friend of Allah. Likewise, a man may be a prophet’s successor who commands obedience, or a prophet’s successor who is weak and oppressed; or he may be a tyrant who commands obedience yet has no connection whatsoever with prophethood. A man may also be a scholar who does not engage in discourse contrary to the words of the prophets, or a scholar whose discourse consists of the words of the prophets.

“Those of you who live after me will see much disagreement. So adhere to my Sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs who come after me.”

It is well known that when “those in authority,” who govern people’s lives and property, remain upright, people generally remain upright. Thus, as al-Bukhārī relates in his Sahīh, when the woman from the Ahmas tribe asked Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, “How long will we continue in this good state?” he replied, “As long as your leaders remain upright in governing you.”

A transmitted report states:

“There are two groups who, when they are righteous, bring righteousness to the people: scholars and rulers.”

These are the bearers of scripture and the wielders of iron, as indicated by His words, “We have certainly sent…” and the remainder of the verse. They are also “those vested with authority” in His words:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those vested with authority among you.”

Likewise, corruption arises through them, as stated in a hadith attributed to the Prophet and in reports from several Companions:

“What I fear most for you is a scholar’s lapse, a hypocrite’s disputing by means of the Quran, and leaders who lead people astray.”

The leaders who lead people astray are the rulers, while the scholar and the disputant belong to the ranks of scholars. However, (the first) holds sound beliefs but makes mistakes: this is the scholar, as happens among the leading jurists of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. And (the second) is like the philosophers and speculative theologians who dispute using specious arguments drawn from the Quran, although in reality they have cast off Allah’s signs. They invoke it only to rebut their opponent, not to seek its guidance or rely upon it. This is why he said:

“A hypocrite’s disputing by means of the Quran.”

For the Sunnah and scholarly consensus refute his specious argument.

The religion established in the heart—faith, both as knowledge and as an inward state—is the “root,” while outward deeds are the “branches,” and they constitute the perfection of faith. Religion is thus first built upon its foundations and brought to completion through its branches. Accordingly, in Mecca Allah revealed its foundations: monotheism; parables, which are rational analogies; narratives; promises of reward; and warnings of punishment. Then, in Medina—once the religion had gained strength—He revealed its outward branches: Friday prayer, congregational prayer, the call to prayer, the announcement that prayer is about to begin, jihad, fasting, the prohibition of wine, unlawful sexual intercourse and gambling, and its other obligations and prohibitions.

translated_text:
Its roots thus nourish and strengthen its branches, while its branches perfect and preserve its roots. Whenever an outward deficiency occurs in it, it begins in its branches. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The first thing you will lose from your religion is trustworthiness, and the last thing you will lose from your religion is prayer.”

It is also reported that he said:

“The first thing to be taken away is trustworthy governance.”

“Governance” is the work of rulers and those in authority, as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice.”

As for prayer, it is the first obligation prescribed and is among the foundations of religion and faith, coupled with the two testimonies of faith. It therefore disappears only at the end, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Islam began as something strange and will return to being strange as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers.”

He thus stated that its return would resemble its beginning. When the rule of the Rightly Guided Caliphs ended and gave way to kingship, deficiency appeared among the rulers; it was therefore inevitable that it would also appear among people of knowledge and religious devotion. Thus, toward the end of ‘Alī’s caliphate, the two innovations—those of the Khawārij and the Rāfidah—arose, for they concern leadership, the caliphate, and the practices and rulings of Islamic law that follow from them.

Mu‘āwiyah’s rule was a merciful kingship. When Mu‘āwiyah—may Allah have mercy on him—passed away and Yazīd’s rule began, there occurred during it the turmoil surrounding the killing of al-Husayn in Iraq and the turmoil involving the people of al-Harrah in Medina. They also laid siege to Mecca when ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr rose up.

Then Yazīd died, and the Muslim community became divided: Ibn al-Zubayr held the Hijāz, the house of al-Hakam held Syria, and al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ‘Ubayd and others rose up in Iraq. It was during this period, towards the end of the era of the Companions, while men such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abbās, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, and others were still alive, that the innovations of the Qadariyyah and the Murji’ah arose. The surviving Companions, such as Ibn ‘Abbās, Ibn ‘Umar, Jābir, Wāthilah ibn al-Asqa‘, and others—may Allah be pleased with them—refuted these innovations, alongside their own and others’ refutations of the innovations of the Khawārij and the Rāfidah.

At that time, the Qadariyyah’s discussions chiefly concerned people’s deeds, just as the Murji’ah’s did. Their discussions thus concerned obedience and disobedience, the believer and the sinner, and similar questions of “religious designations and rulings” and “the promise of reward and the threat of punishment.”

They did not discuss their Lord or His attributes until towards the end of the era of the younger Successors, in the closing years of the Umayyad state, when most of the third generation—the successors of the Successors—began to pass away—for the three generations are reckoned according to the majority of the people of each generation, who belong to its middle period. Most of the Companions had passed away by the end of the caliphate of the four caliphs, so that only a few of those who had fought at Badr remained. Most of the Successors, who followed them in righteousness, had passed away towards the end of the era of the younger Companions, during the rule of Ibn al-Zubayr and ‘Abd al-Malik. Some foreign books—Persian, Indian, and Greek—were translated into Arabic, and what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had foretold came to pass: “Then lying will become widespread, until a man gives testimony without being asked and swears an oath without being asked”—three things emerged: “juristic opinion,” “speculative theology,” and “Sufism.” “Jahmism” also emerged, namely the denial of the divine attributes, and, at the opposite extreme, “likening Allah to His creation.”

Most proponents of juristic opinion were from Kufa, where it predominated, alongside the excessive Shi‘i partisanship and widespread lying in transmitted reports found among its people. Nevertheless, the best of its people possessed a tremendous measure of knowledge, truthfulness, adherence to the Sunnah, understanding of religious law, and devotion to worship. The point, however, is that Kufa was where widespread lying in transmitted reports, a proliferation of juristic opinions, and Shi‘i leanings in matters of doctrine developed.

Speculative theology and Sufism were chiefly found in Basra. Shortly after the deaths of al-Hasan and Ibn Sīrīn, ‘Amr ibn ‘Ubayd and Wāsil ibn ‘Atā’ emerged, together with their followers among the speculative theologians and Mu‘tazilah. Ahmad ibn ‘Atā’ (1) al-Hujaymī also emerged; he had been a companion of ‘Abd al-Wāhid ibn Zayd,

I have previously written in “The Principles” about the deviations in the paths of those devoted to speculative theology and rational inquiry, and those devoted to spiritual aspiration and practice, when these are not accompanied by following the Messenger. Likewise, I explained in “a lengthy treatise” that the foundation of knowledge, guidance, and religion is faith in Allah and His Messenger, and maintaining that faith throughout all one’s words and states.

The people of Medina were closer to the right path in word and deed than either group, for they did not deviate as the two groups among the Kufans and Basrans did in their inclinations, transmitted reports, opinions, speculative theology, and devotional listening. Although some of them displayed a degree of deviation, they were nevertheless closer to the right path.

As for the people of Syria, most were engaged in jihad and devoted to acts of the heart, closer to the religiously prescribed spiritual state than the Basran Sufis of that time. Thus, one finds that books on “speculative theology and Sufism” originally emerged from Basra.

The leading Muʿtazilī theologians were Basrans, such as Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, his son Abū Hāshim, Abū ʿAbd Allāh . . . (1), and Abū al-Husayn,

Likewise, the books of “the Sufis and those who combined Sufism with hadith and speculative theology” originated there, such as the works of al-Hārith ibn Asad al-Muhāsibī, Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim, Abū Sa'īd al-A'rābī, and Abū Tālib al-Makkī. Many people from Baghdad, Khurasan, and Syria shared in their pursuits, but the point is that the origins lay there.

Similarly, “prophetic knowledge”—faith and the Quran, together with the jurisprudence, hadith, and acts of the heart that follow from them—originated only in the centres where the majority of the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, lived: the two Holy Sanctuaries, the two Iraqi cities, and Syria—that is, Medina, Mecca, Kufa, Basra, and Syria. All other centres followed their lead.

The seven Quran reciters came from these centres, as did the leading scholars of hadith. The most reliable among the latter were those of Medina and Basra, such as al-Zuhrī, Mālik, Qatāda, Shu'ba, Yahyā ibn Sa'īd, and 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī.

translated_text:
And among the people of Kufa were both truthful narrators and liars. Among the people of Syria there were not many liars, nor were there great leading authorities in Quranic recitation and hadith.

The same applies to the leading jurists: Mālik was the scholar of Medina; al-Thawrī, Abū Hanīfa and others were from Kufa; Ibn Jurayj and others were from Mecca; Hammād ibn Salama and Hammād ibn Zayd were from Basra; and al-Awzā'ī and his contemporaries were in Syria. It has been said that Mālik modelled his Muwatta' on the book of Hammād ibn Salama; it has also been said that Ibn Jurayj’s book preceded that.

Then came al-Shāfi'ī. Although he had Meccan origins, he studied jurisprudence according to the approach of the scholars of hadith, without confining himself to his own city. Likewise, although Imam Ahmad’s forebears were from Basra, he studied jurisprudence according to the approach of the scholars of hadith, without confining himself to the scholars of Basra or any other group. The same applies to 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm, Muhammad ibn Ismā'īl al-Bukhārī and other scholars from Khurasan.

Likewise, the leading ascetics and devoted worshippers came from these centres, as Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī mentioned in Safwat al-Safwa (The Choicest of the Choice).

Thus, knowledge and devotion sanctioned by the religion are derived from the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. As for what has come down from those after them, it should not be made

translated_text:
a foundation, even if its proponent is excused—indeed, rewarded—for exercising independent judgment or following an authority.

Whoever bases scholarly discussion of fundamentals and subsidiary matters on the Quran, the Sunnah and the reports transmitted from the early predecessors has followed the prophetic path. Likewise, whoever bases aspiration, worship, action and listening—in relation to the fundamentals and particulars of practice, encompassing states of the heart and bodily actions—on faith, the Sunnah and the guidance followed by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions, has followed the prophetic path. This is the way of the leading scholars of guidance.

Thus, when Imam Ahmad discusses the foundations of the Sunnah, you find him saying: “They consist in holding fast to the way followed by the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” He compiled works of Quranic commentary based on what was transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions and the Successors. He also recorded hadiths and reports transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions and the Successors. These are what he relies upon in the fundamentals and subsidiary matters of his scholarship. He even said in his letter to al-Mutawakkil, the caliph of his time:

“I do not like to speak about any of these matters except on the basis of what is in Allah’s Book or in a report from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or from the Companions or the Successors. As for anything beyond that, discussing it is not praiseworthy.”

translated_text:
The same applies to “asceticism,” “heart-softening exhortations,” and “spiritual states.” In his Book of Asceticism, he relied on reports transmitted from the prophets—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—from Adam to Muhammad, and then on the way of the Companions and the Successors, without mentioning those who came after them. Likewise, he instructed the student of knowledge to record what was transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then from the Companions, then from the Successors. In another version, he said: “Then, regarding the Successors, you have a choice.”

He also made statements concerning “speculative theology,” “juristic opinion,” “Sufi books,” and “Sufi listening practices,” which this is not the place to discuss. A precise treatment requires elaboration and an explanation of how his statements apply in some circumstances but not others. This rests on the principle we have already stated: good deeds may be accompanied by sins, whether forgiven or unforgiven. A spiritual wayfarer may find it impossible or difficult to follow the purely prescribed path without some newly introduced practice, because there is no one who upholds the prescribed path in knowledge and practice.

If pure light is unavailable, and the only light to be found is not pure, while a person would otherwise remain in darkness, one should not disparage or forbid a light mingled with darkness unless a light free of darkness is available. Otherwise, how many who turn away from this leave the light altogether when someone else turns away from it because of the darkness he has seen in people’s ways!

translated_text:
I have set out this “principle” only so that the early generations’ and scholars’ condemnation of a thing may be understood in its proper context, and so that it may be recognized that departure from the full realization of succession to prophethood, as prescribed by the revealed law, sometimes results from negligence in omitting good in knowledge and action, and sometimes from transgression in committing evil in knowledge and action. Either may occur because a person is overwhelmed, or despite having the ability to act otherwise. The “former” may result from inability and limited capacity, or occur despite having the ability and opportunity. The “latter” may occur under conditions of need and necessity, or despite having sufficient means and ample alternatives.

Both the person unable to attain the full measure of good and the person compelled by necessity to commit some evil are excused, for Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And He says:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity”—in al-Baqarah and al-Talāq (1).

And He says:

“But those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity—those are the people of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

And He, glorified be He, says:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

And He says:

“Allah does not intend to place you in hardship.”

And He says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And He says:

“But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, incurs no sin.”

And He says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”
translated_footnote: (1) The verse in Surah al-Talāq is Allah Most High’s statement: “Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it.”

translated_text:
And this is a great principle: to recognize what is good in itself, in knowledge and action, whether obligatory or recommended; and to recognize what is evil in itself, in knowledge, speech, and action, whether prohibited or not—if what is not prohibited may be called evil. Religion consists in securing good and benefit, and preventing evil and harm.

These two aspects often coexist in a single act or a single person. Blame, prohibition, and punishment may be directed at the evil contained in either, but the good within it must not be overlooked. Likewise, praise, commands, and reward may be directed at the good contained in either, but the evil within it must not be overlooked. A man may be praised for refraining from certain evils involving religious innovation and wickedness, yet he may lack the good deeds, in accordance with the Sunnah and righteousness, for which another is praised. This is the way of weighing things fairly and giving each its due. Whoever follows it upholds the justice for which Allah sent down the Book and the Balance.

and the Sunnah and transmitted reports, for relatively little time had elapsed. The light of the prophetic reports still shone clearly, and their proof was compelling, even though, for some people, their light had become mingled with the darkness of other things.

As for later writers, many of them presented their predecessors’ formulations in isolation. Some later authors on “speculative theology,” for example, mentioned only innovated principles and turned away from the Book and the Sunnah. They either treated these two as secondary, affirmed them only in general terms, or eventually drifted into a form of heresy. The earlier speculative theologians were better than their later counterparts.

Likewise, some authors on “opinion” mentioned only the views of the imam they followed and his associates, turning away from the Book and the Sunnah and judging their teachings by their imam’s opinions. This was the case with many followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others.

Similarly, some authors on “Sufism” and “asceticism” took reports about later ascetics as their foundation and turned away from the path of the Companions and the Successors. This was done by Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī, the author of The Epistle; Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Kalābādhī; Ibn Khamīs al-Mawsilī in Virtues of the Righteous; and Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī in History of the Sufis. However, Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān also compiled Biographies of the Early Generations, concerning Allah’s friends and the righteous, and biographies of righteous people from the early generations, just as he compiled biographies of righteous people from later generations. translated_text:
“asceticism and spiritual states” after the first three generations, beginning with Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād, Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī, Ma‘rūf al-Karkhī, and those who followed them, while disregarding the lives of the Companions and Successors, whom the Book and the Sunnah expressly praise and commend, declaring Allah’s pleasure with them.

It would have been better for them to follow Abū Nu‘aym al-Asbahānī’s example in The Adornment, mentioning both earlier and later generations. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī likewise did this in The Choicest of the Chosen, as did Abū al-Qāsim al-Taymī in Biographies of the Early Generations … (1), and likewise Ibn Asad ibn Mūsā—even if they did not rise to the standard of ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Hannād ibn al-Sarī, and others in their books on asceticism. So much for this. Allah knows best and is most wise.

Knowing the origins and beginnings of things, and knowing the religion, its foundation, and the origins of what subsequently developed within it, are among the most beneficial branches of knowledge. For until a person thoroughly understands the realities of the matters he needs to know, a thorn of unease remains in his heart.

The ascetics had several names: in Syria they were called “al-Jū‘iyyah”; in Basra, “al-Faqriyyah” and “al-Fikriyyah”; and in Khurāsān, “al-Maghāribah.” They were also called “Sufis” and “the poor.”

First: the phrase containing the blank reads: “and likewise [Kitāb al-Zuhd (The Book of Asceticism)] by Asad ibn Mūsā.” The word ibn (son of) appears to be a corruption of al-zuhd (asceticism), since Asad ibn Mūsā al-Umawī—may Allah have mercy on him—known as Asad al-Sunnah (the Lion of the Sunnah), wrote a book on asceticism.

translated_text:
The name “Sufis” is derived from sūf (wool), since wool was the usual clothing of ascetics. It has also been said to derive from Sūfah ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tābikhah, an Arab tribe whose members used to reside around the Sacred House.

As for those who derive it from suffah (the shaded platform), the objection has been raised that the proper form would be Suffiyyah. Likewise, those who derive it from safāʾ (purity) are told that the proper form would be Safāʾiyyah. If the word ended instead in an unhamzated long ā, the form would be Safawiyyah; if derived from safwah (the elect), it would be Safwiyyah. Those who derive it from saff, meaning the foremost rank before Allah, are told that the proper form would be Saffiyyah. There is no doubt that these would be the required forms of attribution and affiliation if due regard were given to the rules of Arabic.

The correct explanation, however, is that these derivations were proposed on the basis of greater and intermediate derivation, rather than minor derivation. This resembles Abū Ja‘far’s statement that al-‘āmmah (the common people) is a name derived from ‘amā (blindness). Such derivations take account either of shared letters without regard to their order—which is intermediate derivation—or of letters belonging to the same kind without being identical—which is greater derivation. An example of intermediate derivation is the Kufan grammarians’ assertion that ism (name) derives from simah (mark). The same applies when “Sufi” is said to derive from safāʾ (purity). If, however, it is said to derive from suffah or saff, this falls under greater derivation.

A number of the leading scholars, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, used this designation.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī and others also used this designation. As for al-Shāfi‘ī, what is reported from him is criticism of the Sufis, and likewise from Mālik—as far as I recall. Ahmad used this designation when addressing Abū Hamzah al-Khurāsānī, Yūsuf ibn al-Husayn al-Rāzī, and Badr ibn Abī Badr al-Maghāzilī. Their path was criticized by a number of scholars and devout worshippers among the followers of Ahmad, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Abū Hanīfah, as well as by hadith scholars and other devout worshippers, while others praised it.

The sound assessment is that, like other paths, it contains both praiseworthy and blameworthy elements. Its blameworthy elements may or may not result from independent scholarly judgment. In this respect, they are comparable to jurists in their use of legal opinion, for many groups of scholars and devout worshippers have criticized legal opinion. The principle I set out earlier encompasses all of this. Among those who bear this designation are countless allies of Allah, His chosen ones, and the finest of His servants, just as among those who employ legal opinion are people of knowledge and faith whose number none but Allah can count. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

This makes it clear to you that, although innovation in religion is in principle blameworthy—as the Book and the Sunnah indicate, whether such innovations involve words or deeds—and I have written elsewhere that it is imperative to uphold the general scope of the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Every innovation is misguidance,” that one must act upon its general scope, and that whoever begins dividing innovations into good and bad and makes that

This is what some of those engaged in jurisprudence, speculative theology, Sufism, and devotional worship do: when forbidden from engaging in “innovated acts of worship” and “discourse concerning innovated forms of religious observance,” they claim that no innovation is blameworthy unless it has been prohibited. The hadith would then amount to saying: “Everything that has been prohibited,” or “Everything that has been forbidden,” or “Everything that contradicts a prophetic text is misguidance.” This is too obvious to need explanation. Rather, everything in religion that has not been prescribed is misguidance.

As for anything called an “innovation” whose goodness is established by the evidence of revelation, one of “two things” must follow. Either it is said that it is not an innovation in religion, even though it may be called an innovation in the linguistic sense—as ‘Umar said, “What an excellent innovation this is!”—or it is said that this is a general statement from which this particular case has been excepted on the strength of outweighing counterevidence. It then retains its general application to everything else, like other general statements in the Book and Sunnah. I have explained this in Iqtidā’ al-Sirāt al-Mustaqīm (Following the Straight Path), Qā‘idat al-Sunnah wa-l-Bid‘ah (A Treatise on Sunnah and Innovation), and elsewhere.

translated_text:
because of an excusable exercise of independent judgment or reliance on another’s judgment, or because of a lack of ability, as I have explained elsewhere. I have also explained this under the principle of “declaring someone an unbeliever or a sinful transgressor,” which rests on the principle governing threats of punishment.

The texts containing “threats of punishment” in the Book and Sunnah, and the statements of the leading scholars declaring people unbelievers or sinful transgressors and the like, do not entail that their consequences apply to a particular individual unless the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent. There is no distinction in this respect between fundamentals and subsidiary matters.

This concerns punishment in the Hereafter. One who deserves the threatened chastisement, curse, and wrath of Allah in the Hereafter will either remain in the Fire eternally or not. The corresponding designations of disbelief and sinful transgression fall under this “rule,” whether they arise from an innovation in belief or worship, or from sinful conduct in worldly life—that is, sinful transgression through deeds.

The same also applies to rulings in this world. Fighting unbelievers must be preceded by calling them to Islam, since punishment applies only to those whom the message has reached. Likewise, punishment of sinful transgressors is not warranted until the proof has been established against them.

translated_text:
There is an important principle here that deserves careful attention: for sins that harm others in their religion and worldly affairs, the punishment we impose in this world is more severe. As for sins through which a person harms himself, his punishment in the Hereafter may be more severe, even though we do not punish him in this world.

Harming a person in his religion and worldly affairs constitutes wrongdoing against others. Anyone who wrongs another necessarily deserves punishment in this world, to prevent people from wronging one another. Such wrongdoing is of two kinds:

First: withholding the rights due to others, which is neglect.

Second: doing what harms another, which is aggression. Thus, neglect of people’s rights . . . (1)
translated_footnote: (1) A lacuna in the original manuscript.

translated_text:
For this reason, one who promotes religious innovations is subjected to punishments not imposed on one who remains silent; one who openly commits wrongdoing is subjected to punishments not imposed on one who conceals it; and we refrain from punishing the religious hypocrite, even though he will be in the lowest depth of the Fire.

This is because, in principle, punishment is administered by Allah Most High: He recompenses people for their deeds in the Hereafter, and He may also recompense them in this world. As for us, we punish people only to the extent needed to secure the performance of obligations and the abandonment of prohibited acts, as far as we are able. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they do so, they safeguard their lives and property from me, except where a rightful claim warrants otherwise, and their reckoning rests with Allah.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and religion is wholly devoted to Allah.”

And He said:

“Persecution is worse than killing.”

For this reason, if unbelievers, those who wage war, or other transgressors repent before they are apprehended, the punishment pertaining to Allah’s right is waived. Thus, if an unbeliever at war with the Muslims embraces Islam before being captured, he thereby safeguards his life, family, and property. The same applies to highway robbers, those who commit unlawful sexual intercourse, thieves, and those who drink intoxicants, if they repent before being apprehended, because repentance achieves the intended purpose.

But if they repent after being apprehended, the punishment is not entirely waived, because that would lead to the prescribed penalties being rendered ineffective and to the spread of corruption, and because such repentance cannot be relied upon. For this reason, if an unbeliever at war with the Muslims embraces Islam during battle, his acceptance of Islam is valid, because he embraced Islam before being captured

translated_text:
unlike one who embraces Islam after being taken captive: although his life is protected, his enslavement is not precluded.

It follows from this “principle” that some disbelievers and hypocrites may be left unpunished, even though their punishment in the Hereafter will be more severe, provided their harm does not extend to others. Examples include those who pay the jizyah willingly while humbled, and those who outwardly profess Islam and observe its laws despite their hypocrisy. These two groups have withheld their harm from Muslims in both religious and worldly affairs, and they will be punished in the Hereafter for the disbelief and hypocrisy they have committed.

As for anyone who openly engages in harmful conduct, his harm must be prevented, even through punishment—even if he is a Muslim who is flagrantly sinful or disobedient, or an upright person who errs in exercising independent judgment; indeed, even if he is righteous or a scholar. This applies equally to those who can be apprehended and those who resist apprehension.

As an example concerning those who can be apprehended, people who openly commit unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, false testimony, highway robbery, and similar acts are punished only because these acts violate lives, property, and sexual inviolability. This is so even though the sinful Muslim’s condition in the Hereafter is better than that of disbelievers under covenant and hypocrites, for the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish that a sinful Muslim is better than a disbeliever or hypocrite.

Likewise, anyone who promotes a religious innovation that harms people in their religion is punished, even though he may in fact be excused for it on account of his independent judgment or his following another’s opinion.

translated_text:
Likewise, it is permissible to fight “rebels”: those who rise against the ruler or others on the basis of a defensible interpretation, even though they remain upright, we uphold their judicial rulings, and we recognize as valid their collection of jizyah, land tax, and other revenues. There is no disagreement that the Companions retained their upright standing; their defensible interpretation precluded judging them to be flagrantly sinful.

As for fighting them, its purpose is to make them fulfil the obligations they have neglected and desist from the prohibited acts they have committed, even though they act on an interpretation. Likewise, we enforce the prescribed punishment upon someone who drinks a fermented beverage whose permissibility is disputed, even if those who do so are righteous people.

Consider, then, how people are punished in this world for neglecting an obligation or committing an act clearly forbidden in religious or worldly affairs, even though they may be excused for it. This is done to avert the worldly harm caused by their actions. Similarly, the prescribed punishment is enforced upon someone who repents after his case has been brought before the ruler, even if his repentance is entirely sincere. Likewise, an army will march against this House, and while they are on a stretch of open ground, the earth will swallow them up. Among them will be people compelled to accompany them, but they will be resurrected according to their intentions. Likewise, the armies of the disbelievers are fought even though their ranks include people compelled to join them, as at Badr, when al-ʿAbbās and others were among them.

The same applies if the disbelievers use Muslims as shields and their harm cannot be repelled except by fighting them. Thus, punishments prescribed by religious law and those divinely decreed may, in this world, extend to people who do not deserve them in the Hereafter. For such people, they count among the calamities that befall them. As has been said concerning some of them: “The killer is striving in Allah’s cause, and the one killed is a martyr.”

Accordingly, the instruction given by the later adherents of the Sunnah—that an advocate of religious innovation

translated_text:
is to be shunned—his testimony is not to be sought, no narrations are to be transmitted from him, no legal opinions are to be sought from him, and prayer is not to be performed behind him—may fall into this category. Shunning him is a disciplinary measure and a punishment intended to deter people from that sin, whether it is a religious innovation or something else, even if he has in fact repented or is excused.

For shunning serves one of two purposes: either avoiding the sins that must be shunned and those who commit them, or punishing the offender and making an example of him. As for shunning him by refraining from . . . (1) elsewhere.

This category includes Imām Ahmad’s shunning of those who yielded during the inquisition before being put in fetters, those who repented after yielding, and those who committed some religious innovation, even though they included leading figures in hadith, jurisprudence, Sufism, and worship. His shunning them, together with the Muslims who joined him, does not preclude recognizing their merit. Similarly, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the Muslims to shun the three who had been left behind, this did not negate their earlier merits.

Indeed, it has been said that two of them participated in Badr, and Allah said to the people of Badr:

“Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.”

One of the three was Kaʿb ibn Mālik, the Prophet’s poet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and one of those present at al-ʿAqabah.

This, then, is “a fundamental principle”: a worldly punishment prescribed by religious law, ranging from shunning to execution, does not preclude the person punished from being upright or righteous. This accords with the distinction I have explained between worldly punishment—whether prescribed by religious law or divinely decreed—and punishment in the Hereafter. Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

translated_text:
Section

Related to this subject is the saying: “So-and-so’s state is to be accepted without objection,” or “His state is not to be accepted without objection.” Disputes over this frequently arise concerning things done by certain shaykhs, spiritual mendicants, and Sufis that are said to contravene the Sharia.

Someone who considers these things reprehensible, and regards forbidding wrongdoing as part of religion, condemns those acts and censures both the man concerned and anyone who thinks well of him. He hates him, denounces him, and punishes him. By contrast, someone who sees the man’s righteousness and devotion—his asceticism, spiritual states, scrupulous piety, and knowledge—does not condemn those acts. Rather, he considers them permissible or good, or turns away from the matter.

Either of these two may go to extremes. The first may be carried by his condemnation to the point of declaring people unbelievers or grave sinners in matters open to scholarly judgment, following the apparent meaning of evidence from the Sharia. The second may be carried by his acceptance to the point of approving things contrary to the religion of Islam—things indisputably known to contradict what the Messenger brought—claiming to follow something resembling the account of Moses and al-Khidr.

The first tendency is common among those whose approach resembles that of Moses, and those among them who have strayed into Judaism. The second is common among those whose approach resembles that of Jesus, and those among them who have strayed into Christianity.

translated_text:
And the (first) tendency often occurs among people of knowledge, but coupled with hardness of heart and the pursuit of personal desires. The (second) often occurs among people of compassion, but coupled with misguidance and ignorance. As for the “community of the middle way,” they possess both knowledge and mercy, as Allah has described Himself in the words:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

And He, Most High, says:

“My mercy encompasses all things.”

And He says:

“Your only God is Allah, other than whom there is no deity. He encompasses all things in knowledge.”

Likewise, He described the servant whom Moses met, saying:

“We had granted him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our own presence.”

The just approach in “this matter,” in both word and deed, is to recognize that accepting someone’s state without objection has two meanings:

The first is to absolve him of blame, so that he is neither censured nor held sinful . . . (1).

The second is to judge what he has done to be correct, so that he deserves praise and reward. Thus, the “first” means the absence of censure and punishment, while the “second” means the presence of praise and reward. The “first” means the absence of Allah’s displeasure and punishment, while the “second” means the presence of His pleasure and reward. For this reason,

translated_text:
you will often find those who object affirming displeasure, censure, and punishment, while those who approve affirm pleasure, praise, and reward. Both may be mistaken, with the correct view lying in “a third, intermediate position”: that there is neither praise nor censure, neither reward nor punishment.

The explanation is this: when something a person says or does is known to contradict the Quran and Sunnah, constituting a false statement or a forbidden act, he may nevertheless be excused in two circumstances: (the first) is his inability to obtain the relevant knowledge; (the second) is his inability to follow the truth prescribed by the revealed law.

An example of (the first) is when the person experiencing the state is bewildered and insane, and is no longer held accountable. If it is said of him, “His state should be accepted without objection,” meaning that he is neither censured nor punished—not that he is judged correct in it—then this is sound, just as it is said of other insane people. But if what is meant is that the statement itself is correct, then this is mistaken.

The same applies when his state results from an exercise of independent judgment, as in matters disputed among people of knowledge and religion. If it is said, “His state should be accepted without objection,” just as one says, “He is allowed to maintain his independent judgment,” meaning that he is neither censured nor punished, then this is sound.

But if this is said to mean that it is correct or sound, evidence must be provided to establish its correctness. A statement or action proceeding from anyone other than the Messenger is not, in itself, proof that the speaker or doer is correct. If that exercise of independent judgment is known to be mistaken, accepting his state means exempting him from censure, not declaring him correct.

Likewise, accepting his state and allowing him to continue may mean letting his judicial ruling stand without overturning it, allowing his legal opinion to stand without objection, or permitting those entitled to rely on his authority and follow him to do so. Those lacking the requisite knowledge may rely on and follow scholars and religious teachers whom it is permissible to follow, in matters they have not recognized as mistaken. Some of this, however, falls within the second category: that which is not known to contravene the revealed law.

In such cases, his state is accepted when he is known to be excused, or known to be sincere in his path and the matter may be an exercise of independent judgment on his part. These, then, are “three circumstances” in which his state is accepted because he is unable to obtain the relevant knowledge and the truth is hidden from him in a way that excuses him.

An example of (the second)—his inability to comply—is when he experiences states that compel him to tear his clothes, slap his face, utter objectionable cries, or shake violently. If it is known that the cause of this was not forbidden and that he is overcome by it, his state is accepted. If there is doubt whether he is overcome or merely pretending, but he is known to be truthful, it is said, “His state should be accepted without objection,”

In sum, these matters must be accorded their due under the Quran and Sunnah. Whatever the Quran and Sunnah convey—whether statements, commands, or prohibitions—must be followed. No consideration is to be given to anyone who opposes it, whoever he may be, nor may anyone be followed in contradicting it, whoever he may be. This accords with what the Quran, Sunnah, and consensus of the Muslim community establish concerning following and obeying the Messenger.

At the same time, the person responsible for such conduct must be excused wherever the revealed law excuses him: if he has lost his reason or discernment; if he has erred in exercising independent judgment, whether in word or deed; or if he is so overcome in committing that act or neglecting that duty that, through no sin of his own, he cannot prevent the objectionable act he commits, or, through no sin of his own, he cannot perform that obligation.

The general principle governing this matter must be safeguarded: whatever contradicts the Quran and Sunnah must neither be followed nor made into a religious law or a path to follow. Rather, there is no path to Allah and no religious law except what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. As for those individuals who have contravened some of this in the circumstances described above, they are excused, and are neither blamed nor punished.

For the words and deeds of anyone may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Every imam has said or done things in which he is not to be followed, even though he is not blamed for them.

Yet he cannot bind others to what has become clear to him but not to them. Thus, in one respect, such a matter belongs to the first category, and in another to the second. These matters may also remain open to independent judgment in his own view. In such cases, those exercising independent judgment, together with those who follow them, are allowed their respective approaches as a general concession, without being censured for them, just as an individual concession is granted in the first category.

As for someone whose state is not to be accepted as an excuse, this includes one who is known to be of sound mind but feigns derangement to escape blame—as do many who affiliate themselves with Shaykh Ahmad ibn al-Rifāʿī and the “Yūnusiyya” regarding the forbidden acts they commit and the obligations they neglect. It also includes one who is known to affect ecstasy and feign intoxication in that state so that others will think well of him and excuse the objectionable acts he commits; or one who is known to have recognized the truth but follows his own desires; or one who is known to regard deviation from the requirements of Muhammad’s revealed law as permissible, who may utter statements contrary to it, and who holds that some men can dispense with the Messenger, oppose him, or simply go along with the divine decree in opposition to religion.

Thus, some misguided liars relate that the people of the Suffa fought against the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, alongside the disbelievers when his Companions were defeated, saying: “We are with Allah; whoever prevails, we are with him.” They also relate that, on the morning following the Night Journey, the intimate discourse that had taken place between him and his Lord was heard from him,

and that he gave himself over to ecstasy in heaven until his cloak fell from him; and that he deposited the secret communicated to him in a patch of earth where reeds grew, so that the flute came to bear the meaning of that secret. Or they hold that anyone after Muhammad may depart from his revealed law, just as al-Khidr was permitted to depart from Moses’ command. Moses, however, had not been sent to al-Khidr, whereas Muhammad was sent to all humankind.

These people, and others like them who violate the revealed law and turn away when the truth becomes clear to them, must be opposed in accordance with what the revealed law prescribes: by physical intervention, by speech, and in the heart. Likewise, anyone who follows those previously mentioned whose contrary statements and actions were excusable must be censured, for the excuse that applied to them does not apply to him. He therefore has no grounds for following them in this.

When it is unclear to which of the two categories someone belongs, judgment concerning him should be withheld, for it is better for a ruler to err in pardoning than to err in punishing. However, there should be no hesitation in rejecting whatever contradicts the Book and Sunnah, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever performs an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected.”

It is therefore impermissible to depart, on doubtful grounds, from what the general and unqualified wording of the Book and Sunnah requires. Nor is it permissible to condemn or punish on doubtful grounds, or to declare something true or false, right or wrong, on such grounds.

May Allah guide us to the straight path—the path of those whom He has blessed among the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous—not those who have incurred His anger, nor those who have gone astray.

translated_text:
There remains here a “question” that often causes confusion: someone whose circumstances are unknown may outwardly do something contrary to the revealed law, yet possibly have an excuse recognized by that law. Examples include a state of ecstasy in which he transgresses the revealed law, when it is unclear whether his state is genuine or feigned; or taking property apparently without its owner’s permission, when he may know that the owner willingly consents.

If it is said that such a person should be censured, he may in fact have an excuse. But if it is said that he should not be censured, this entails allowing people whose circumstances are unknown to persist in apparent violations of the revealed law. In such cases, one must first address the person gently, saying: “Outwardly, this is wrong. As for the inward reality, Allah has entrusted you with responsibility for yourself. So explain your circumstances to us, or refrain from displaying this where doing so would cause confusion and temptation.” In doing so, you should follow a course that neither condones wrongdoing nor blames the innocent.

The governing principle is that someone habitually known for truthfulness and trustworthiness should be left unchallenged unless his words or actions are known to be false or unlawful. Someone known for lying or dishonesty should not be left unchallenged when the facts are unclear. As for someone whose character is unknown, judgment concerning him should be withheld.

The shaykh, imam, learned scholar and great authority, Shaykh al-Islām, an heir to the noble early generations, the godly scholar into whose heart the light of the Quran had been cast, Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah al-Harrānī—may Allah sanctify his soul, illuminate his grave, and grant him an abode in the spacious Gardens of Paradise—also said:

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help, ask His forgiveness, and seek His guidance. We seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. We bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, with no partner, and we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. He sent him with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and Allah suffices as a witness.

He conveyed the message, fulfilled the trust, sincerely counselled the community, dispelled its distress, strove in Allah’s cause as he ought, and worshipped Allah with sincere devotion until death came to him from his Lord. May Allah bestow His blessings and abundant peace upon him until the Day of Judgment.

Section: “Acts of Worship” and “The Distinction between Their Prescribed and Innovated Forms”

Much confusion has arisen in this area, just as it has concerning what is lawful and unlawful. Some people have deemed lawful certain things Allah has forbidden, while others have forbidden certain things Allah Most High has made lawful. Likewise, some have introduced acts of worship that Allah has not prescribed but has, rather, prohibited.

The “foundation of religion” is that what is lawful is what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful; what is unlawful is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden; and religion consists of what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. No one may depart from the straight path with which Allah sent His Messenger.

Allah Most High says:

“And this is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path. This is what He has commanded you, so that you may be mindful of Him.”

In the hadith of ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—it is reported: “The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—drew a line, then drew other lines to his right and left. He then said: ‘This is Allah’s path, and these are other paths. On each of these paths is a devil calling

In Sūrat al-An‘ām, Sūrat al-A‘rāf, and elsewhere, Allah Most High mentions the grounds on which He condemned the polytheists: they prohibited what Allah Most High had not prohibited, such as the bahīrah and sā’ibah; deemed lawful what Allah had forbidden, such as killing their children; and instituted a religion that Allah had not authorized. Allah Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have ordained for them a religion that Allah has not authorized?”

This included forbidden things that they made into acts of worship, such as associating partners with Allah and committing indecencies, including circumambulating the House naked, and other such practices. The discussion of “the lawful and the unlawful” belongs elsewhere. Our concern here is “acts of worship,” so we say:

Among the acts of worship by which people seek nearness to Allah Most High are those that Allah and His Messenger love and approve of. These are either obligatory or recommended, as reported in the Sahīh from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He:

“My servant draws near to Me through nothing like the performance of what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks

It is well known that some prayers are obligatory—namely, the five daily prayers—while others are voluntary, such as the night prayer. Likewise, some fasting is obligatory, namely fasting the month of Ramadan, while some is voluntary, such as fasting three days each month. Similarly, travelling to the Sacred Mosque is obligatory, while travelling to the other two mosques—the Mosque of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the mosque in Jerusalem—is recommended.

Likewise, some charity is obligatory and some is recommended, the latter being what is given from one’s surplus, as Allah Most High says:

“They ask you what they should spend. Say, ‘Whatever is beyond your needs.’”

An authentic hadith reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O son of Adam, spending your surplus is better for you, while withholding it is worse for you. You are not to blame for retaining what suffices for your needs. The upper hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those you support.”

The distinction between what is obligatory and what is recommended belongs elsewhere. Our concern here is the distinction between what is prescribed, whether obligatory or recommended, and what is not prescribed. What is prescribed is that by which one draws near to Allah Most High, and it is Allah’s path

, and it is righteousness, obedience, good deeds, goodness, and right conduct. It is the path of spiritual wayfarers and the way of seekers and worshippers. It is followed by everyone whom Allah wills to guide and who takes the path of asceticism and worship, and what is called poverty, Sufism, and the like.

Undoubtedly, this includes the prescribed prayers, both obligatory and recommended. It includes the prescribed night prayer, reciting the Quran in the prescribed manner, and the prescribed remembrances and supplications. Some of these are assigned particular times, such as the beginning and end of the day; others are connected with particular occasions, such as the prayer upon entering a mosque, the prostration of recitation, the eclipse prayer, and the prayer for guidance in making a choice, together with the prescribed remembrances and supplications transmitted for these occasions. This encompasses many things, whose various forms would take a long time to describe.

It likewise includes prescribed fasting, such as fasting half the time, a third, two thirds, or a tenth—the last being fasting three days each month. It includes prescribed travel, such as travelling to Mecca and to the other two mosques. It includes jihad in its various forms; most Prophetic hadiths concern prayer and jihad. It also includes reciting the Quran in the prescribed manner.

The foundations of “religious acts of worship” are prayer, fasting, and recitation, as mentioned in the hadith of Abdullāh ibn Amr ibn al-Ās in the two Sahīh collections. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to him and said:

“Have I not been told that you said, ‘I will certainly fast
