translated_text:
Stranger still is what one of these mistaken people once said to me concerning His words:

“None knows its interpretation except Allah.”

He said that this meant: “None knows the interpretation of ‘He’”—meaning the name “He” used in the invocation “He, He.” Ibn ‘Arabī wrote a book about this “He.” I replied to him—though I was very young at the time—“If it were as you say, it would have been written in the Quran as two separate words, ta’wīlu huwa (‘the interpretation of “He”’), rather than as one word, ta’wīlahu (‘its interpretation’).”

The falsity of what this man said is self-evident. Many mistaken Sufis offer similar false interpretations of the Quran and Sunnah. The meaning they intend may be sound, but the wording does not indicate it, nor is it what the speaker intended; or the meaning itself may be unsound. Thus, the error sometimes lies in the conclusion and sometimes in the evidence.

For example, some interpret:

“Because he sees himself as self-sufficient”

to mean: “Because he sees his Lord, he becomes self-sufficient.” Yet the meaning is that he transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient.

Likewise, some interpret “If you do not see Him” (fa-in lam takun tarāhu) to mean: “If your awareness of yourself is effaced, you will see your Lord.”

This is not the meaning of the hadith. Had that been intended, the wording would have been fa-in lam takun tarahu, whereas it says tarāhu. Moreover, what would he do with the result clause, namely, “He certainly sees you”?

Furthermore, according to their false interpretation, the verb kāna (‘to be’) would express existence in its own right. Thus, “If you are not” would mean: “If you do not occur or exist.” This is an impossible interpretation, for the servant exists; he is not nonexistent. Even if what was intended was his detachment from his desires, or the effacement of his awareness of other things, this would not be expressed by denying his existence, for that is impossible.

Whenever the meaning is sound, but the wording was not intended to convey it, this may be called an “allusion.”

 مِنْ هَذَا قِطْعَةً. وَلَيْسَ الْمَقْصُودُ الْآنَ الْكَلَامَ فِي هَذَا فَإِنَّهُ بَابٌ آخَرُ. وَإِنَّمَا الْغَرَضُ بَيَانُ حُكْمِ ذِكْرِ الِاسْمِ وَحْدَهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ كَلَامٍ تَامٍّ وَقَدْ ظَهَرَ بِالْأَدِلَّةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ أَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُسْتَحَبٍّ. وَكَذَلِكَ بِالْأَدِلَّةِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ الذَّوْقِيَّةِ؛ فَإِنَّ الِاسْمَ وَحْدَهُ لَا يُعْطِي إيمَانًا وَلَا كُفْرًا وَلَا هُدًى وَلَا ضَلَالًا وَلَا عِلْمًا وَلَا جَهْلًا وَقَدْ يَذْكُرُ الذَّاكِرُ اسْمَ نَبِيٍّ مِنْ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ أَوْ فِرْعَوْنَ مِنْ الْفَرَاعِنَةِ أَوْ صَنَمٍ مِنْ الْأَصْنَامِ وَلَا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِمُجَرَّدِ اسْمِهِ حُكْمٌ إلَّا أَنْ يَقْرِنَ بِهِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى نَفْيٍ أَوْ إثْبَاتٍ أَوْ حُبٍّ أَوْ بُغْضٍ وَقَدْ يَذْكُرُ الْمَوْجُودَ وَالْمَعْدُومَ. وَلِهَذَا اتَّفَقَ أَهْلُ الْعِلْمِ بِلُغَةِ الْعَرَبِ وَسَائِر اللُّغَاتِ عَلَى أَنَّ الِاسْمَ وَحْدَهُ لَا يَحْسُنُ السُّكُوتُ عَلَيْهِ؛ وَلَا هُوَ جُمْلَةٌ تَامَّةٌ؛
 وَلَا كَلَامًا مُفِيدًا وَلِهَذَا سَمِعَ بَعْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُؤَذِّنًا يَقُولُ:
 أَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ.
 قَالَ:
 فَعَلَ مَاذَا فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا نَصَبَ الِاسْمَ صَارَ صِفَةً وَالصِّفَةُ مِنْ تَمَامِ الِاسْمِ الْمَوْصُوفِ فَطَلَبَ بِصِحَّةِ طَبْعِهِ الْخَبَرَ الْمُفِيدَ؛ وَلَكِنَّ الْمُؤَذِّنَ قَصَدَ الْخَبَرَ وَلَحَنَ.
translated_text:
And Shaykh Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī included a selection of such interpretations in his Haqā’iq al-tafsīr. Discussing this, however, is not our present purpose, for it is a separate subject. Our purpose is only to explain the ruling on invoking the name alone, without a complete utterance. The scriptural evidence has shown that this is not recommended, as has rational and experiential evidence.

The name alone conveys neither faith nor unbelief, guidance nor misguidance, knowledge nor ignorance. Someone may mention the name of a prophet, a pharaoh, or an idol, yet no judgment attaches to merely mentioning the name unless he adds something indicating negation or affirmation, love or hatred. He may also name something existent or nonexistent. Thus, scholars of Arabic and all other languages agree that a name alone cannot properly stand on its own: it is neither a complete sentence nor an informative utterance.

For this reason, when an Arab heard a caller to prayer say, “I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,” he asked, “What did he do?” By putting the noun in the accusative, the caller had made it a descriptive qualifier, and a qualifier forms part of the noun phrase it describes. The Arab’s sound linguistic instinct therefore led him to ask for an informative predicate. The caller, however, had intended it as the predicate but made a grammatical error.

translated_text:
Even if a person repeated the name “Allah” a million times, he would not thereby become a believer or merit Allah’s reward or His Paradise. Unbelievers of every nation mention the name alone, whether or not they acknowledge Him and His oneness.

Even when He commanded us to mention His name, as in His words:

“So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it,”

and His words:

“And do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned,”

and His words:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,”

and His words:

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great,”

and similar passages, mentioning His name was to be done through a complete utterance, such as saying, “In the name of Allah,” or, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High,” and, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,” and the like. He never prescribed mentioning the name alone. Doing so neither fulfills a command nor establishes [the lawfulness of game] (1) or of a slaughtered animal, or anything else of that kind.

If it is said: A person who utters or hears the name alone may experience a stirring of love and reverence for Allah, and similar feelings.

I reply: Yes, and he is rewarded for that lawful inward experience and state of faith, not because mentioning the name alone is recommended. Hearing it stirs what lies dormant in the heart. Yet what lies dormant may also be stirred by hearing an utterance that is forbidden or disliked. A Muslim may even hear someone associating partners with Allah or reviling Him, and a state of deep feeling and love for Allah surges in his heart because of the intensity of his aversion

{فَانْقَلَبُوا بِنِعْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَفَضْلٍ}
 الْآيَةَ. فَهَذَا الْإِيمَانُ الزَّائِدُ وَالتَّوَكُّلُ كَانَ سَبَبَ تَخْوِيفِهِمْ بِالْعَدُوِّ وَلَيْسَ ذَلِكَ مَشْرُوعًا بَلْ الْعَبْدُ يَفْعَلُ ذَنْبًا فَيُورِثُهُ ذَلِكَ تَوْبَةً يُحِبُّهُ اللَّهُ بِهَا وَلَا يَكُونُ الذَّنْبُ مَأْمُورًا بِهِ وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ جِدًّا. فَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَ أَنْ يَكُونَ نَفْسُ السَّبَبِ مُوجِبًا لِلْخَيْرِ وَمُقْتَضِيًا وَبَيْنَ
translated_text:
and hatred of what he has heard. The Companions said to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him):

“One of us finds within himself thoughts that he would rather be burned to a cinder or fall from heaven to earth than utter.”

He asked, “Have you really experienced that?”

They replied, “Yes.”

He said, “That is clear faith.” In another narration, he said, “Praise be to Allah, who has reduced his plotting to mere whispering.”

When Satan cast blameworthy whispers into their hearts, the faith within them stirred in aversion to those thoughts and horror at their enormity. That was clear faith. This does not imply that the cause—those whispers—was something commanded. Likewise, a person may be prompted to disbelief or disobedience, yet seek protection and resist, thereby gaining faith and piety. The cause itself, however, is not something commanded.

Allah Most High said:

“Those to whom people said, ‘Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them.’ But this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

“So they returned with favor from Allah and bounty,” to the end of the verse.

This increase in faith and reliance on Allah arose from their being frightened with the prospect of facing the enemy, yet such intimidation is not prescribed. Indeed, a person may commit a sin that leads him to repent, and Allah loves him for that repentance; this does not mean that the sin was commanded. This is a very broad subject. translated_text:
its not doing so, with the good arising instead from the recipient. The good words and righteous deeds that are commanded bring about goodness, mercy, and reward. When accompanied by the strength of the servant’s faith and the sweetness and savor of faith that he experiences, goodness, mercy, and blessing are multiplied.

As for things that are not commanded—whether the servant’s own actions, be they forbidden, disliked, or permissible; the actions of others toward him, whether humans or jinn; or heaven-sent events with which the Lord afflicts him—if they encounter faith and certainty within him, stirring that faith and certainty so that his faith increases, this does not mean that those causes should be loved, praised, or commanded if they are not otherwise deserving of such regard. They do not themselves entail that good; their effect is merely to stir what lies dormant. Often, they have led to evil and harm.

Similar to this is speaking of love, longing, and fear in unqualified terms, together with the poetry and prose expressing them. This too is non-specific: it is shared by believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked. For this reason, Allah and His Messenger have neither prescribed nor commanded such things. Allah commands only goodness, righteous deeds, and piety, and that does not belong to this category. The poetry of lovers, however, is shared by lovers of faith, lovers of idols, lovers of women, lovers of beardless youths, lovers of homelands, and lovers of paramours.

translated_text:
What we have stated thus establishes that invoking the name in isolation is not recommended, let alone being the remembrance of the elect. Still further removed is invoking the “pronominal name,” namely “He.” By itself, this does not designate anyone in particular; its referent depends on something mentioned or known that explains it. Its meaning therefore depends on the speaker’s purpose and intention. Thus, someone who believes that the Real is absolute existence may use it in remembrance.

He may say, “There is no He but He,” while his heart drifts into “the oneness of existence” and the doctrine of Pharaoh, the Ismā‘īlīs, and the heretics among these latter-day Sufis, so that his saying “He” is equivalent to saying “His existence.” By saying, “There is no He but He,” he may mean that He is existence, that there is no creation whatsoever, and that the Lord and the servant, the Real and creation, are one and the same—as I have explained elsewhere when discussing the doctrine of the Ittihādiyya (adherents of union).

Among the causes of these corrupt beliefs and spiritual states is departure from the law and the way with which the Messenger was sent to us, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Religious innovations are the beginnings of disbelief and places where it is likely to arise, just as the prescribed sunnahs are manifestations of faith and strengthen it. Faith increases through obedience and decreases through disobedience, as Allah has told us of its increase in such verses as His saying:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this increased them in faith.”

And His saying:

“Which of you has this increased in faith?”

translated_text:
and His saying:

“He is the One who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they might increase in faith along with their existing faith,”

and other such verses.

If it is asked, “If this form of remembrance is not prescribed, is it disliked?” I reply: In the case of someone who is overwhelmed, it is not deemed disliked. The heart may experience states in which speech becomes difficult, even while it is filled with states of faith. A person may then be able to invoke the name alone, but not a complete expression. Such people offer what their hearts contain of faith and whatever their tongues are capable of uttering.

For people fall into four categories with regard to remembrance:

(First) Remembrance with both heart and tongue. This is what is commanded.

(Second) Remembrance with the heart alone. If this is because the tongue is unable to speak, it is good; but if the tongue is capable, it means forgoing what is better.

(Third) Remembrance with the tongue alone: keeping one’s tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah. In this connection, there is the account of one in whom the angels found no good except the movement of his tongue in remembrance of Allah. Allah Most High says:

“I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move in remembrance of Me.”

(Fourth) Neither form of remembrance. This is the condition of those who are losers.

translated_text:
But when a complete expression can readily be uttered, restricting oneself to repeating the name alone is an innovation, and the default ruling on innovations is that they are disliked. The reports of Abū Yazīd, al-Nūrī, al-Shiblī and others invoking the name alone are to be understood as cases in which they were overwhelmed, for their states bear this out. Moreover, the shaykhs who were sounder and more accomplished than these men used only complete expressions of remembrance.

When disagreement arises, the matter must be referred back to Allah and the Messenger. The actions of anyone other than the Messenger do not constitute unconditional proof. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Chapter: The Straight Path in Asceticism, Worship, Scrupulousness in Abstaining from Forbidden Things and Desires, and Moderation in Worship

Adherence to the Sunnah protects against the evil of the self and Satan, without recourse to innovated paths. Those who follow such paths inevitably become entangled in burdens and shackles, even if they act on an interpretation; they cannot avoid following their desires. For this reason, the proponents of innovation are called the followers of desires. The way of the Sunnah is knowledge, justice, and guidance, whereas innovation contains ignorance, injustice, and the pursuit of conjecture and whatever the soul desires.

The Messenger has neither gone astray nor erred. Misguidance goes hand in hand with waywardness: everyone who is wayward is misguided. Right conduct is the opposite of waywardness, and guidance is the opposite of misguidance. This entails avoiding the path of the wicked and the proponents of innovation, both of whom the early generations used to warn against.

Allah Most High says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will therefore meet with ruin.”

And ghayy (waywardness) is originally the verbal noun in the conjugation ghawā–yaghwī–ghayyan (“to be wayward”), just as one says lawā–yalwī–layyan (“to twist”). It is the opposite of right conduct, as Allah Most High says:

“If they see the way of right conduct, they do not take it as their way; but if they see the way of waywardness, they take it as their way.”

Right conduct is action that benefits the person who performs it, while waywardness is action that harms the person who performs it. Thus, doing good is right conduct, and doing evil is waywardness. For this reason, the jinn said:

“We do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends a right course for them.”

They thus contrasted evil with right conduct. And He says at the end of the surah:

“Say: I have no power to bring you harm or guide you to a right course.”

From the same root comes rashīd (a person of sound judgment), to whom his property is handed over: someone who spends his wealth on what is beneficial, not on what is harmful.

Satan said:

“I will surely lead them all astray, except Your chosen servants among them.”

This means that he commands them to do the evil that harms them, and they obey him, as Allah Most High says:

“I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me.”

And He says:

“And Hell will be brought into full view of the wayward,”

until He says:

“Then they and the wayward will be hurled headlong into it, together with all the forces of Iblīs.”

And He says:

“Those against whom the sentence has been passed will say: ‘Our Lord, these are the ones we led astray. We led them astray just as we ourselves went astray.’”

And He says:

“Your companion has neither gone astray nor erred.”

translated_text:
the consequence of evil is called evil, and the consequence of good is called good; the consequences of good deeds are called hasanāt (good things), and the consequences of evil deeds sayyi’āt (bad things).

Thus, in the Book of Allah, “hasanāt and sayyi’āt” refer to good and evil deeds, as well as to blessings and calamities. Recompense corresponds to the deed: whoever does good and performs good deeds encounters good and good things, while whoever does evil and performs evil deeds encounters evil and bad things. Likewise, whoever acts waywardly encounters waywardness. Neglecting prayer and following desires are forms of waywardness whose perpetrator will encounter waywardness.

For this reason, al-Zamakhsharī said:

“To the Arabs, every evil is waywardness, and every good is right conduct.”

As the poet said:

“Whoever encounters good, people praise his conduct;
Whoever goes astray will never lack someone to blame him for his waywardness.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “Its recompense is waywardness,” in accordance with His words:

“He will meet a penalty,”

meaning recompense for sins. And the transmitted hadith states:

“Ghayy is a valley in Hell from which its other valleys seek refuge.”

This expresses the encounter with evil.

He, glorified be He, says:

“They neglected prayer and followed desires.”

Prayer entails seeking the Face of Allah, as Allah Most High says:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

That is, they perform the dawn and afternoon prayers. The one who supplicates directs himself toward his Lord and seeks Him. Thus, in these acts, hearts seek their Lord and love Him.

Following desires means following what the soul craves. The word shahawāt (desires) is the plural of shahwah, which is originally a verbal noun. The object of desire is also called shahwah, thus applying the verbal noun to its object. Allah Most High says:

“Those who follow their desires wish you to stray far away.”

He thus contrasts repentance with following desires, for He wishes to accept our repentance—that is, Allah loves this for us, is pleased with it, and commands it. “Those who follow their desires”—who are the wayward—“wish you to stray far away”: to turn you far away from the straight path toward following desires. The basic meaning of mayl (inclination) is deviation, which is inevitable for those who follow desires. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Remain steadfast, though you will never fully attain it. Know that the best of your deeds is prayer, and none but a believer consistently maintains his ablution.”

Ahmad and Ibn Mājah narrated this from Thawbān. He thus tells us that we cannot fully sustain steadfastness—or encompass its reward if we remain steadfast.

Allah also says:

“You will never be able to treat your wives with complete fairness, however hard you try. But do not incline wholly toward one, leaving another in limbo.”

His words, “incline wholly,” refer to the utmost extent of deviation: straying from the path and turning away from the straight way toward the furthest reaches of evil. Rather, if you are afflicted with this, exercise moderation and return to the path through repentance. As related in the hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“A believer’s straying is like that of a tethered horse: it wanders, then returns to where it is tethered. Likewise, the believer wanders, then returns

to his Lord.” Allah Most High says:

“Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous,”

through to His words:

“How excellent is the reward of those who work!”

He did not say that they never do wrong or commit sins. Rather, He said:

“When they commit an indecency or wrong themselves”—

that is, through another sin besides indecency. He thus joins the general to the specific. Similarly, Moses said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself.”

And Bilqīs said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself.”

Allah Most High also says generally of the inhabitants of the towns that were destroyed:

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.”

They wronged themselves by committing what they had been forbidden, disobeying their prophets, and failing to repent to their Lord. And Allah Most High says:

“They remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins.”

Hence He says:

“Allah wishes to accept your repentance.”

Then He says:

“Allah wishes to lighten your burden, for man was created weak.”

Mujāhid and others said that “following desires” refers to fornication. Ibn Zayd said: “They are the followers of falsehood.” Al-Suddī said: “They are the Jews and Christians.” All these interpretations are correct, for following desires may be accompanied by disbelief, or by acknowledgment that it is a sin.

He then mentions that “man was created weak.” The context indicates that man is weak when it comes to abstaining from desires. He therefore needs a lawful outlet for desire that enables him to dispense with what is forbidden. Hence Tāwūs and Muqātil said: “His weakness lies in his limited patience in abstaining from women.” Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Kaysān said: “His resolve is too weak to overcome desire.”

It has also been said: “He is weak in his original constitution, because he was created from a lowly fluid.” This is reported

The “one who seeks self-sufficiency” does not inwardly look to what others possess. The “one who exercises self-restraint” does not ask people for anything with his tongue. The “one who practices patience” is the one who does not force himself to be patient. He thus stated that whoever strives to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. This appears to concern patience in poverty: enduring the bitterness of need without becoming distraught over the poverty with which one has been afflicted. This is patience in poverty and hardship. The Most High says:

“And those who are patient in poverty and hardship and during battle.”

“Hardship” here means illness. This is patience in the need, illness, and fear with which one is afflicted.

As for patience in trials one voluntarily undertakes, such as jihad, patience in these is better than patience in an illness with which one is afflicted without choosing it. Thus, if someone experiences hardship during jihad, patience in that hardship is better than patience in it while in his own land, because such patience is part of fully carrying out jihad. Likewise, if he is afflicted during jihad with poverty or illness resulting from it, patience in that is better, as has been explained at length elsewhere. The same applies to the harm a person suffers while performing acts of obedience, such as prayer and enjoining what is right

Likewise, when his soul urges him toward prohibited things—whether leadership, taking wealth, or committing sexual immorality—his patience in resisting them is better than his patience in lesser matters. For the greater the righteous deeds, the greater the patience exercised in them compared with lesser deeds.

For “knowledge,” “governance,” “jihad,” “enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong,” “prayer,” “pilgrimage,” “fasting,” and “zakah” involve temptations of the soul and other trials not found in other pursuits. In these undertakings, the soul may develop an inclination toward leadership, wealth, and physical beauty. When the soul cannot attain these things, it does not covet them as it does when it can. When it has the ability, it seeks those prohibited things, unlike when it lacks that ability. Exercising patience when one has the ability is jihad; indeed, it is among the best forms of jihad.

It is also more complete in three respects:

(First): Patience in refraining from prohibited things is better than patience in afflictions.

(Second): Refraining from prohibited things when one can engage in them and the soul desires them is better than refraining from them without those circumstances.

(Third): When the soul’s desire for them arises because of a religious undertaking—as in the case of someone who

This is unlike the case in which his soul inclines toward it without his being engaged in a righteous deed.

For this reason, Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd would offer three counsels, saying:

“Do not visit a ruler, even if you say, ‘I will enjoin him to obey Allah.’ Do not visit a woman, even if you say, ‘I will teach her the Book of Allah.’ And do not lend your ear to a proponent of religious innovation, even if you say, ‘I will refute him.’”

His advice, then, was to guard against “the causes of temptation,” for when a person exposes himself to them, he may succumb and fail to remain safe. If he happens to be tested in this way without choosing it, or enters into it by choice and is then tested, he must fear Allah, exercise patience, be sincere, and strive. His patience in this and his remaining safe from temptation while fulfilling his duty are among the best deeds. Examples include someone who assumes authority and exercises it justly; someone who refutes proponents of religious innovation with the pure Sunnah without being led astray by them; or someone who teaches women their religion in the prescribed manner, without temptation.

Yet when Allah tests a servant and decrees a trial for him, He helps him; whereas when the servant exposes himself to a trial, Allah leaves him to his own devices. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Samura:

“Do not ask for authority, for if you are given it at your request, you will be left to bear it unaided; but if you are given it without asking, you will be helped in carrying it out.”

Likewise,

he said concerning the plague:

“If it breaks out in a town where you are, do not leave to flee from it; and if you hear of it in a land, do not go there.”

Whoever does what Allah has commanded and then encounters a trial without choosing it will receive Allah’s help in facing it, unlike someone who deliberately exposes himself to it. Yet the door of repentance remains open. A man may ask for authority and be left to bear it unaided, then regret having asked and repent. Allah then accepts his repentance and helps him either to fulfil his duty or to relinquish that authority. The same applies to all other trials.

As He says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

These matters require a fuller discussion than space permits here. And (the point) is that Allah, glorified is He, wishes to make things clear to us and guide us to the ways of those before us, of whom He said:

“Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, so follow their guidance.”

They are those to whose path He has commanded us to ask Him to guide us, in His words:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed.”

He loves us to follow their path and commands us to do so. It is the way of those who turn to Him. Thus, He mentions three matters here: clarification, guidance, and repentance.

It has also been said that the ways intended here are those of both the people of truth and the people of falsehood. That is, He wishes to make clear to us the ways of both groups, guiding His believing servants to the truth

“We have never sent a messenger except in the language of his people, so that he might make things clear to them. Then Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

And He says:

“Allah would never lead a people astray after guiding them until He has made clear to them what they must avoid.”

On this interpretation, “ways”—meaning the ways of the people of falsehood—would be grammatically connected to “make clear,” not to “guide,” while the people of truth would be connected to His words, “and guide you.”

Al-Zajjāj said: “The ‘ways’ are paths. Thus, the meaning is that He directs you to obey Him, just as He directed the prophets and their followers.” This interpretation is preferable, because when two verbs precede a shared object, the first is not made its sole governing verb. Rather, either the second alone governs it, or both do, as in His words:

“Bring me [copper], that I may pour molten copper over it.”

Alternatively, if the intended construction is, “He makes clear to you the ways of those before you and guides you to ways,” this still indicates that He guides us to their ways. What is meant here is the ways of the people of truth, unlike His words:

“There have been precedents before you.”

For He says immediately afterwards:

“So travel through the land and see what was the end of those who denied the truth.”

There, He intended to make the punishment of the wrongdoers known through direct observation. Here, however, He has sent down to us passages of the Quran through which He guides us to the ways of those before us: those whom Allah has blessed.

He mentions three matters: “clarification,” “guidance,” and “repentance.” This is because a person first needs to know good and evil, what he has been commanded to do, and what he has been forbidden to do. Then, after that, he needs

to be guided, so that he pursues the truth and acts upon it rather than falsehood. This is the way of the prophets and the righteous. Thereafter, he will inevitably commit sins and wish to purify himself of them through repentance. Thus, he needs knowledge, action upon it, and repentance alongside both. He will inevitably fall short or become heedless in following those ways to which Allah has guided him, and must therefore repent of whatever negligence he has shown in following each of them.

These “ways” include both obligatory and recommended deeds. Whoever follows them will inevitably fall short and become heedless, so he seeks Allah’s forgiveness and repents to Him. However hard a servant strives, he cannot fully discharge the duty Allah has imposed upon him. He therefore has no recourse but to seek forgiveness and repent after every act of obedience.

The meaning is: “I desire for you the good that benefits you, whereas these people desire for you the evil that harms you—like Satan, who desires to lead you astray. His followers are those who follow their desires. So do not take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me. Rather, follow the paths of guidance and rectitude, and beware of the paths of error and corruption.”

As the Most High says:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor fall into misery,”

and the verses that follow.

His words, “follow their desires,” occur in both passages. Following one's appetites is akin to following one's desires, as the Most High says:

“They only follow their own desires. And who is further astray than one who follows his desires without guidance from Allah?”

He also says:

“If the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would fall into ruin.”

The Most High says:

“Do not follow the desires of people who went astray before.”

And the Most High says:

“Is someone who stands upon clear proof from his Lord like those whose evil deeds have been made appealing to them and who follow their own desires?”

And the Most High says:

“Do not follow the desires of those who do not know.”

This occurs frequently in the Quran. The word hawā (desire) is the verbal noun of hawā, yahwī (to desire). The object of desire itself—what one desires—is also called hawā. Following it is thus like following a path, as the Most High says:

“Do not follow

the desires of people who went astray before.” As with the word “appetite,” following desire means following what the verbal noun itself denotes: following one’s will and love, which constitute one’s desire. Following one’s will means doing what the soul desires. This is like His words, the Most High:

“Follow the path of those who turn to Me.”

And His words:

“This is My path, perfectly straight, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, for they will lead you away from His path.”

He also says:

“Do not follow any protectors besides Him.”

The term “following” can thus apply to the one who commands and forbids, to the commands and prohibitions themselves, and to what is commanded and forbidden—the straight path. Likewise, desire has its commands and prohibitions, which are the soul’s commands and prohibitions. As the Most High says:

“I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul persistently commands evil, except where my Lord shows mercy. Indeed, my Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

As for the blameworthy deeds it commands, the one entails the other: following a command means doing what is commanded, and following the soul’s command means doing what it desires. Thus, it becomes clear that following appetites and following desires means following the soul’s appetite and desire by doing what it craves and desires.

Indeed, one may say that this is the only possible meaning of the expression “following appetites and desires.” For what a person craves and desires only comes into existence after he craves and desires it, and a person is censured only when he does what he craves and desires, when it comes into existence

Commenting on the Most High’s words, “Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,” the Quran commentators explained that this means neither taking anything Allah has forbidden nor withholding anything Allah has commanded one to give. Thus, avarice commands the opposite of what Allah and His Messenger command: Allah forbids injustice and commands kindness, whereas avarice commands injustice and forbids kindness.

(While circumambulating the House and standing at ‘Arafah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf would frequently say, “O Allah, protect me from the avarice of my own soul.” When asked about this, he replied, “If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I am protected from injustice, stinginess, and severing ties of kinship.” In another report from him, he said, “I fear that I am already ruined.” He asked, “Why is that?” He replied, “I hear Allah say, ‘Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,’ yet I am an avaricious man: hardly anything leaves my hand.” He replied, “That is not the avarice Allah mentions in the Quran. Avarice is to consume your brother’s wealth unjustly. This is merely stinginess—and what an evil thing stinginess is!”) (*).

The Most High mentions avarice in the context of envy and giving others preference over oneself, saying:

“They harbour no desire in their hearts for what the others have been given, and give them preference over themselves, even though they are in need.”

Then He says:

“And whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul—it is they who will be successful.”

Thus, whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul will not be envious and transgress against the person he envies. Envy is fundamentally hatred of the person envied.

(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 84):
An omission has occurred here, as two points demonstrate:
First, the apparent wording of the second report indicates that the speaker who said, “I fear that I may have been ruined,” was ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, since it says, “In another report from him, he said”—meaning Ibn ‘Awf, may Allah be pleased with him. Who, then, explained the verse to him by saying, “That is not the avarice Allah mentioned…”? It is this person’s statement that is being cited as evidence.
Second, a page later (p. 590), the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, said, “Ibn Mas‘ūd treated stinginess as distinct from avarice,” although Ibn Mas‘ūd had not previously been mentioned in this passage!
Thus, the second report from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, has been omitted here, together with the beginning of the report from Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him—the person whose statement is being related. His report was joined to the preceding report, causing the confusion.
It appears—and Allah knows best—that the corrected text should read as follows:
“While circumambulating the House and standing at ‘Arafah, ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf would frequently say, ‘O Allah, protect me from the avarice of my own soul.’ When asked about this, he replied, ‘If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I am protected from injustice, stinginess, and severing ties of kinship.’ In another report from him, he said: [‘If I am protected from the avarice of my own soul, I will neither steal nor commit adultery nor do…’] [A man came to ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, and said to him:] ‘I fear that I may have been ruined.’ He asked, ‘Why is that?’ The man replied, ‘I hear Allah say, “Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own soul,” yet I am an avaricious man: hardly anything leaves my hand.’ He replied, ‘That is not the avarice Allah mentions in the Quran. Avarice is to consume your brother’s wealth unjustly. This is merely stinginess—and what an evil thing stinginess is!’”

and avarice in a person is accompanied by greed, an intense desire for wealth, hatred of others, and injustice toward them. As the Most High says:

“Allah certainly knows those among you who hold others back and those who say to their brothers, ‘Come over to us,’ yet hardly ever join in battle, withholding their help from you”—through the verses up to His words: “begrudging any good. Those have not believed, so Allah has rendered their deeds worthless.”

Their avarice toward the believers and toward good entails aversion and hatred. Hatred of good urges one toward evil, while hatred of a person urges one to wrong him and sever ties with him, as does envy. For the envier urges the one who envies him to wrong the person envied and sever ties with him, as in the case of Adam’s two sons and Joseph’s brothers.

Envy and avarice thus entail hatred and aversion, prompting one to withhold what is due and to wrong that person. Here the action springs from hatred, unlike desire, where the action springs from love: a person loves something, pursues it, and acts accordingly. The former’s aim is an absence, and absence brings no benefit. Yet that intention commands an actual deed, and its command is obeyed.

Ibn Mas‘ūd regarded stinginess as distinct from avarice, whereas the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described avarice as commanding stinginess.

as he claimed. Rather, what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Ibn Mas‘ūd said is more deserving of being followed. A stingy person may withhold his wealth out of love for the pleasure and comfort it affords him. Or he may derive neither pleasure nor comfort from it, but simply feel reluctant to spend it and dislike doing so, to the point that he dislikes even benefiting himself from it despite his abundant wealth. This may be accompanied by pleasure in amassing wealth and a fondness for looking at it. Or there may be no pleasure at all; rather, he dislikes showing kindness to anyone. Even if someone else wishes to give, he resents it out of hatred for goodness—not for the giver or the recipient, but for goodness itself. Alternatively, this may arise from hatred and envy of the recipient or the giver. This is avarice, and it is certainly what commands stinginess. Yet every instance of stinginess arises from avarice. Thus, every avaricious person is stingy, but not every stingy person is avaricious.

Al-Khattābī said: “Avarice is more extreme in withholding than stinginess. Stinginess concerns individual matters and particular things, whereas avarice is pervasive: it is like an enduring trait rooted in a person’s nature and disposition.”

Al-Khattābī also related that someone said: “Stinginess is for a person to begrudge his wealth, while avarice is for him to begrudge both his wealth and his kindness.” It has also been said: “Avarice is to begrudge the kindness that others show to someone else, whereas stinginess is to withhold one’s own kindness from others.”

what they loved and desired without knowledge, never considering whether it would ultimately benefit or harm them. Hence Allah said:

“Know that they only follow their own desires.”

Then He said:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desires without guidance from Allah?”

Following one’s desires has varying degrees. Among those who do so are the polytheists and those who worship, besides Allah, whatever appeals to them, without knowledge or proof. As Allah said:

“Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god?”

That is, he takes as the god he worships whichever deity he desires. Allah did not say that his desire itself is his god. Not everyone who desires something worships it, for desire takes different forms. Rather, the meaning is that he makes whatever he desires the object of his worship, so that his worship follows his own desires concerning worship. For he has neither worshipped what Allah loves to be worshipped nor performed the worship he was commanded to perform.

Such is the condition of the people of religious innovation: they have worshipped other than Allah and devised forms of worship through which they claim to worship Allah. They have merely followed their own desires. Each follows his own inclinations, inner experiences, feelings, and desires, without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book. Had he followed knowledge and the illuminating Book, he would have worshipped none but Allah, in the manner He willed, not through newly introduced practices and innovations.

A person seeks what he loves and repels what he dislikes. Hope attaches to what is loved, and fear to what is disliked. None but Allah brings good, and none but Allah removes harm:

“If Allah afflicts you with harm, none can remove it but Him; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty. He grants it to whomever He wills of His servants. And He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.”

When a servant asks his Lord to grant what he seeks and ward off what he fears, Allah grants him faith in Him, love for Him, knowledge of Him, affirmation of His oneness, and hope in Him, while enlivening his heart and illuminating it with the light of faith. These benefits may be greater than what he sought, if it was some worldly possession. But if he asks Allah to help him remember Him, thank Him and worship Him well, and for related matters, then what he seeks may be more beneficial than the act of seeking it—that is, supplication. What he seeks is remembrance, gratitude, worship performed in the best possible manner, and other such things. This is a subject to be discussed at length elsewhere.

And (the point) is that whatever a servant desires and loves, or fears and dreads, may engulf and overpower his heart, whatever it may be. Hence Allah Most High says:

“But their hearts are steeped in heedlessness of this, and they have other deeds besides this that they persist in doing.”

Their hearts are immersed in what distracts them from that of which they have been warned. It engulfs them, keeping them from remembering Allah and the Hereafter, with its bliss and painful punishment.

Allah Most High says:

“So leave them in their heedlessness for a time.”

That is, leave them immersed in the love of wealth and children that engulfs their hearts and prevents them from hastening to good deeds and righteous works.

And He Most High says:

“May the liars be destroyed—
those who are engulfed in confusion and heedless.”

And the following verses. That is, they are heedless of the Hereafter and engulfed in what distracts them from it: love of this world and its enjoyments overwhelms their hearts, while they remain heedless of the Hereafter and of the purpose for which they were created.

Hence some have said: “Inattention means being heedless of something and having one’s heart turn away from it.” These two—heedlessness and desire—sum up all evil. Heedlessness of Allah and the Hereafter closes the door to goodness, namely remembrance and wakefulness. Desire opens the door to evil, inattention and fear. It becomes preoccupied with something other than Allah; its affairs fall into disorder, and love of this world covers its heart.

As related in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May the slave of the dinar perish! May the slave of the dirham perish! May the slave of the plush covering perish! May the slave of the cloak perish! May he perish and fall headlong, and if a thorn pricks him, may he be unable to remove it! If he is given, he is pleased; if he is denied, he is displeased.”

He described such a person as the slave of whatever pleases him when he possesses it and displeases him when he loses it. Thus he becomes the slave of the dirham and of the other things mentioned in this hadith. The plush covering is something one sits upon, yet he becomes its servant. As one of the early Muslims said: “Wear clothes that serve you; do not wear clothes that you have to serve.” This covering is like a rug upon which one sits, while the cloak is something one wraps around oneself. the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned these to draw attention to things of greater worth, of which a person likewise becomes a slave. He is subject to disparate lords and quarrelsome partners. Hence the Prophet said:

“If he is given, he is pleased; if he is denied, he is displeased.”

Whatever a person is pleased to obtain and displeased to lose, he is its slave, for a slave is pleased through attachment to such things and displeased when deprived of them. As for the true object of worship, besides whom there is no deity, when the believer worships and loves Him, this brings faith, monotheism, love, remembrance and worship into his heart. He is pleased with this and becomes angry if prevented from it. Likewise, anyone who loves something necessarily forms a conception of it in his heart and desires to be connected to it as far as possible.

Al-Junayd said: “A servant does not truly become a servant until he is free of everything besides Allah Most High.” This accords with the hadith: a person cannot be exclusively Allah’s servant, devoting his religion entirely to Him, until he is no longer a slave to anything besides Him and retains not the slightest trace or fraction of servitude to anything besides Allah. If something other than Allah determines his pleasure and displeasure, he is a slave to that other thing. He therefore has a share of polytheism proportionate to his love for it, and his worship of it adds to that.

Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl said:

“Shall I worship one Lord or a thousand lords,
when paths diverge?”

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī and al-Tabarānī narrated from Asmā’ bint ‘Umays that she said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wretched is the servant who is conceited and arrogant, forgetting the Most Great, the Most Exalted. Wretched is the servant who acts tyrannically and transgresses, forgetting the Compeller, the Most High. Wretched is the servant who is heedless and distracted, forgetting the graves and decay. Wretched is the servant who oppresses and transgresses, forgetting his beginning and his end. Wretched is the servant who deceitfully seeks worldly gain through religion. Wretched is the servant who undermines religion by exploiting doubtful matters. Wretched is the servant whose craving humiliates him and turns him away from the truth. Wretched is the servant whose greed leads him. Wretched is the servant whose desires lead him astray.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “It is singular.” The authentic hadith quoted earlier contains support for it. Allah knows best. Many other hadiths and reports have likewise been narrated to this effect.

As Allah Most High says:

“Yet among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals to Him, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Someone who seeks leadership—even through falsehood—is pleased by words that exalt him, even if they are false, and angered by words that disparage him, even if they are true.

But the believer is pleased by truthful words, whether they favour him or count against him, and angered by false words, whether they favour him or count against him. For Allah Most High loves truth, honesty, and justice, and hates falsehood and injustice.

Thus, when truth, honesty, and justice—which Allah loves—are expressed, the believer loves them, even when they run counter to his desires, because his desires have become subordinate to what the Messenger brought. When injustice and falsehood are expressed, Allah hates them, and the believer hates them too, even if they accord with his desires.

The same applies to someone who seeks “wealth”—even through falsehood—as Allah Most High says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the distribution of charity. If they are given some of it, they are pleased; but if they are not given any, they become enraged.”

These are the people of whom he said:

“Wretched is the slave of the dinar,”

and the rest of the hadith.

What, then, if the heart is overcome by desires, passions, and objects of love that enslave it more powerfully than dirhams and dinars, drawing it away from complete love and worship of Allah because they compete with Him and involve associating created beings with Him? How they turn the heart aside and divert it from complete love, worship, and fear of its Lord! For every object of love draws the heart of the one who loves it towards itself and diverts it from loving anything else. Likewise, an object of hatred repels the heart, unsettles it, and distracts it from worshipping Allah Most High.

For this reason, Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad, as did others, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

said to his Companions:

“Is it poverty that you fear? I do not fear poverty for you. Rather, I fear this world for you, for whenever the heart of any one of you goes astray, it is this world alone that leads it astray.”

The same applies to those who love a person, such as his friends, and those who hate him, such as his enemies. Those who love him draw him towards themselves. If their love for him is not for Allah’s sake, this becomes something that cuts him off from Allah. Those who hate him harm him and show him hostility, distracting him from Allah through the harm they cause. If his friends who love him for reasons other than Allah’s sake treat him kindly, their kindness makes him love them and draws his heart towards them—even if this is not in keeping with upright conduct—and obliges him to repay them. Thus they cut him off from Allah and His worship.

The heart is not freed from temptation unless the servant’s religious devotion is entirely for Allah, Almighty and Majestic. He must love for Allah’s sake and love what Allah loves, hate for Allah’s sake and hate what Allah hates; the same applies to his allegiance and enmity. Otherwise, his love for a created being draws him towards that being, while people’s love for him is a means that draws them towards him. Either of these may be stronger than the other.

If he has mastered his desires, someone overcome by his own desires will not draw him in, nor will the things he loves draw him towards them. This is because he masters his desires and restrains himself from following them, owing to the fear and love of Allah in his heart that prevent him from being drawn towards those things.

As for people’s love for him, it leads them to draw him towards themselves with their own strength. If he does not possess the strength, born of love and fear of Allah, to fend them off

This is the familiar pattern of human conduct, with the warfare, disputes, disagreements and strife that arise among people. Some support Zayd and oppose Amr, while others do the reverse, all to serve their own ends. Once they have obtained what they want from the one they support—what they seek from Zayd—they turn to Amr. Amr’s supporters do likewise, as happens among all kinds of people.

Likewise, the “leader” on either side inclines towards those who support him. Yet unless their allegiance is for Allah’s sake, they are more harmful to him than his opponents. His opponents seek only to ruin his worldly life, whether by killing him, taking his wealth or removing him from office. All this is worldly harm, of no consequence so long as the servant’s religion remains intact. This is the opposite of the attitude of worldly people and those who love this world: they attach no importance to the corruption of their religion so long as their worldly affairs remain intact. They are unconcerned about it. As for “the servant’s religion,” which is between him and Allah, his opponents have no power over it.

His allies, however, whose allegiance serves their own ends, seek from him only what corrupts his religion, through his helping them achieve their aims and in other ways. If he does not comply, they turn into enemies. Thus harm comes upon him from “two directions”:

Unless he inwardly does good to them, patiently bears their harm, and meets their needs for Allah’s sake, while seeking Allah’s help against them fully and placing his complete trust in Him, they will corrupt both his religion and his worldly life. translated_text:
from Mujāhid:

“They are the bonds of affection that were not for Allah’s sake, and the ties that existed between them in this world.”

“Those who followed will say, ‘If only we could return, we would disown them as they have disowned us.’ Thus will Allah show them their deeds as a source of bitter regret, and they will never emerge from the Fire.”

The deeds that Allah shows them as a source of regret are those they performed for one another in this world that were not for Allah’s sake. These include allegiance, companionship and love for other than Allah’s sake. All goodness lies in worshipping Allah alone, associating nothing with Him. There is neither power nor strength except through Allah.

Section

What further establishes these matters is that the lover draws, while the beloved is drawn. Whoever loves something draws it towards himself according to his strength. Whoever loves a form is drawn by that form towards the beloved existing in the external world, according to his strength. For the lover functions as an efficient cause, and the beloved as a final cause; each contributes to bringing about the effect.

The lover draws the beloved only through the image of the beloved that he holds in his heart. That image draws him in the sense that he is drawn towards it, not that the image itself has intention or acts. For the beloved possesses a quality suited to the lover that draws him towards it, just as a person is drawn to food to eat it, to a woman to be intimate with her, and to

his friend to enjoy his company, and just as the hearts of those who love Allah and His Messenger are drawn to Allah, His Messenger, and His righteous servants because of the attributes of Allah—glory be to Him—for which He deserves to be loved and worshipped.

Indeed, nothing in existence may be loved for its own sake except Him—glory and praise be to Him. Everything else that is loved in this world may be loved only for the sake of something else, not for its own sake. The Lord Most High alone must be loved for His own sake. This is one of the meanings of His divinity and of His words:

“Had there been in the heavens and the earth gods besides Allah, both would have fallen into ruin.”

For loving anything else for its own sake is to associate partners with Allah. None, then, is to be loved for His own sake except Allah, for this is a prerogative of His divinity, which none but Allah alone deserves. Anything loved besides Him, unless it is loved for His sake or for the sake of something loved for His sake, is loved with a corrupt love.

Allah Most High has instilled in human souls a love of food and a love of women, because these preserve their bodies and perpetuate humankind. Were it not for the love of food, people would not eat, and their bodies would perish. Were it not for the love of women, they would not marry, and procreation would cease. The purpose of these inclinations is to preserve the life of each of them so that they may worship Allah alone, and He may be the One loved and worshipped for His own sake—a distinction none but He deserves.

The prophets and the righteous are loved only as a consequence of loving Him, for loving what He loves is part of the completeness of love for Him. He loves the prophets and the righteous, and He loves righteous deeds, so loving them

for Allah’s sake is part of the completeness of love for Him. Loving others alongside Him, however, is the love of the polytheists, who love their rivals to Allah as they love Allah. When a created being loves for Allah’s sake, that love draws him toward loving Allah. They may be addressed with good things as a bribe from Satan. They are not addressed with what they recognize as false, lest they be repelled by him. Rather, Satan addresses each of them with what that person considers true.

When a monk disciplines himself, he sometimes sees within himself an image of the Trinity and may even be addressed by it. This is because he had previously pictured it to himself; once his soul was polished through spiritual discipline, it appeared to him. The believer who loves Allah and His Messenger sees the Messenger in his dreams in accordance with his faith. Likewise, he sees Allah Most High in his dreams in accordance with his faith, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

For this reason, many who practise asceticism and devotion become helpers of the disbelievers. They claim that they have been commanded to do this and are addressed with such instructions, imagining that Allah is the One who commanded them. Allah is far exalted above that. Rather, what commands them to do this is the self, Satan, and the polytheism within their souls. Had they been sincere in their devotion to Allah, none of this would have befallen them. This happens only to someone whose worship contains some association of partners with Allah, or who follows a religious innovation. It never happens to someone who is sincere and adheres to the Sunnah.

As for worshipping through what Allah loves and is pleased with, they neither love it nor desire it alone. They believe that worshipping Allah as He and His messengers have commanded would lower them from the station of being His allies. Thus they cultivate intense love, devotion, worship, longing, and renunciation, but these contain polytheism and religious innovation.

Love grounded in “monotheism,” however, is directed to Allah alone, in accordance with following His Messenger. As the Most High says:

“Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.”

For this reason, those who follow the Messenger combine their love with striving and intention: they love for Allah’s sake and hate for His sake. They follow the faith of Abraham and those with him:

“When they said to their people: We disavow you and whatever you worship besides Allah. We reject you, and enmity and hatred have arisen between us and you forever, until you believe in Allah alone.”

Those others, however, mix their love with polytheism; they neither follow the Messenger nor strive in Allah’s cause. Their love is therefore not the love of pure devotion, for such love is inseparable from monotheism. This is why Abū Tālib al-Makkī entitled his book “Nourishment of the Hearts: Dealing with the Beloved and Describing the Seeker’s Path to the Station of Monotheism.”

And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

I have written a section in the notebook on events concerning “The Essence of Renunciation and Scrupulousness,” explaining that “renunciation” means abstaining from what brings no benefit: either because it has no benefit at all, or because its benefit is outweighed, since it causes one to forgo something more beneficial or brings about something whose harm exceeds its benefit.

As for things whose benefit is unalloyed or outweighs their harm, renouncing them is foolish. “Scrupulousness,” by contrast, means refraining from what may cause harm. This includes prohibited and doubtful matters, since they may cause harm. Whoever guards against doubtful matters safeguards his honour and religion, while whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing around a protected pasture who is liable to stray into it.

As for “scrupulousness” concerning what involves no harm, or harm that is outweighed—owing to what

This encompasses “three categories” from which one should not abstain out of scrupulousness: benefits that equal their attendant harms, outweigh them, or are unalloyed—such as what is simply permissible, recommended, or obligatory. Abstaining from these out of scrupulousness is misguidance.

I shall explain this in detail here:

“Renunciation” is the opposite of desire. One says, “So-and-so renounces such-and-such,” and “So-and-so desires it.” “Desire” is a form of volition. Renouncing something therefore means having no desire for it, whether accompanied by aversion to it or by the absence of both desire and aversion, so that one neither desires nor dislikes it. Anyone who does not desire or want something renounces it.

Just as, on Allah’s path, it is praiseworthy to renounce those worldly excesses that Allah has encouraged people to renounce, so too is it praiseworthy to desire and seek what Allah has praised people for wanting and desiring. This is why volition is the foundation of the path. As Allah Most High says:

“And do not turn away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is those whose striving will be appreciated.”

There are numerous similar passages.

He has likewise encouraged “renunciation” and condemned its opposite in His words:

“Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornments—We will repay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Competition for more distracts you”—and the rest of the surah.

Allah Most High says:

“And you devour inheritance altogether, and love wealth with immense love.”

He also says:

“Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he himself bears witness to that. And indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth.”

Allah Most High says:

“Know that the life of this world is but play, amusement, adornment, and boasting among yourselves”—and the rest of the verse.

This is a vast subject. The purpose here is simply to distinguish “renunciation prescribed by the revealed law”—which is praiseworthy—from other forms of renunciation, and “desire prescribed by the revealed law”—which is praiseworthy—from other forms of desire. Renunciation is often confused with laziness, incapacity, and idleness in fulfilling the commands of the revealed law. Likewise, prescribed desire is often confused with greed, covetousness, and activity whose undertaking amounts to misguided striving.

As for “scrupulousness,” it means avoiding an action, guarding against it, refraining and holding back from it, and being wary of it. It comes down to disliking something, feeling averse to it, and hating it. This, too, is a positive reality—although there is disagreement over what a prohibition requires: is it the nonoccurrence of the prohibited act, or the performance of its opposite? Most proponents of affirmation hold the latter view. There is thus no doubt that a person cannot be described as scrupulous, as exercising scrupulous restraint, or as guarding against sin unless he actually refrains and holds back, which constitutes doing the opposite of what is prohibited.

translated_text:
And the “correct analysis” is that when the prohibited act does not occur, a person is spared its harmful consequences—censure, punishment, and the like. When he actively refrains, guards against it, and avoids it, he has performed a righteous deed, an act of obedience and piety, and so receives the benefits of that deed—praise, reward, and so forth. Thus, the absence of harm results from the absence of evil deeds, while the attainment of benefit results from the performance of good deeds.

In sum, “renunciation” consists in not wishing for or desiring what one renounces, whereas “scrupulousness” consists in feeling aversion and dislike toward what one scrupulously avoids. The absence of desire is appropriate only toward something that offers no unmixed or predominant benefit. By contrast, aversion is appropriate only toward something that entails unmixed or predominant harm.

If we suppose that something has neither benefit nor harm, or that its benefit and harm are equal in every respect, then it is appropriate neither to desire it nor to dislike it. Renunciation is therefore appropriate toward it, but scrupulousness is not. It thus becomes clear that everything toward which scrupulousness is appropriate is also something toward which renunciation is appropriate, but not vice versa. This is plain: whatever it is appropriate to dislike and feel averse to, it is also appropriate not to desire or wish for. For where aversion is appropriate, the absence of desire is all the more so; and the presence of aversion entails the absence of desire, but not vice versa.

Not everything that it is appropriate not to desire is something that it is appropriate to dislike. Indeed, matters may arise that it is appropriate neither to desire nor to dislike, neither to love nor to hate, and neither to command nor to forbid.

translated_text:
This makes it clear that neither renunciation nor scrupulousness is appropriate toward obligatory or recommended acts, whereas both are appropriate toward forbidden or disliked acts. As for permissible acts, renunciation is appropriate, but scrupulousness is not. This much is clear and can be understood with the slightest reflection.

The real issue arises when conflicting considerations bear on an act: is it commanded, forbidden, or permissible? It also arises when something ordinarily permissible is accompanied by a factor that makes it commanded or forbidden, or when something commanded is accompanied by a factor that makes it forbidden, and vice versa. Thus, when good and ill effects, benefits and harms, coexist and conflict, discernment is needed.

Section

The claim made by some that “reward is proportionate to hardship” is not unconditionally correct. Some groups may invoke it to justify various forms of “monastic austerities and innovated acts of worship” that Allah and His Messenger have not prescribed. These resemble the prohibitions imposed by the polytheists and others on the wholesome things Allah has made lawful, as well as the excessive rigor and extremism condemned by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he said:

“Those who go to extremes have perished.”

He also said:

“Had the month been prolonged for me, I would have continued fasting without a break in a manner that would make those who pursue excessive rigor abandon it.”

Examples include excessive hunger or thirst that harms the mind and body and prevents the performance of obligatory or recommended acts more beneficial than it. The same applies to going barefoot, going unclothed, and walking in ways that harm a person without any benefit. An example is the report of Abū Isrā’īl, who vowed to fast and to remain standing without sitting down, seeking shade, or speaking. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Tell him to sit down, seek shade, speak, and complete

As for reward being proportionate to obedience, obedience to Allah and His Messenger may consist in an easy deed, just as Allah has made the “two phrases” easy for Muslims, although they are the best of deeds. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: ‘Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him; glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.’”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both related it in their Sahīh collections.

If it were said, “Reward is proportionate to the benefit and usefulness of the deed,” that would be correct. The “former” characterization concerns its relation to the command, and the “latter” its inherent quality. A deed’s benefit and usefulness may derive solely from its being commanded, from its inherent quality, or from both. From the first perspective, deeds are classified as obedience or disobedience; from the second, as good or evil. Obedience and disobedience describe a deed in relation to the command, whereas good and evil describe it in itself. ... (1)

Yet many people affirm only the “first,” as do the Ash'arīs and a group of jurists from our school and others. Some affirm only the “second,” as do the Mu'tazilah and a group

As for a deed’s being arduous, this is not what gives it merit or makes it superior. A meritorious deed may, however, be arduous; its merit then derives from something other than its hardship. Persevering in it despite the hardship increases its reward and recompense. Thus, reward increases with hardship, just as someone who travels farther to the Sacred House for Hajj or ‘umrah receives a greater reward than someone nearby. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ‘Ā’ishah concerning ‘umrah:

“Your reward is proportionate to your exertion.”

This is because the reward is proportionate to the effort involved in covering the distance: the greater the distance, the greater the exertion, and thus the greater the reward. The same applies to jihad, and to his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The one proficient in the Quran is with the noble, righteous scribes, while the one who recites it, stumbling over it and finding it difficult, has two rewards.”

Reward therefore often increases in proportion to hardship and fatigue—not because fatigue and hardship are themselves the purpose of the deed, but because the deed necessarily entails them. This applies to our revealed law, in which burdens and shackles have been lifted from us, no hardship has been imposed upon us, and no difficulty is intended for us. Under the revealed laws of those before us, however, hardship may have been required of them.

Many worshippers regard hardship, pain, and fatigue in themselves as things sought for their own sake and as means of drawing closer to Allah, because they cause the soul to turn away from pleasures and from attachment

If, however, the meaning were “Successful indeed is whoever Allah has purified,” there would no longer be any pronoun in the clause referring back to “whoever.” On this interpretation, the subject pronoun refers to Allah, who is not the referent of “whoever,” while the object pronoun refers to the soul previously mentioned. Thus neither the subject pronoun nor the object pronoun refers back to “whoever.” The relative clause would therefore lack a pronoun referring back to its antecedent, which is impermissible.

Admittedly, had it said, “Successful indeed is whoever Allah has purified his soul,” or, “whoever Allah has purified it for,” or something similar, the construction would have been sound. It is astonishing that this escaped those grammarians who advocated that interpretation.

He did not say, “Successful indeed is a soul He has purified.” In that case, “He has purified” would be an adjectival clause describing “a soul,” rather than a relative clause. Instead, He said:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies it.”

The clause is therefore a relative clause attached to “whoever,” not an adjective describing it.

Nor did He say, “Successful indeed is the soul which He has purified.” Had that been said, with the subject pronoun in “has purified it” referring back to Allah’s name, the construction would have been sound.

and to singular and plural, with the pronoun thus referring to its feminine sense, its femininity being grammatical rather than natural—hence “Successful indeed is” uses the masculine form qad aflaha rather than the feminine qad aflahat—the answer to them is: Besides departing from eloquent Arabic, this construction is valid only when the wording indicates that meaning, as in “And whoever …” (1), on the understanding that what is intended is “for us”; likewise in His words:

“Among them are those who listen to you,”

and similar expressions.

Here, however, neither the word “whoever” nor what follows it indicates that it refers to the grammatically feminine noun “soul.” Words cannot be assigned an intended meaning for which they provide no indication. The speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is above such a thing.

Even supposing that the pronoun in “purifies it” could refer either to “a soul” or to “whoever”—although nothing in the word “whoever” requires the pronoun to refer back to it—referring it to the feminine noun would be more appropriate than referring it to a word that admits both masculine and feminine reference. Indeed, the latter is more evidently masculine, since it gives no indication of femininity.

When a statement admits two meanings, it must be understood according to the more apparent of the two. Whoever forces another interpretation departs from established Arabic usage, and the Quran is above that. Departing without evidence from what the wording plainly indicates to something it does not indicate is absolutely impermissible. How much more so when its meaning is unequivocal! Allah has stated that He inspires both piety and wickedness. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

translated_text:
The point here is to command people to purify their souls and warn them against corrupting them, as in His words:

“Successful indeed is he who purifies himself.”

If the meaning were assumed to be, “Successful indeed is he whose soul Allah has purified,” this would contain neither a command nor a prohibition addressed to them, neither encouragement nor warning. When the Quran commands or prohibits, it does not speak merely of “divine decree.” It does not say, “Whomever Allah has made a believer.” Rather, it says:

“Successful indeed are the believers.”

“Successful indeed is he who purifies himself.”

Mentioning divine decree alone in this context would defeat the intended purpose. Such speech would be unworthy even of someone with the weakest intellect—how, then, could it befit the speech of Allah? Do you not see that, when commanding, prohibiting, encouraging, and warning, He mentions the corresponding promises and threats, praise and blame? He mentions divine decree only when explaining His blessings upon them, whether blessings unrelated to their own actions or His blessing of faith and righteous deeds. He also mentions it when speaking of His power and will. In the context of commands, however, He mentions it only in connection with His blessings, as in His words:

“Were it not for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, there would have been no purification…”

—and the rest of the verse. This is appropriate to that context.

His words, “Successful indeed is he who purifies himself,” and the verse under discussion belong to the second category, not the first.

The point is to discuss purification. Allah Most High says:

“Tell the believers to lower…”

—and the rest of the verse. He also says:

“Then go back; that is purer for you.”

And:

“Those who do not give zakah.”

And:

“You are not responsible if he does not purify himself.”
