الْمَالُ إذَا نَمَا. وَلَنْ يَنْمُوَ الْخَيْرُ إلَّا بِتَرْكِ الشَّرِّ وَالزَّرْعُ لَا يَزْكُو حَتَّى يُزَالَ عَنْهُ الدَّغَلُ فَكَذَلِكَ النَّفْسُ وَالْأَعْمَالُ لَا تَزْكُوَا حَتَّى يُزَالَ عَنْهَا مَا يُنَاقِضُهَا وَلَا يَكُونُ الرَّجُلُ مُتَزَكِّيًا إلَّا مَعَ تَرْكِ الشَّرِّ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يُدَنِّسُ النَّفْسَ وَيُدَسِّيهَا.
 قَالَ الزَّجَّاجُ:
 (دَسَّاهَا جَعَلَهَا ذَلِيلَةً حَقِيرَةً خَسِيسَةً وَقَالَ الْفَرَّاءُ: دَسَّاهَا؛
 لِأَنَّ الْبَخِيلَ يُخْفِي نَفْسَهُ وَمَنْزِلَهُ وَمَالَهُ قَالَ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ:
 أَيْ أَخْفَاهَا بِالْفُجُورِ وَالْمَعْصِيَةِ فَالْفَاجِرُ دَسَّ نَفْسَهُ؛ أَيْ قَمَعَهَا وَخَبَّاهَا وَصَانِعُ الْمَعْرُوفِ شَهَرَ نَفْسَهُ وَرَفَعَهَا وَكَانَتْ أَجْوَادُ الْعَرَبِ تَنْزِلُ الرُّبَى لِتُشْهِرَ أَنْفُسَهَا وَاللِّئَامُ تَنْزِلُ الْأَطْرَافَ وَالْوُدْيَانَ فَالْبِرُّ وَالتَّقْوَى يَبْسُطُ النَّفْسَ وَيَشْرَحُ الصَّدْرَ بِحَيْثُ يَجِدُ الْإِنْسَانُ فِي نَفْسِهِ اتِّسَاعًا وَبَسْطًا عَمَّا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا اتَّسَعَ بِالْبِرِّ وَالتَّقْوَى وَالْإِحْسَانِ بَسَطَهُ اللَّهُ وَشَرَحَ صَدْرَهُ. وَالْفُجُورُ وَالْبُخْلُ يَقْمَعُ النَّفْسَ وَيَضَعُهَا وَيُهِينُهَا بِحَيْثُ يَجِدُ الْبَخِيلُ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُ ضَيِّقٌ.
 وَقَدْ بَيَّنَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ ذَلِكَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ فَقَالَ:
 
{مَثَلُ الْبَخِيلِ وَالْمُتَصَدِّقِ كَمَثَلِ رَجُلَيْنِ عَلَيْهِمَا جُبَّتَانِ مِنْ حَدِيدٍ قَدْ اُضْطُرَّتْ أَيْدِيهمَا إلَى تَرَاقِيهِمَا. فَجَعَلَ الْمُتَصَدِّقُ كُلَّمَا هَمَّ بِصَدَقَةِ اتَّسَعَتْ وَانْبَسَطَتْ عَنْهُ حَتَّى تَغْشَى أَنَامِلَهُ. وَتَعْفُوَ أَثَرَهُ وَجَعَلَ الْبَخِيلُ كُلَّمَا هَمَّ بِصَدَقَةِ قلصت وَأَخَذَتْ كُلُّ حَلْقَةٍ بِمَكَانِهَا وَأَنَا رَأَيْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ بِإِصْبَعِهِ فِي جَيْبِهِ فَلَوْ رَأَيْتهَا يُوَسِّعُهَا فَلَا تَتَّسِعُ}
 أَخْرَجَاهُ.
translated_text:
wealth when it increases. Goodness will never grow except by abandoning evil. Crops do not flourish until the tangled growth among them is removed. Likewise, the soul and its deeds do not flourish until whatever opposes their goodness is removed. A person cannot purify himself without abandoning evil, for evil sullies and debases the soul.

Al-Zajjāj explained dassāhā (he debased it) as making the soul lowly, contemptible, and base. Al-Farrā explained the expression by noting that the miser conceals himself, his home, and his wealth. Ibn Qutayba explained it as concealing the soul through wickedness and disobedience. The wicked man buries his soul—that is, he suppresses and hides it—whereas the doer of good makes himself known and elevates his soul. Generous Arabs would settle on hilltops to make themselves known, while the mean-spirited would settle in outlying places and valleys.

Righteousness and piety expand the soul and bring ease to the heart, so that a person finds within himself a spaciousness and openness beyond what he experienced before. As he opens himself through righteousness, piety, and goodness, Allah expands his soul and brings ease to his heart. Wickedness and miserliness, by contrast, suppress, abase, and humiliate the soul, leaving the miser feeling constricted within himself.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, illustrated this in an authentic hadith, saying:

“The miser and the giver of charity are like two men wearing coats of iron, with their hands pressed up against their collarbones. Whenever the giver intends to give charity, his coat expands and loosens around him until it covers his fingertips and wipes away his footprints. But whenever the miser intends to give charity, his coat contracts, and each ring grips its place.”

“I saw Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gesturing with his finger inside the neck opening of his garment. If only you could have seen it as he tried to widen it, yet it would not widen!”

Reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

original_text:
وَإِخْفَاءُ الْمَنْزِلِ وَإِظْهَارُهُ تَبَعًا لِذَلِكَ.
 قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{يَتَوَارَى مِنَ الْقَوْمِ مِنْ سُوءِ مَا بُشِّرَ بِهِ}
 الْآيَةَ. فَهَكَذَا النَّفْسُ الْبَخِيلَةُ الْفَاجِرَةُ قَدْ دَسَّهَا صَاحِبُهَا فِي بَدَنِهِ بَعْضِهَا فِي بَعْضٍ وَلِهَذَا وَقْتَ الْمَوْتِ تُنْزَعُ مِنْ بَدَنِهِ كَمَا يُنْزَعُ السَّفُّودُ مِنْ الصُّوفِ الْمُبْتَلِّ وَالنَّفْسُ الْبَرَّةُ التَّقِيَّةُ النَّقِيَّةُ الَّتِي قَدْ زَكَّاهَا صَاحِبُهَا فَارْتَفَعَتْ وَاتَّسَعَتْ وَمَجَّدَتْ وَنَبُلَتْ فَوَقْتَ الْمَوْتِ تَخْرُجُ مِنْ الْبَدَنِ تَسِيلُ كَالْقَطْرَةِ مِنْ فِي السِّقَاءِ وَكَالشَّعْرَةِ مِنْ الْعَجِينِ.
 قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ:
 
" إنَّ لِلْحَسَنَةِ لَنُورًا فِي الْقَلْبِ وَضِيَاءً فِي الْوَجْهِ وَقُوَّةً فِي الْبَدَنِ وَسَعَةً فِي الرِّزْقِ وَمَحَبَّةً فِي قُلُوبِ الْخَلْقِ وَإِنَّ لِلسَّيِّئَةِ لَظُلْمَةً فِي الْقَلْبِ وَسَوَادًا فِي الْوَجْهِ وَوَهَنًا فِي الْبَدَنِ وَضِيقًا فِي الرِّزْقِ وبغضة فِي قُلُوبِ الْخَلْقِ "
 قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{وَالْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ}
 الْآيَةَ. وَهَذَا مَثَلُ الْبَخِيلِ وَالْمُنْفِقِ.
 قَالَ:
 
{فَمَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أَنْ يَهدِيَهُ يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ}
 الْآيَةَ.
 وَقَالَ:
 
{اللَّهُ وَلِيُّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا}
 الْآيَةَ.
 وَقَالَ لَهُ فِي سِيَاقِ الرَّمْيِ بِالْفَاحِشَةِ وَذَمِّ مَنْ أَحَبّ إظْهَارَهَا فِي الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُتَكَلِّمِ بِمَا لَا يَعْلَمُ:
 
{وَلَوْلَا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ وَرَحْمَتُهُ مَا زَكَا مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ أَبَدًا}
 الْآيَةَ.
 فَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ الزَّكَاةَ إنَّمَا تَحْصُلُ بِتَرْكِ الْفَاحِشَةِ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ:
 
{قُلْ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَغُضُّوا مِنْ أَبْصَارِهِمْ}
 الْآيَةَ. وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ تَرْكَ السَّيِّئَاتِ هُوَ مِنْ أَعْمَالِ النَّفْسِ فَإِنَّهَا تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ السَّيِّئَاتِ مَذْمُومَةٌ وَمَكْرُوهٌ فِعْلُهَا وَيُجَاهِدُ نَفْسَهُ إذَا دَعَتْهُ إلَيْهَا إنْ كَانَ مُصَدِّقًا لِكِتَابِ
translated_text:
Concealing or displaying one’s home follows from this. Allah Most High says:

“He hides himself from the people because of the bad news he has received,” to the end of the verse.

Likewise, the owner of a miserly, wicked soul has buried it within his body, folded in upon itself. Thus, at death, it is pulled from his body as a skewer is pulled from wet wool. By contrast, the righteous, God-fearing, pure soul, which its owner has purified so that it has risen, expanded, and grown in dignity and nobility, flows out of the body at death like a drop from the mouth of a waterskin, or slips out like a hair from dough.

Ibn ʿAbbās said:

“A good deed brings light to the heart, radiance to the face, strength to the body, abundance in provision, and love in the hearts of people. An evil deed brings darkness to the heart, blackness to the face, weakness to the body, scarcity in provision, and hatred in the hearts of people.”

Allah Most High says:

“And the good land,” to the end of the verse.

This illustrates the miser and the one who spends. He says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart,” to the end of the verse.

He also says:

“Allah is the Guardian of those who believe,” to the end of the verse.

He also said to him, in the context of accusations of sexual immorality and the condemnation of those who wish to spread it among the believers and those who speak without knowledge:

“Were it not for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, not one of you would ever have become pure,” to the end of the verse.

He thus made clear that purification is attained only by abandoning sexual immorality. Hence He says:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze,” to the end of the verse.

This is because refraining from evil deeds is itself an act of the soul: it knows that evil deeds are blameworthy and that committing them is hateful. A person struggles against his soul when it urges him toward them, if he believes in the Book of

 وُجُودِيٌّ وَهُوَ التَّرْكُ وَهَذَا قَوْلُ الْأَكْثَرِ.

 الْمَطْلُوبُ عَدَمُ الشَّرِّ وَهُوَ أَنْ لَا يَفْعَلَهُ. وَ 
" التَّحْقِيقُ "

(١)
 وُجُودِيٌّ لَكِنْ قَدْ لَا يَكُونُ مُرِيدًا لَهُ كَمَا يُكْرَهُ أَكْلُ الْمَيْتَةِ طَبْعًا وَمَعَ ذَلِكَ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ اعْتِقَادِ التَّحْرِيمِ وَالْعَزْمِ عَلَى تَرْكِهِ لِطَاعَةِ الشَّارِعِ وَهَذَا قَدْرٌ زَائِدٌ عَلَى كَرَاهَةِ الطَّبْعِ وَهُوَ أَمْرٌ وُجُودِيٌّ يُثَابُ عَلَيْهِ؛ وَلَكِنْ لَيْسَ كَثَوَابِ مَنْ كَفَّ نَفْسَهُ وَجَاهَدَهَا عَنْ طَلَبِ
original_footnote: (١) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
his Lord and has faith in what has come from his Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This affirmation, faith, aversion, and struggle against the soul involve deeds performed by the purified soul, through which it becomes purer still. By contrast, when it commits evil deeds, it becomes defiled, buried, and stunted, like crops among which tangled growth has sprung up. Reward is granted only for an actual deed, and the same applies to punishment.

As for the mere absence of action, it entails neither reward nor punishment, but rather the absence of both. Allah, glorified be He, has commanded good and forbidden evil. There is agreement that a command requires an actual deed, but disagreement over whether a prohibition requires something positive or merely an absence. One view holds that it requires something positive—namely, refraining. This is the majority view. Another holds that what is required is the absence of evil: that one simply does not commit it.

“The correct analysis” is that when a believer forbids wrongdoing, he must not approach it, must resolve to refrain from it, and must find its commission abhorrent. This is undoubtedly something positive. It is therefore inconceivable that a believer who knows that it is . . . (1) positive in nature. Yet he may have no desire for it, just as one has a natural aversion to eating carrion. Even so, he must believe that it is forbidden and resolve to refrain from it in obedience to the Lawgiver. This goes beyond natural aversion: it is something positive for which he is rewarded. His reward, however, is not like that of someone who restrains his soul and struggles against it to keep it from pursuing

As for someone whose aversion to forbidden things springs from faith, and whose faith has overcome the influence of his natural disposition, his is the highest of these three states. He possesses the tranquil soul and ranks above the possessor of the self-reproaching soul, which commits a sin and reproaches its possessor for it, wavering and hesitating over whether to commit it. As for someone to whom it has not occurred that Allah has forbidden a thing, and who has no desire for it but simply does not do it, he is neither punished nor rewarded, since he has performed no actual deed for which he might be rewarded or punished.

Thus, if someone says, “What is required is that he does not do it,” and means that this suffices to escape punishment, he is correct. But if he means that one is rewarded for this mere absence of action, that is not so. When a disbeliever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, he inevitably occupies himself with deeds that distract him from faith; abandoning deeds is disbelief for which punishment is incurred. Hence, when Allah mentions the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire, He mentions actual deeds, which defile and bury the soul. Thus, affirming Allah’s oneness and having faith are the greatest means of purifying the soul, while associating partners with Him is the greatest cause of its defilement. The soul is also purified through righteous deeds and charity. All of this was mentioned by the early generations.

Concerning the words,

they said: he purifies himself of associating partners with Allah and of disobedience through repentance. Abū Sa‘īd, ‘Atā’, and Qatādah explained it as the alms given at Eid al-Fitr.

They did not mean that the verse referred exclusively to these alms. Rather, they meant that whoever gives these alms and performs the Eid prayer falls within the scope of this verse and the one that follows it. Thus,

Al-Hasan explained the words,

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself,”

as referring to one whose deeds are pure. Abū al-Ahwas said: “Purification in all matters.” Al-Zajjāj said: “He purifies himself by obeying Allah, Mighty and Majestic.” The word zākī denotes growth and abundance.

They offered similar explanations of His words:

“And woe to those who associate partners with Allah, who do not give zakat.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “They do not testify that there is no god but Allah.” Mujāhid said: “They do not purify their deeds,” meaning that their deeds are not pure. It was also said: “They do not purify them through sincere devotion.” It seems that he meant—and Allah knows best—those who act to be seen by others, for this is a form of associating partners with Allah.

Al-Hasan explained it as: “They neither believe in zakat nor acknowledge it.” Al-Dahhāk said: “They neither give charity nor spend in obedience to Allah.” Ibn al-Sā’ib said: “They do not pay zakat on their wealth.” He said: “They used to perform Hajj and ‘umrah, but did not pay zakat.”

The correct understanding is that the verse encompasses everything through which a person purifies himself, including affirming Allah’s oneness and performing righteous deeds. It is like His words:

“Would you be willing to purify yourself?”

and His words:

“Successful indeed is the one who purifies himself.”

The obligatory alms had not yet been prescribed when this verse was revealed.

If it is objected that “give” is a transitive verb, the answer is that this resembles His words:

“Then, if they were asked to lapse into disbelief, they would readily do so.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“O Allah, cleanse me with water, hail, and snow.”

He would offer this supplication at the opening of prayer, when standing upright after bowing, and when bathing. These things cool whatever is washed with them, and hail imparts strength and firmness. Things that bring joy are described in terms of coolness and as a delight to the eyes. Thus, tears of joy are cold, whereas tears of sorrow are hot: what distresses the soul brings it sorrow and grief, while what pleases it brings it joy and gladness, which cool the inner self. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, therefore asked Allah to wash away sins in a manner that would cool hearts to the utmost, through the joy and gladness of having the sins that distress the soul removed.

His words, “with snow, hail, and cold water,” express this through a likeness drawn from things possessing this quality; sins themselves are not washed away with these substances. His words:

“Take from their wealth”

show that doing good deeds cleanses the soul and purifies it of past sins, for He said this after His words, “And others have acknowledged,” to the end of the verse. Repentance and righteous deeds thus bring about cleansing and purification. This is why, in the passage beginning, “Tell the believing men to lower their gaze,” and the subsequent verses, He said, “And turn to Allah in repentance,” to the end of the verse. He commanded them all to repent in connection with what He had mentioned, because no one is free of shortcomings of this kind. As recorded in the Sahīh:

“Allah has decreed for the son of Adam his share of unlawful sexual conduct,”

and the rest of the hadith.

It is likewise recorded in the Sahīh that His words:

“Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds”

were revealed on account of a man who had engaged in every form of intimacy with a woman except intercourse. He then felt remorse, whereupon the verse was revealed.

In this regard, a Muslim needs to fear Allah and restrain his soul from its desires. Mere inclination and desire are not punishable; rather, punishment is for following them and acting upon them. If his soul desires something and he restrains it, his restraint is an act of worship devoted to Allah and a righteous deed.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet said:

“The fighter in Allah’s cause is the one who struggles against his own soul for Allah’s sake.”

He is therefore commanded to struggle against his soul

just as he is commanded to struggle against those who command sinful acts and call others to them. Yet his need to struggle against his own soul is greater, for this is an individual obligation, whereas the other is a collective obligation. Perseverance in this is among the finest deeds, for this struggle is the very essence of that other struggle: whoever perseveres in it will persevere in the other.

As he said:

“The emigrant is the one who abandons evil deeds.”

In this struggle, however, a person is praiseworthy only if he prevails, unlike in the former, for:

“Whoever is killed or prevails, We shall grant him a great reward.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The strong man is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling,”

and so on.

This is because Allah has commanded a person to restrain his soul from its desires and to fear standing before his Lord. He thus acquires faith that helps him in this struggle. If he is overcome, it is because his faith is weak, and he is therefore remiss in neglecting what he was commanded to do. This is unlike facing a disbelieving enemy, whose body may be stronger. Sins occur only when the soul fails to comply with what it has been commanded to do. When it complies with the command, it does not commit what is forbidden, for the two are opposites.

Allah Most High said:

“Thus We would turn evil away from him,”

and the rest of the verse.

And he said—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them.”

Thus Satan does not lead Allah’s sincere servants astray. Going astray is the opposite of following right guidance; it consists in following one’s desires. Whoever finds his soul inclining toward something forbidden should worship Allah as Allah has commanded, devoting his religion sincerely to Him. This will turn evil and indecency away from him. … (1) out of fear and love; and worship is for Him

alone, and this prevents sins. If he is repentant, then, should [his faith] be deficient and he commit sins, it effaces them after they occur. It is like an antidote that wards off the effects of poison and removes them once they occur; like nourishment from food and drink; and like lawful enjoyment, which prevents the soul from seeking what is forbidden. If such a desire arises, he seeks to remove it. It is also like knowledge, which prevents doubt and dispels it once it arises, and like medicine, which preserves health and wards off illness. Likewise, the faith within the heart is preserved by kindred qualities present within it. If an illness involving doubts and desires develops within it, these remove it. Illness arises only when the means of maintaining health are deficient; likewise, the heart becomes ill only because its faith is deficient.

Faith and disbelief are likewise opposites. With any pair of opposites, one sometimes prevents the other and at other times removes it, as with blackness and whiteness … (1) takes its place and removes it if it is already present. The same applies to good deeds, evil deeds, and nullification … (2) and the Mu‘tazilah [hold] that a major sin nullifies good deeds, even faith itself, and that whoever dies persisting in it would not be … (3) al-Jubbā’ī and his son, regarding the weighing of deeds against one another.

However, they said:

“Whoever’s evil deeds outweigh his good deeds will remain in the Fire forever.”

Weighing deeds against one another without eternal punishment is a view. As for nullification, what is unanimously agreed upon is that all good deeds are nullified by disbelief, as He said:

“Whoever among you turns back from his religion,”

and the rest of the verse. And His saying:

“And whoever rejects faith

translated_text:
then his deeds have come to nothing,” and the rest of the verse. He also said:

“Had they associated partners with Allah, all they used to do would have come to nothing.”

And He said:

“If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely come to nothing,” and the rest of the verse.

What the Muʿtazilah claim contradicts the statements of the early generations. For Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prescribed punishment for the adulterer and other offenders, but did not declare them disbelievers whose deeds were nullified, nor command that they be killed as He commanded that apostates be killed. The hypocrites did not openly display their disbelief. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that funeral prayers be offered for someone who had misappropriated war booty and someone who had killed himself. Had they been disbelievers and hypocrites, offering funeral prayers for them would not have been permissible. Thus, it is known that their faith was not entirely nullified.

He said concerning a man who drank wine:

“Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.”

That love is among the greatest branches of faith. Thus, it is known that his persistent drinking did not destroy all its branches.

It is established through numerous chains of transmission:

“Whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will be brought out of the Fire.”

Had their faith been nullified, none of it would have remained in their hearts.

Allah Most High said:

“Then We gave the Scripture as an inheritance,” and the rest of the verse.

Thus, he was counted among the chosen. Since evil deeds do not nullify all good deeds, do they nullify a corresponding amount of them? And can some good deeds be nullified by a sin short of disbelief? Those who affiliate themselves with the Sunnah hold two views on this: some deny it, while others affirm it, as the revealed texts indicate.

For example, He said:

“Do not nullify your charitable gifts with reminders of your generosity and hurtful words,” and the rest of the verse.

This indicates that this evil deed nullifies the charitable gift. He illustrated it with the example of someone who acts to be seen by others. And ʿĀ’ishah said:

“Tell Zayd that his jihad has been nullified,” and the rest of the hadith.

translated_text:
As for His words:

“Lest your deeds come to nothing,”

and the hadith concerning the ‘Asr prayer, there is disagreement over this.

Allah Most High said:

“And do not nullify your deeds.”

Al-Hasan explained: “Through sins and major sins.” It is reported from ‘Atā’: “Through associating partners with Allah and hypocrisy”; from Ibn al-Sā’ib: “Through showing off and seeking renown”; and from Muqātil: “Through reminders of favors.” This was because some people regarded their acceptance of Islam as a favor. What is reported from al-Hasan thus indicates that sins and major sins cause deeds to come to nothing.

If it is said, “He meant only nullifying them through disbelief,” the reply is: Disbelief is forbidden in its own right and entails remaining in the Fire forever. Its prohibition would therefore not be expressed in these terms; rather, it would be stated in stern terms, as in His words:

“Whoever among you turns back from his religion,”

and similar passages. In this verse and the verse concerning reminders of generosity, Allah, glorified is He, calls it ibtāl (nullification), not ihbāt (rendering deeds fruitless). Hence, He mentions disbelief afterward, saying:

“Indeed, those who disbelieved and barred others from the way of Allah, then died as disbelievers,”

and the rest of the verse.

If it is said, “The intended meaning is: once you begin these deeds, complete them”—and this verse is cited as evidence by those who hold that a voluntary act of worship becomes obligatory once begun—the reply is: Even supposing that the verse indicates that nullifying part of a deed is forbidden, nullifying the whole deed would all the more clearly fall within its scope. How, then, can that interpretation stand when, before its completion, it is not called a prayer or a fast?

What they have cited is a command to complete the act, whereas nullification means nullifying its reward. We do not concede that someone who fails to complete an act of worship loses all its reward. Rather, it may be said that he is rewarded for whatever he has done of it. The authentic collection also contains the hadith about the bankrupt person, “who comes with good deeds like mountains.”

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

A man studied Islamic jurisprudence and learned what Allah has commanded and forbidden. He then embraced renunciation, abandoning worldly life, wealth, family, and children, fearing unlawful and doubtful earnings and resurrection in the Hereafter, and seeking the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger. He wandered through Allah’s earth, from land to land. Is it permissible for him to sever ties of kinship and wander about as described, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah alone.

“Renunciation as prescribed by Islam” means leaving everything that brings no benefit in the Hereafter and placing one’s heart’s trust in what is with Allah. As stated in the hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhī:

“Renouncing worldly life does not mean declaring lawful things forbidden or squandering wealth. Rather, renunciation means having greater confidence in what is in Allah’s hand than in what is in your own, and desiring the reward for a calamity that befalls you more than you would desire to have retained what you lost.”

For Allah Most High says:

“So that you may not grieve over what you have missed, nor exult in what He has given you.”

This, then, describes the state of the “heart.”

translated_text:
As for its “outward” expression, it means foregoing superfluous food, clothing, wealth, and other things that do not help one obey Allah. As Imam Ahmad said:

“It is only a matter of simpler food, simpler clothing, and patience for a few short days.”

All of this is embodied in the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is authentically reported in the Sahīh that he would say:

“The best speech is Allah’s speech, and the best guidance is Muhammad’s guidance. The worst matters are those newly introduced, and every innovation is misguidance.”

His practice regarding food was neither to refuse what was available nor to go to trouble to obtain what was unavailable. He wore whatever clothing was readily available, whether cotton, wool, or other materials, though cotton was his favourite.

“Whenever he learned that some of his Companions wished to overstep the bounds by exceeding what was prescribed in renunciation or worship, saying, ‘Which of us is like the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’ he would become angry at this and say, ‘By Allah, I fear Allah more than any of you and know best the limits Allah Most High has set.’”

“He learned that one of his Companions had said, ‘As for me, I shall fast without ever breaking my fast.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall spend the nights in prayer and never sleep.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall not marry women.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I shall not eat meat.’ He therefore said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘But I fast and break my fast, pray at night and sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me.’”

As for turning away from one’s family and children, this is not something Allah and His Messenger love, nor is it part of the religion of the prophets. Rather, Allah Most High has said:

Spending on one’s dependants and earning a living for them is sometimes obligatory and sometimes recommended. How, then, could abandoning something obligatory or recommended be part of religion? Likewise, wandering through the lands without a religiously sanctioned purpose, as some ascetics practise, is prohibited. Imam Ahmad said:

“Wandering has no place in Islam, nor was it the practice of the prophets or the righteous.”

[As for the siyāhah (journeying) mentioned in the Quran in His words:

“Those who repent, worship, praise, and fast,”

and in His words:

“Women who submit to Allah, believe, are devoutly obedient, repentant, devoted to worship and fasting—previously married women and virgins,”

this does not mean this innovated practice of wandering. Allah described in these terms the women whom His Messenger would marry, yet it is not prescribed for a married woman to travel through the wilderness as a wanderer. Rather, siyāhah has two intended meanings. One of them is fasting.

As ‘Amr ibn Dīnār narrated from Yahyā ibn Ja‘dah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said:

“What is lawful is clear, and what is unlawful is clear. Between them are doubtful matters that many people do not understand. Whoever avoids doubtful matters has safeguarded his honour and his religion, while whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing his flock around a protected pasture, on the verge of straying into it. Another omission occurs here. The missing material comprises the remainder of the discussion of the first meaning of siyāha (devotional journeying), namely fasting, and the discussion of its second meaning. He then moved on to doubtful matters, citing the hadith as evidence. This is apparent because he said, “Siyāha has two meanings,” then mentioned the first and supplied a chain of transmission that does not belong to the hadith following it. That hadith is unrelated both to siyāha and to the chain of transmission: it concerns doubtful matters, not siyāha, and is transmitted by al-Sha‘bī from al-Nu‘mān—may Allah be pleased with him—as recorded in the two Sahīh collections, not by ‘Amr ibn Dīnār from Yahyā ibn Ja‘da. This indicates that the omission begins here. The two meanings are:
Fasting: Numerous chains of transmission report that Ibn ‘Abbās, Abū Hurayra, Ibn Mas‘ūd, al-Hasan, Mujāhid and others interpreted Allah’s words “al-sā’ihūn” as referring to those who fast.
Jihad: Several hadiths convey this meaning, including the report recorded by Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan from Abū Umāma—may Allah be pleased with him—who attributed it to the Prophet: “The siyāha of my community is jihad.”

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about the words of Allah Most High, “true certainty,” “certainty of sight,” and “knowledge of certainty”: What does each of these stations mean, and which station is highest?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. People have expressed various well-known views concerning these terms.

(One explanation is that “knowledge of certainty” is what one knows through hearing, reports, analogy, and reasoning; “certainty of sight” is what one witnesses and sees with one’s own eyes; and “true certainty” is what one directly encounters, experiences, tastes, and comes to know through examination.

The first is like someone who is told that there is honey somewhere and believes the person reporting it, or who sees traces of honey and infers its existence.

The second is like someone who sees the honey itself, witnessing it with his own eyes. This is higher, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“One who is told is not like one who sees for himself.”

heard about. As one of the shaykhs said:

“I once experienced a state in which I said: ‘If the people of Paradise experience a state like this in Paradise, they truly enjoy a pleasant life.’”

Another said:

“There are times when the heart dances with joy.”

Another said:

“Those who spend their nights in worship find greater delight in their nights than people of amusement find in their amusements.”

People stand at three degrees regarding what they have been told about the Hereafter:

The first is knowing of these things through what the messengers have told them and the evidence establishing their existence.

The second is when they see for themselves the reward and punishment, Paradise and Hell, that they were promised.

The third is when they experience these things directly: the people of Paradise enter Paradise and taste what they were promised, and the people of Hell enter Hell and taste what they were promised. Thus, people stand at these three degrees regarding both what is experienced within the heart and what exists outside it.

The same applies to worldly matters. Someone who knows of passionate love or sexual intercourse by report, without having witnessed or tasted it, has knowledge of it. If he witnesses it without tasting it, he has firsthand observation of it. If he tastes it himself, he has personal experience of it. Anyone who has not tasted something does not know its true nature, for

words can offer only analogies and approximations. Knowledge of a thing’s true nature cannot be gained through words alone, except by someone who has already tasted, known, and experienced the thing being described.

This is why they are called people of knowledge: through experience and tasting, they know what others know through reports and reflection. An authentic hadith relates:

“Among the questions Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantines, asked Abū Sufyān ibn Harb about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was: ‘Does any of them renounce his religion out of aversion to it after embracing it?’ He replied, ‘No.’ Heraclius said, ‘Such is faith: once its joy permeates the heart, no one feels aversion to it.’”

When faith touches the heart and its joy permeates it, the heart feels no aversion to it; rather, it loves it and is content with it. Faith brings the heart a sweetness, pleasure, happiness, and delight that cannot be expressed to someone who has not tasted it. People differ in how deeply they taste it. The joy and happiness within the heart bring a corresponding delight; when that delight permeates the heart, the heart feels no aversion to faith. Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘In Allah’s bounty and mercy—in that let them rejoice. It is better than all they accumulate.’”

And He Most High says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture rejoice in what has been revealed to you, but among the factions are those who reject part of it.”

And He Most High says:

“Whenever a surah is revealed, some of them ask, ‘Which of you has this increased in faith?’ As for those who believe, it increases them in faith, and they rejoice.”

He, glorified is He, thus tells us that they rejoice in what has been revealed of the Quran. This rejoicing is joy and happiness, arising from the sweetness, pleasure, and delight they find in their hearts through what Allah has revealed.

And “pleasure” always follows love: whoever loves something and attains what he loves finds pleasure in it. Tasting is thus the experience of what one loves. With outward pleasures, such as eating, a person desires food and loves it, then tastes and eats it, and at that point experiences its pleasure and sweetness. The same applies to sexual intercourse and similar things.

No love among created beings is greater, more perfect, or more complete than the believers’ love for their Lord. Nothing in existence deserves to be loved for its own sake in every respect except Allah Most High. Love for anything besides Him is subordinate to love for Him. The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is loved, obeyed, and followed only for Allah’s sake. As He Most High says:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

And in the hadith:

“Love Allah for the blessings with which He nourishes you; love me out of love for Allah; and love the members of my household out of love for me.”

He Most High also says:

“Say: If your fathers”—up to His words—“are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command. Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his children, his parents, and all people.”

And in a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhī and others:

“Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

He Most High says:

“Among people are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Thus, the believers’ love for Allah is stronger than any lover’s love for the beloved. We have discussed this at length in several places.

translated_text:
they turn to Allah with a sincere sense of their need for Him and seek His aid, devoting their worship sincerely to Him, He answers their supplication, removes their suffering, and opens the doors of mercy to them. Such a person has tasted the reality of reliance upon Allah and supplication to Him in a way that others have not. Likewise, whoever has tasted sincere devotion to Allah and sought His countenance alone experiences spiritual states, results, and benefits unknown to those who have not done so.

By contrast, whoever follows his desires—seeking leadership and supremacy, becoming attached to beautiful forms, or amassing wealth—experiences, in the process, indescribable worry, distress, sorrow, pain, and anguish. His heart may refuse to relinquish its desires, yet he obtains nothing that brings him happiness. Rather, he lives in constant fear and sorrow: while pursuing what he desires, he is sorrowful and pained because he has not yet attained it; once he attains it, he fears losing it and being parted from it. But the allies of Allah have nothing to fear, nor will they grieve.

If this person, or anyone else, tastes the sweetness of sincere devotion to Allah, of worshipping Him, of remembering Him and speaking privately to Him; understands His Book; and submits himself to Allah while doing good, so that his deeds are righteous and sincerely performed for Allah’s sake, then he experiences happiness, delight, and joy greater than that experienced by someone whose supplication and reliance upon Allah have secured some worldly benefit or warded off some harm. For the sweetness of that is proportionate to what he has received in the way of

benefit or the harm that has been averted from him. Nothing benefits the heart more than affirming Allah’s oneness and devoting worship sincerely to Him, and nothing harms it more than associating partners with Him.

When a person experiences the reality of sincere devotion embodied in “You alone we worship,” together with the reality of reliance upon Allah embodied in “You alone we ask for help,” his experience surpasses that of anyone who has not experienced the like. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
The Question of Abū al-Qāsim al-Maghribī

Would the shaykh and imam, a living legacy of the early generations and an exemplar for later ones, the most learned person I have met in the lands of the East and West, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah, kindly advise me on what will set right my religious and worldly affairs? I also ask him to direct me to a book on which I may rely in the science of hadith, and likewise in the other Islamic sciences; to point out to me the best righteous deeds after the obligatory duties; and to explain to me the most preferable means of earning a livelihood—all in the form of brief pointers. May Allah Most High preserve him. Noble greetings of peace be upon him, and Allah’s mercy and blessings.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. As for “advice,” I know of no counsel more beneficial than the counsel of Allah and His Messenger for one who understands it

and follows it.

Allah Most High says:

“We have enjoined those who were given the Scripture before you, and you yourselves, to fear Allah.”

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, sent Mu‘ādh to Yemen, he advised him, saying: “O Mu‘ādh, fear Allah wherever you are, follow a bad deed with a good deed—it will erase it—and treat people with good character.”

Mu‘ādh, may Allah be pleased with him, held a lofty position with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He said to him: “O Mu‘ādh, by Allah, I love you,” and would have him ride behind him.

It is related concerning him that “he is the most knowledgeable of this community about what is lawful and unlawful, and that he will be gathered one step ahead of the scholars.” Among his distinctions was that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, sent him to the people of Yemen to convey his teachings, preach, teach religious understanding, issue legal opinions, and serve as a judge. He would liken him to Abraham, Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him; and Abraham is a leader for mankind.

Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: “Mu‘ādh was a model to be followed, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright in faith, and was not one of the polytheists,” likening him to Abraham.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, gave him this counsel, which shows that it is comprehensive. Indeed, it is so for anyone who understands it; moreover, it explains the Quranic counsel.

Its comprehensiveness becomes clear from the fact that the servant owes two duties:

translated_text:
a duty to Allah, Almighty and Majestic, and a duty to His servants.

Yet a person will inevitably fall short at times in some of what he owes, either by neglecting something commanded or by doing something forbidden. Thus the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Fear Allah wherever you are.”

This is a comprehensive statement. His words “wherever you are” emphasize the servant’s need to fear Allah both in private and in public.

Then he said:

“Follow a bad deed with a good deed—it will erase it.”

Whenever a patient consumes something harmful, the physician prescribes something to counteract it. Sin is, as it were, inevitable for the servant. The wise person therefore continually performs good deeds that erase bad ones. In the wording of the hadith, “a bad deed” is mentioned first, even though it is the object, because the focus here is on erasing it, rather than on performing the good deed. This is like his instruction concerning the Bedouin’s urine: “Pour a bucket of water over it.”

Good deeds should be of the same kind as the bad deeds, for this is more effective in erasing them. The consequences of sins are removed through several means:

(First) Repentance.

(Second) Seeking forgiveness without repentance. Allah Most High may forgive a person in answer to his supplication, even if he has not repented. When repentance and seeking forgiveness are combined, however, that is the most complete course.

(Third) Righteous deeds that expiate sins. As for “prescribed expiations”

As for “general expiations,” Hudhayfah said to ‘Umar:

“A man’s trials involving his family, wealth, and children are expiated by prayer, fasting, charity, enjoining good, and forbidding evil.”

This is established by the Quran and authentic hadiths concerning the expiation of sins through the five daily prayers, Friday prayer, fasting, Hajj, and all the other deeds about which it is said: “Whoever says such-and-such and does such-and-such will be forgiven,” or “will have his past sins forgiven.” Such reports are numerous for anyone who gathers them from the hadith collections, especially works devoted to the virtues of deeds.

Know that paying close attention to this is among a person’s most pressing needs from the time he reaches puberty, especially in times such as these and similar periods of religious decline that resemble the age of pre-Islamic ignorance in certain respects. Even someone who grows up among people of knowledge and religious commitment may become tainted by several practices of that age of ignorance—so what of someone who does not?

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Sa‘īd, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, the Jews and Christians?” He replied, “Who else?”

This prediction is borne out by Allah’s words:

“So you have enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed theirs, and you have indulged in idle talk as they did.”

This is corroborated by other authentic and sound hadiths. Such tendencies may spread even among the religious elite, as more than one of the early scholars, including Ibn ‘Uyaynah, has stated. Some who identify with religious learning have been afflicted with many of the traits of the Jews, while some who identify with religious devotion have been afflicted with many of the traits of the Christians. This is apparent to anyone who understands the religion of Islam with which Allah sent Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and then applies that understanding to people’s circumstances.

Since this is so, anyone whose heart Allah has opened to Islam, who thus follows a light from his Lord, and who was dead before Allah brought him to life and gave him a light by which to walk among people, must examine the practices of the age of ignorance and the ways of the two communities—those who incurred Allah’s wrath and those who went astray, the Jews and Christians. He will then recognize that he has been afflicted with some of these things.

What benefits the elite and ordinary people most, therefore, is knowing what delivers souls from these predicaments: following bad deeds with good ones. Good deeds encompass the actions, character traits, and qualities that Allah has encouraged through the Seal of the Prophets.

translated_text:
Among the things that remove the consequences of sins are “expiatory afflictions”: anything that causes pain, whether worry, sorrow, or harm to one’s wealth, honor, body, or anything else. These, however, are not acts performed by the servant.

Having addressed Allah’s right through these two injunctions—doing good and rectifying wrongdoing—he said:

“Treat people with good character.”

This is the right owed to people. Good character in dealing with people consists, in essence, of maintaining ties with those who sever them with you—by greeting them, honoring them, supplicating for them, seeking forgiveness for them, speaking well of them, and visiting them; giving to those who withhold from you, through teaching, providing benefit, and giving wealth; and pardoning those who wrong you in your person, property, or honor. Some of this is obligatory, and some is recommended.

As for the exalted character with which Allah described Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, it is the religion encompassing everything Allah has commanded, without exception. This is what Mujāhid and others said. It is putting the Quran into practice, as ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“His character was the Quran.”

Its essence is to hasten to carry out what Allah Most High loves, willingly and with an open heart.

As for explaining how all of this is included in Allah’s counsel, the term “fearing Allah” encompasses doing everything Allah has commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation, and refraining from everything He has prohibited as unlawful

However, since fearing Allah sometimes means fearing punishment in a way that leads one to refrain from unlawful acts, its meaning is elaborated upon in the hadith of Mu‘ādh and likewise in the hadith of Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with them both—which al-Tirmidhī narrated and graded authentic:

He replied, ‘Fear of Allah and good character.’
He was asked, ‘And what most often brings people into the Fire?’

In an authentic report, ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with them both—said that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The believers with the most complete faith are those with the best character.”

He thus linked completeness of faith to perfection of good character. It is well known that faith, in its entirety, consists of fearing Allah. This is not the place to detail the foundations and branches of fearing Allah, for they encompass the entire religion.

Nevertheless, the fountainhead and foundation of goodness is the servant’s sincere devotion to his Lord in worship and in seeking help, as in His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

And His words:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And His words:

“In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn.”

And His words:

“So seek provision from Allah, worship Him, and be grateful to Him.”

The servant should thus sever his heart’s attachment to created beings, whether in seeking benefit from them or acting for their sake, and direct his aspirations to his Lord, Most High. This is achieved by continually supplicating to Him in every matter of poverty, need, fear, or anything else

 أَنَّ مُلَازَمَةَ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ دَائِمًا هُوَ أَفْضَلُ مَا شَغَلَ الْعَبْدَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ فِي الْجُمْلَةِ وَعَلَى ذَلِكَ دَلَّ حَدِيثُ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ الَّذِي رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌ: 
{سَبَقَ الْمُفَرِّدُونَ قَالُوا يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ وَمَنْ الْمُفَرِّدُونَ؟
 قَالَ:
 الذَّاكِرُونَ اللَّهَ كَثِيرًا وَالذَّاكِرَاتُ}
 وَفِيمَا رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد عَنْ أَبِي الدَّرْدَاءِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: 
{أَلَا أُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِخَيْرِ أَعْمَالِكُمْ وَأَزْكَاهَا عِنْدَ مَلِيكِكُمْ وَأَرْفَعُهَا فِي دَرَجَاتِكُمْ وَخَيْرٌ لَكُمْ مِنْ إعْطَاءِ الذَّهَبِ وَالْوَرِقِ وَمِنْ أَنْ تَلْقَوْا عَدُوَّكُمْ فَتَضْرِبُوا أَعْنَاقَهُمْ وَيَضْرِبُوا أَعْنَاقَكُمْ؟
 قَالُوا:
 بَلَى يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ قَالَ: ذِكْرُ اللَّهِ}
 . وَالدَّلَائِلُ الْقُرْآنِيَّةُ وَالْإِيمَانِيَّةُ بَصَرًا وَخَبَرًا وَنَظَرًا عَلَى ذَلِكَ كَثِيرَةٌ. وَأَقَلُّ ذَلِكَ أَنْ يُلَازِمَ الْعَبْدُ الْأَذْكَارَ الْمَأْثُورَةَ عَنْ مُعَلِّمِ الْخَيْرِ وَإِمَامِ الْمُتَّقِينَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَالْأَذْكَارِ الْمُؤَقَّتَةِ فِي أَوَّلِ النَّهَارِ وَآخِرِهِ
translated_text:
and by doing for His sake all that He loves. If a person masters this, the fruits that follow are beyond description.

As for your question about the best deeds after the obligatory duties, this varies from person to person according to their abilities and what is appropriate at different times. No single comprehensive, detailed answer can therefore apply to everyone. However, there is something approaching a consensus among those knowledgeable about Allah and His commands: constant remembrance of Allah is, as a general rule, the best occupation for a servant. This is indicated by the hadith of Abū Hurayrah narrated by Muslim:

“The mufarridūn have forged ahead.”
They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, who are the mufarridūn?”
He replied, “The men and women who remember Allah often.”

Abū Dāwūd also narrated from Abū al-Dardā’, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Shall I tell you which of your deeds is best, purest in the sight of your Sovereign, and raises you highest in rank; better for you than giving gold and silver, and better than meeting your enemies and striking their necks while they strike yours?”
They said, “Yes, O Messenger of Allah.”
He replied, “Remembering Allah.”

The evidence for this from the Quran and from faith—through direct observation, transmitted reports, and reflection—is abundant. At the very least, the servant should consistently recite the remembrances transmitted from the teacher of goodness and leader of the God-fearing, peace and blessings be upon him, such as the remembrances prescribed for specific times at the beginning and end of the day

" لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ "
.
 وَقَدْ تَعْرِضُ أَحْوَالٌ يَكُونُ بَقِيَّةُ الذِّكْرِ مِثْلُ:
 
" سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَاَللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إلَّا بِاَللَّهِ "
 أَفْضَلُ مِنْهُ. ثُمَّ يَعْلَمُ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ اللِّسَانُ وَتَصَوَّرَهُ الْقَلْبُ مِمَّا يُقَرِّبُ إلَى اللَّهِ مِنْ تَعَلُّمِ عِلْمٍ وَتَعْلِيمِهِ وَأَمْرٍ بِمَعْرُوفِ وَنَهْيٍ عَنْ مُنْكَرٍ فَهُوَ مِنْ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ. وَلِهَذَا مَنْ اشْتَغَلَ بِطَلَبِ الْعِلْمِ النَّافِعِ بَعْدَ أَدَاءِ الْفَرَائِضِ أَوْ جَلَسَ مَجْلِسًا يَتَفَقَّهُ أَوْ يُفَقِّهُ فِيهِ الْفِقْهَ الَّذِي سَمَّاهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فِقْهًا فَهَذَا أَيْضًا مِنْ أَفْضَلِ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ. وَعَلَى ذَلِكَ إذَا تَدَبَّرْت لَمْ تَجِدْ بَيْنَ الْأَوَّلِينَ فِي كَلِمَاتِهِمْ فِي أَفْضَلِ الْأَعْمَالِ كَبِيرَ اخْتِلَافٍ. وَمَا اشْتَبَهَ أَمْرُهُ عَلَى الْعَبْدِ فَعَلَيْهِ بِالِاسْتِخَارَةِ الْمَشْرُوعَةِ فَمَا نَدِمَ مَنْ اسْتَخَارَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى.
 وَلْيُكْثِرْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَمِنْ الدُّعَاءِ فَإِنَّهُ مِفْتَاحُ كُلِّ خَيْرٍ وَلَا يُعَجِّلُ فَيَقُولُ:
 قَدْ دَعَوْت فَلَمْ يُسْتَجَبْ لِي وَلْيَتَحَرَّ الْأَوْقَاتَ
translated_text:
and when going to bed, upon waking from sleep, and after the prayers, as well as the remembrances prescribed for particular occasions, such as eating, drinking, dressing, marital intercourse, entering and leaving the home, the mosque, or the lavatory, and during rain and thunder, among other occasions. Books entitled Devotions of the Day and Night have been compiled for this purpose. Beyond these, one should remain constant in remembrance generally, the best of which is:

“There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.”

Circumstances may arise, however, in which other remembrances are better than this, such as:

“Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, Allah is the Greatest, and there is no power nor strength except through Allah.”

One should also understand that everything uttered by the tongue and conceived in the heart that brings one closer to Allah—such as acquiring and imparting knowledge, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong—is remembrance of Allah. Thus, whoever occupies himself with seeking beneficial knowledge after fulfilling the obligatory duties, or attends a gathering to acquire or impart religious understanding in the sense intended by Allah and His Messenger, is also engaged in one of the finest forms of remembering Allah. If you reflect on this, you will find little disagreement among the early Muslims in their statements about the best deeds.

Whenever a servant is uncertain about a matter, he should seek Allah’s guidance in the prescribed manner, for no one who seeks the guidance of Allah Most High regrets doing so. Let him do this often and supplicate frequently, for supplication is the key to all good. He should not grow impatient and say, “I have supplicated, but I have received no answer.” And he should seek out the times

of special merit: the latter part of the night, after the prayers, at the call to prayer, when rain falls, and the like.

As for the best means of earning a livelihood, it is to rely upon Allah, trust that He will suffice, and expect good from Him. Whoever is concerned about his provision should turn to Allah concerning it and supplicate to Him, as He, glorified be He, says in what His Prophet relates from Him:

“All of you are hungry except those whom I have fed, so ask Me for food and I shall feed you. O My servants, all of you are naked except those whom I have clothed, so ask Me for clothing and I shall clothe you.”

Al-Tirmidhī narrated from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

“Let each of you ask his Lord for everything he needs, even the strap of his sandal when it breaks, for if He does not make it possible, it will not be possible.”

Allah Most High has said in His Book:

“Ask Allah of His bounty.”

And He, glorified be He, said:

“When the prayer is concluded, disperse throughout the land and seek Allah’s bounty.”

Although this concerns the Friday prayer, its meaning applies to all prayers. For this reason—and Allah knows best—

“The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) instructed whoever enters the mosque to say, ‘O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy,’ and upon leaving to say, ‘O Allah, I ask You of Your bounty.’”

Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend (peace and blessings be upon him), said:

“So seek provision from Allah, worship Him, and be grateful to Him.”

This is a command, and a command entails obligation. Thus, seeking Allah’s help and turning to Him in matters of provision and all other affairs is a fundamental principle.

He should then receive wealth with a contented heart, so that it may be blessed for him, rather than with eager longing and anxious greed. Wealth should be to him like a privy: something he needs, but which holds no place in his heart. When he strives to acquire it, his efforts should be like attending to the upkeep of the privy.

In a hadith traced back to the Prophet and narrated by al-Tirmidhī and others:

“Whoever begins his day with this world as his greatest concern, Allah will throw his affairs into disarray and disrupt his livelihood, and nothing of this world will come to him except what has been decreed for him. Whoever begins his day with the Hereafter as his greatest concern, Allah will bring his affairs together, place richness in his heart, and make this world come to him despite itself.”

One of the early generations said:

“You need this world, but you have an even greater need for your share of the Hereafter. If you begin with your share of the Hereafter, it will encompass your share of this world and bring it into proper order.”

Allah Most High says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

“I seek no provision from them, nor do I wish them to feed Me.”

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Lord of Power, the Ever-Strong.”

As for choosing one means of earning a livelihood over another—whether a craft, trade, construction, farming, or anything else—this varies from person to person, and I know of no universal rule concerning it. But when an opportunity presents itself, a person should seek Allah Most High’s guidance concerning it through the prayer taught by the teacher of goodness (peace and blessings be upon him), for it contains blessings beyond measure. Then, whatever is made easy for him, he should not strain to pursue something else, unless there is something objectionable about it under Islamic law.

As for the books on which you should rely in the various disciplines, this is a broad subject. It also varies according to where a person grows up: knowledge, or particular methods and approaches to acquiring it, may be available to him in one land but not in another. Yet the key to all good is to seek Allah’s help in acquiring the knowledge inherited from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), for this is what truly deserves to be called knowledge. Anything else is either knowledge that brings no benefit, or not knowledge at all, even if it is called such. If it is beneficial knowledge, then the legacy of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) must contain something comparable and better that makes it unnecessary.

His aim should be to understand the Messenger’s intent in his commands, prohibitions, and all his other statements. Once his heart is assured that this is what the Messenger intended, he should not depart from it, either in his relationship with Allah Most High or in his dealings with people, whenever he is able to do so. In every branch of knowledge, he should strive to hold firmly to a foundation transmitted from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him).

If he is uncertain about a matter over which people have differed, let him offer the supplication narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ʿĀ’ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who reported that when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) rose to pray at night, he would say:

“O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen! You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differed. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which they have differed. Indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

For Allah Most High

translated_text:
has said, as reported from Him by His Messenger:

“O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I have guided. So seek My guidance, and I will guide you.”

As for assessing books and their authors, we have already offered, in the course of discussion, such assessments as Allah, Glorified be He, has enabled us to give. Among books compiled and arranged by topic, none is more beneficial than the Sahīh of Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl al-Bukhārī. Yet this book alone does not suffice to cover the foundations of knowledge, nor does it fully meet the needs of a scholar deeply versed in its various branches. One must also know other hadiths and the statements of jurists and scholars concerning matters in which particular scholars have specialized knowledge.

The Muslim community has produced comprehensive works in every branch of knowledge. Whoever has his heart illuminated by Allah will be guided by Him through whatever reaches him of this knowledge. But whoever has his heart blinded by Him will gain nothing from a multitude of books except greater confusion and misguidance. As the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to Abū Labīd al-Ansārī:

“Do the Jews and Christians not have the Torah and the Gospel? What benefit do these bring them?”

We therefore ask Allah the Almighty to grant us guidance and sound judgment, to inspire us to follow the right course, and to protect us from the evil within ourselves. We ask Him not to let our hearts deviate after He has guided us, and to bestow upon us mercy from Himself. Indeed, He is the Bestower. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may His blessings be upon the noblest of the messengers.

The shaykh and imam, the scholar who practised what he knew, the consummate learned authority, Shaykh al-Islām and mufti to the people, Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah strengthen him and increase him from His immense bounty—was asked about “beautiful patience,” “gracious forgiveness,” and “gracious withdrawal,” and about the various forms of piety and patience found among people.

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

All praise is due to Allah. To proceed:

Allah commanded His Prophet to observe gracious withdrawal, gracious forgiveness, and beautiful patience. (*) “Gracious withdrawal” is withdrawal without causing harm; “gracious forgiveness” is forgiveness without reproach; and “beautiful patience” is patience without complaint.

Jacob, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“I complain of my anguish and sorrow only to Allah.”

Yet he also said:

“So I shall bear this with beautiful patience. And Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe.”

Thus, complaining to Allah does not contradict beautiful patience. It is reported that Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say: “O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You complaints are addressed, You are the One whose help is sought, and through You
translated_footnote:

deliverance is sought, and upon You we rely.” Among the supplications of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was:

“O Allah, to You I complain of my feebleness, my lack of resourcefulness, and the contempt with which people regard me. You are the Lord of the downtrodden, and You are my Lord. O Allah, to whom will You entrust me? To a stranger who treats me harshly, or to an enemy whom You have given power over me? If You are not angry with me, I do not mind, though Your protection would afford me greater ease. I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right, lest Your displeasure descend upon me or Your anger befall me. Yours is the right to reproach until You are pleased.”

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, would recite during the dawn prayer:

“I complain of my anguish and sorrow only to Allah, and I know from Allah”

and would weep until his sobbing could be heard from the back rows. Complaining to created beings, however, is different. During Imam Ahmad’s final illness, a report was read to him stating that Tāwūs disapproved of a sick person’s groaning and said, “It is a complaint.” Ahmad did not groan again before he died.

This is because a person who complains is implicitly asking either for the removal of what harms him or for the attainment of what benefits him. The servant is commanded to ask his Lord, rather than His creation, as Allah Most High says:

“So when you have finished, strive in worship, and turn to your Lord with longing.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to Ibn ʿAbbās: “When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

A person cannot do without two things: obedience to Allah by doing what He has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden, and patience with whatever befalls him by the ordained decree. The first is piety, and the second is patience.

Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, do not take confidants from among

those outside your ranks, who will spare no effort to harm you,” up to His words:

“But if you remain patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all. Surely Allah encompasses all that they do.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Yes, if you remain patient and mindful of Allah, and they come upon you in this sudden rush, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand specially marked angels.”

Allah Most High also says:

“You will surely be tested in your possessions and yourselves, and you will surely hear much abuse from those who were given the Scripture before you and from the polytheists. But if you remain patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed a matter requiring firm resolve.”

Joseph said:

“I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has indeed been gracious to us. Whoever is mindful of Allah and remains patient—Allah certainly does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

For this reason, Shaykh Abd al-Qādir and other upright spiritual masters would generally urge these two principles in their teachings: hastening to do what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden; and patience and contentment with what has been decreed.

Many ordinary people—and even spiritual wayfarers—have erred on this point. Some perceive only the divine decree, contemplating the reality of the created order but not the reality of religion. They recognize that Allah is the Creator and Lord of everything, but do not distinguish between what Allah loves and is pleased with and what angers Him and He hates, even though He has decreed and ordained it. Nor do they distinguish between Allah’s exclusive right to worship and His oneness in lordship. Thus they perceive the common ground shared by all created beings—the blessed and the wretched alike—a commonality shared by the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the truthful prophet and the false claimant to prophethood, the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, Allah’s allies and His enemies, and the angels brought near to Allah and the rebellious devils.

For all of these share this common ground and this “reality of the created order”: Allah is their Lord, Creator, and Sovereign; they have no Lord besides Him. Yet they fail to perceive the distinction Allah has made between His allies and His enemies, between believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, and the people of Paradise and the people of Hell. This is singling Allah out for worship: worshipping Him alone, without any partner; obeying Him and His Messenger; doing what He loves and is pleased with—that is, what Allah and His Messenger have commanded, whether as an obligation or a recommendation; refraining from what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden; showing allegiance to His allies and enmity towards His enemies; enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong; and waging jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites with the heart, hand, and tongue.

Whoever fails to perceive this “reality of religion,” which distinguishes the two groups, and to stand with those who uphold this “reality of religion,” is of the same kind as the polytheists and is worse than the Jews and Christians. For the polytheists acknowledge the reality of the created order, since they acknowledge that Allah is the Lord of everything. As Allah Most High says:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and everyone in it, if you know?’
They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then take heed?’
Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’
They will say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then be mindful of Him?’
Say, ‘In whose hand is the sovereignty over all things, who grants protection, while none can grant protection against Him, if you know?’
They will say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘How then are you deluded?’”

Hence He, glorified be He, says: “Yet most of them do not believe

“You ask them who created the heavens and the earth, and they say, ‘Allah,’ yet they worship others besides Him.”

Whoever acknowledges divine decree and predestination but not the commands and prohibitions prescribed by Allah is greater in disbelief than the Jews and Christians. For they acknowledge the angels and the messengers who brought those commands and prohibitions, but they believe in some and disbelieve in others. As Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to distinguish between Allah and His messengers, saying, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and wish to adopt a way in between—it is they who are truly the disbelievers.”

As for someone who perceives the “reality of the created order” and Allah’s sole lordship over all creation, acknowledges that all His servants are subject to divine decree and predestination, and follows this reality as his path, making no distinction between the believers and the God-fearing who obey Allah’s command, with which He sent His messengers, and the disbelievers and the wicked who disobey Allah and His Messenger—such people are greater in disbelief than the Jews and Christians.

Some people, however, have glimpsed the distinction in certain matters but not in others. A person may distinguish between the believer and the disbeliever but not between the righteous and the wicked, or distinguish between some righteous people and some wicked people but not between others, following his own assumptions and desires. His faith is deficient to the extent that he treats the righteous and the wicked alike, while he possesses faith in the religion of Allah Most High—which makes this distinction—to the extent that he distinguishes between His allies and His enemies.

Whoever acknowledges the religious commands and prohibitions but not divine decree and predestination belongs to the Qadariyya, such as the Mu‘tazila and others, who are the Magians of this community. These resemble the Magians, whereas those others resemble the polytheists, who are worse than the Magians. Whoever acknowledges both yet attributes contradiction to the Lord is a follower of Iblīs, who objected to the Lord—glory be to Him—and disputed with Him, as has been related about him.

This classification concerns statements and beliefs. The same applies to their “states and actions.” The correct state is that of the believer who fears Allah: he does what is commanded, refrains from what is forbidden, and patiently endures whatever befalls him by divine decree. He adheres to the commands and prohibitions, the religion and the revealed law, seeking Allah’s help in doing so. As Allah Most High says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

When he sins, he seeks forgiveness and repents. He does not invoke predestination to excuse the evil deeds he commits, nor does he consider any created being to have an argument against the Lord of all creation. Rather, he believes in predestination without using it as an excuse, as in the authentic hadith which states:

“The foremost supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain faithful to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I confess my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’”

The first consists of those who possess both piety and patience. These are the people whom Allah has blessed with happiness in this world and the Hereafter.

The second consists of those who have some measure of piety but lack patience, such as those who fulfil their obligations of prayer and the like and refrain from forbidden things. Yet when one of them suffers bodily illness or a similar affliction, suffers harm to his wealth or honour, or is tried by an enemy who frightens him, his distress becomes intense and his panic apparent.

The third consists of people who have some measure of patience but lack piety, such as the wicked who patiently endure whatever befalls them in pursuing their desires. These include thieves and highway robbers who endure pain in their pursuit of forcible seizure and unlawful gain, as well as scribes and administrative officials who endure such things in pursuit of the wealth they obtain through dishonesty and other means. Likewise, those who seek leadership and supremacy over others endure forms of suffering that most people cannot bear. Similarly, those enamoured of forbidden forms of beauty, whether passionate lovers or others, endure various kinds of suffering and pain in pursuing the forbidden things they desire. These are the ones who seek supremacy on earth

or corruption—those who seek leadership and supremacy over others, those who pursue wealth through oppression and aggression, and those who seek unlawful enjoyment of physical beauty through looking or physical contact, and other such pursuits. They endure various hardships, but they lack piety, neglecting what is commanded and committing what is forbidden. Likewise, a man may patiently endure afflictions such as illness, poverty, and other hardships, yet show no piety when given power.

(As for the fourth category, it is the worst of all: they neither fear Allah when they have power nor remain patient when they are tried. Rather, they are as Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, man was created anxious: fretful when evil touches him, and withholding when good touches him.”

You find such people among the most unjust and tyrannical when they have power, and among the most abject and panic-stricken when they are overpowered. If you overpower them, they abase themselves before you, act hypocritically toward you, curry favour with you, and beg for your mercy. To protect themselves, they resort to all manner of lies, self-abasement, and exaltation of the person they petition. But if they overpower you, they are among the most unjust and hard-hearted of people, and the least merciful, kind, and forgiving. Muslims have experienced this with all those furthest removed from the realities of faith, such as the Tatars whom the Muslims fought and those who resemble them in many of their ways—even if such a person outwardly wears the garb of Muslim soldiers, scholars, ascetics, merchants, or craftsmen. What matters is the underlying reality:

“For Allah does not look at your appearance or your wealth; rather, He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”
